title: The workspace becomes the firm's record: the portfolio and watchlist leave it
details: The second half of the deck move. /desk stops drawing a portfolio and a watchlist — both render on /vault now — so the workspace is the firm's shelf, its deal board, its contacts and its roster, plus the report chamber below them. The subtitle and the signed-out prompt stopped promising the two things that left. renderMyDesk SURVIVES and still reads the portfolio, which is the whole reason it does: portfolioKeys is what tells a report whether it is already saved, so without the read “Save to portfolio” would offer to re-save a property already in the book on every report a member opens. The read got one rule it did not have before — a FAILED read no longer clears the set. An empty portfolioKeys is a positive claim (“none of your properties are saved”), and making it from a read that did not happen turns an outage into an invitation to create duplicates. The desk-level reading strip and the attention line went with the figures they summed, and their CSS came out rather than being left standing: .dk-ledger, .dk-lfig, .dk-lnote, .dk-attn, .dk-up/.dk-down, .dk-fig and the 2x2 phone rule. .dk-stmt and .dk-addr stay — the shares table and the firm shelf still use them. A FIRM-level strip belongs on that page eventually; it is not this one with the labels changed, which is why it is gone rather than relabelled. Two things had to travel with the surface or they would have lapsed silently. Marking the watch feed SEEN, because last_seen_at is one of the two high-water marks the digest reads and a member reading their comps somewhere that did not stamp it would be mailed about them anyway; vault-page.js does that now, on the same unseen guard. And Refresh, which /vault reaches as ?property=<id>&refresh=1 because that page can neither render a report nor replay a search — both need the real #compForm and every rule hanging off it. That door got a guard the desk's button never needed: refreshPortfolioItem replays payload.meta, and a row whose payload never landed threw on that read. Survivable as a button on a row the page had just drawn; not survivable from a URL anyone can type, where the symptom is a page that visibly does nothing. The bug worth recording is the one the tests could not see. Removing the sections left behind an IIFE that still populated the watch-type select from the property-type one. It ran at TOP LEVEL, so appendChild on null threw before anything below it was defined — and the symptom was not a missing watch form, it was the ENTIRE workspace failing to render, under a cascade of “cannot access X before initialization” hiding the real error. Nothing in the suite could catch it: the assertions there are string matches, and the one place the emitted script is compiled checks syntax, which was fine. It took loading the page. So there is now a standing test that every getElementById in index.html names an id the file actually defines — one-directional, because an id with no reader is ordinary (CSS, anchors, aria-controls) while a dangling read is not. Mutation-checked both ways. Eleven tests moved rather than lapsing. Five are pinned against vault-page.js now (the empty copy naming Save to portfolio, between-checks naming its sample and saying outright it is not a return, the attention line, the one-year stale threshold with its mirrored-constant note, and the checked date reading the same field the count does), and checking them against the move found two rules my version had quietly dropped: an em dash in copy the owner's rule forbids, and the title that says what the between-checks figure is NOT — the exact thing that stops the label reading as a portfolio return. Five retired with the desk's strip and left a note in index-html.test.js saying where each rule went, and portfolioValuesOn's fallback is subsumed rather than dropped: it guarded a stale /api/config body, and vaultReadPayload states the answer from the entitlement in the same process that renders the page. Verified in a browser at both tiers: the workspace renders its four firm decks with no console errors, /vault carries the portfolio with its strip and stale warning, and the Refresh link replays the stored address, type and size into the real form.

title: The Vault becomes your own space: your properties and your watchlist moved into it
details: Slice 1 of “Three Spaces”, the reorganisation into a firm workspace, a personal space and (later) a messaging hub. /vault gains two decks — Your properties (the portfolio) and Your watchlist — which moved off /desk, because the workspace is becoming the FIRM's record and those two are yours. No table and no route changed: portfolio_items and watchlist_items are still user-scoped and still read through the same endpoints; only the surface moved. The change that made it possible is that /vault's single canUseVault gate is now a PER-DECK one. Your book, Your pipeline and Your hubs still refuse without Pro and say so in one panel; Your properties and Your watchlist render regardless, because a member opening their own space and finding their own saved properties behind a paywall is not a paywall, it is a bug. 401 is the only whole-page gate left — signed out there is no portfolio, no watchlist and no book. vaultReadPayload now states portfolioValues on all three of its exits (200, 403, 503) rather than only the success one: it is the single fact the personal decks need, and the 403 is exactly the case that needs it. The nav followed, and had to: #navVault was revealed from canUseVault, so a free member's only route to their own portfolio would have been typing the URL — the same failure the per-deck gate exists to prevent, moved into the navigation. The row opens to every signed-in member now, on both sides of the nav parity (marketBar's ACCOUNT_NAV_JS and index.html's refreshBillingUI). It widened who sees the door, never what is behind it. Two tests that pinned the old rule were updated rather than deleted, and routes.test.js keeps proving the thing it was really there for: bulk and the vault read separate flags. Not a port of renderMyDesk. That one is built out of the desk's dk-* classes and Tailwind utilities, and tailwind.css is purged against index.html alone, so a utility used only in a server-side string silently stops styling. These are the same rules redrawn in this page's own idiom (.strip, .tw, table, .lnk) with no new CSS but one address-colour rule — a{} paints this page's links red and a column of red rows reads as a list of warnings. Four rules came across intact because each was earned on the desk: a failed read renders as a FAILURE and never as an empty portfolio (two elements, and the early return sits above anything that would state a count); “checked” is the last time a VALUE was produced, not updated_at; every figure including the market-movement line is gated on portfolioValues; and the strip and the table footer close on one combined figure computed once. A property row LINKS to /?property=<id> and Refresh is the same door with &refresh=1, because the report engine lives in index.html and a row that opened one in place would silently do nothing. Two things came out of looking at the page rather than the diff. The deck was called “Your markets” and that name was already taken twice: #rollupSec's h2 is where a broker's COMPS are, and #covBox's “Markets you watch” is where they want LEADS from — two identical headings 500px apart meaning different things, so it is Your watchlist, pinned by a test that fails on any duplicate deck label. And the sparkline's explanatory comment named a hex colour, which theme.test.js caught: that comment ships inside the emitted script, and the raw-hex rule scans the generated markup, not just the stylesheet. test/vault-personal-decks.test.js is the new file: it compiles the emitted browser JS in all four boot states (the page is one template literal, so a stray brace ships a blank workspace silently), pins that the lock list names every gated deck and no personal one, and runs the seam against a real server and the fake PostgREST — a free member's 403 carries portfolioValues, their /vault answers 200 with both personal decks intact, and their rail carries the vault row. Verified in a browser at both tiers.

title: Testers get a ninja in the corner that mails their feedback to the three of us
details: An account on a tester code now carries a small ninja badge; clicking it opens a short form (problem / idea / anything else) and POST /api/tester-feedback mails it to Jacob, Chuck and Owen. Recipients live in one env-overridable constant so a change of team is a Render edit rather than a deploy, and reply_to is the TESTER, so answering the mail answers the person — the single thing most likely to keep a beta channel alive. One message per recipient rather than one with three names in `to`, because sendEmail wraps its own `to` in an array and an array argument would post a nested one that reaches nobody. Gated strictly on the tester grant, not on Pro and not on admin: a feedback button everybody can see is a support inbox, which promises answers this does not. The badge is revealed from /api/config's pro.tester through the existing isTesterPro() helper rather than a second copy of the flag test, and the route re-resolves entitlements server-side, since that flag is presentation only. Three decisions came out of actually looking at it rather than reading the diff. It is FIXED rather than a nav item, because the signed-in chrome is a left rail at 900px and up, so there is no top-right header to sit in — and it only takes the top-right corner above 1380px, where that corner is genuinely empty: the rail is 224px and the content column is capped at 1024px and centred in the rest, so at 1280 the first screenshot showed the badge sitting squarely on the desk's "Run a report" button. Below that it tucks bottom-right, which also covers the sub-900px case where the rail becomes a top bar and the badge would have landed on the account circle. Its surface is var(--slab) and not var(--ink): --ink is the TEXT token, so in dark mode it is #E4E9F0 and a white ninja on it would have been invisible — caught by the theme suite's raw-hex rule on the way past, then fixed properly rather than allowlisted. A failed send never clears the box, because retyping a bug report is how a tester stops sending them, and with outbound mail unconfigured the route returns 503 naming an address to use instead rather than thanking somebody for a message that silently went nowhere: sendOutboundEmail is a silent no-op without EMAIL_FROM, so the words are written to the deploy log BEFORE the send is attempted. test/tester-feedback-run.test.js runs the whole thing against a real server and a stub Resend — the refusal ladder, all three recipients, the reply address, the refusals, the unconfigured-mail 503, and that a dark deployment (PRO_ENABLED off) grants no tester and therefore no channel. The boot helper now blanks TESTER_FEEDBACK_EMAIL too, because its default is three live @compninja.co addresses and the day EMAIL_FROM lands in a developer's .env, `npm test` would otherwise start mailing the three of us for real. Verified in a browser end to end: non-tester sees nothing, redeeming the code makes the badge appear, the send reached all three inboxes with the tester's words plus page, viewport and browser, and signing out takes it away again.

title: A hub-note email test that blamed the notifier when the server had died
details: test/hub-note-email-run.test.js failed at random with an empty recipient list where it expected one address. The mail wait was not the problem — that file already polled the Resend stand-in for ten seconds. The problem was that it never checked the POST it was named after had succeeded, so anything that stopped the request (a 503, a test server exiting on its own mid-run, which boot.js documents and prints a ⛔ for) arrived as "nobody was mailed" and read as a broken notifier. Reproduced in a loop, then fixed by asserting the status inside postNote with the server’s own answer attached. The wait itself moved into test/helpers/fake-supabase.js as waitForMail, beside the sent array it waits on: there were four hand-copied copies of that loop across the suites with three different budgets (1.5s, 1.5s, 2s, 10s), and the short ones — watchlist-digest, renewal-watch, org-run — were simply written first. Production is untouched: the send stays fire-and-forget, because a mail provider having a bad afternoon must never turn a saved note into an error. A second defect surfaced while reproducing it: t.after(() => stop()) inside a subtest whose callback takes no argument registers on the PARENT, so all twelve servers and stand-in databases stayed up for the whole run and were closed in one burst at the end — measured twelve live server.js children at peak against the one the suite uses at a time. db.stop() is server.close(), which waits on its connections, and that burst is the state a hung node --test was observed in: it sat for five hours after printing its last test line, which in CI is a job that never ends rather than a build that goes red. Each subtest now owns its own context and closes its own server; peak went 12 to 1. Same shape fixed in watchlist-digest-run and renewal-watch-run.

title: A portfolio holds the properties you own
details: Every signed-in search used to save itself onto My Desk, so "Your properties" was really a log of everything the account had ever looked up. A search now files itself under Recent searches, which moved server-side so it follows you across devices, and you add what is yours from the report or from the row. Bulk valuation lands there too: one click can put fifty addresses through it, and a broker pricing a prospect list owns none of them. Nothing already on a desk was touched.

title: The tenant rep shop is withdrawn
details: A firm could say it was a broker shop, a development shop or a tenant rep shop. The third one is gone, ten days after it landed. The option is out of both places the question is asked — creating a firm and changing it afterwards — the refusal under the select names the two shops that remain, and the /firms page counts its own cards instead of promising three. Nothing about a firm's shelf, invites, auto-share, shared vault comps or seats changed. No database work was needed in either direction, and that is the part worth knowing: an unrecognized kind has always read as a broker shop, on purpose, so a firm that had chosen tenant rep goes back to reading the words every firm read before the kind existed rather than losing a screen, and the route refusing the string is what stops a new one being written. The CHECK that migration 037 widened is deliberately left alone — narrowing it would fail on exactly the rows that would make narrowing worth doing, and a value no code can send is a value no row can gain. The /firms heading now reads its count off the list of shops rather than a typed numeral, because a kind was added and withdrawn inside ten days and a page saying “three” over two cards is the drift that guarantees.

title: Tenant contacts import from an Excel file, with no new dependency
details: Owner’s call, straight after the button was relabelled “Import a spreadsheet”: the label was true about the intent and false about the file, since the input took .csv only. It takes a real .xlsx now. Every library that reads xlsx is an npm dependency and this repo has none outside desktop-app/, so xlsx.js reads the format by hand — an .xlsx is a ZIP of XML and node ships zlib. It is pure apart from that builtin, and test/xlsx.test.js BUILDS its fixtures (real local headers, a real central directory, real deflate streams) rather than committing a binary nobody can read in a diff. What the reader deliberately does NOT do is interpret numbers: Excel stores a date as a day count whose epoch is a per-workbook setting, and whether a number is a date at all is decided by a format string in a different part, so a wrong guess turns a lease expiry into 45678 silently. Contacts are four text fields, so nothing here needs it — and that is exactly why the file’s header forbids pointing this at the broker vault, which is mostly dates and money, until that work is done. The import obeys ONE set of rules: parseContactsCsv was split so parseContactsGrid holds the loop, and the spreadsheet path feeds it a grid in the same shape parseCsv returns. Same header aliases, same email refusals, same 2000-row cap, same note-line counting. Four things the format punishes anybody who skims it, each pinned by a test: Excel OMITS an empty cell rather than writing a blank one, so cells are placed by their r= reference and “Nordic Cold” cannot slide into the email column; sizes come from the central directory, because a data-descriptor entry zeroes them in the local header and a reader that trusts it sees a file with no rows; the sheet read is the first TAB in workbook order, not the file called sheet1, whose number survives reordering; and a shared-string cell with an empty <v> is a blank, not index 0 — Number("") is 0, so the first draft imported the workbook’s first shared string into every empty cell, which in a contacts sheet is the header, “Name”. A test caught that one, not a reading. Refusals name the file: an older .xls (an OLE2 document, not a zip at all) says to save it as .xlsx, a password-protected book says to remove the password, an .ods says what it is. The browser decides which door a file takes from its leading BYTES, never its name, so a spreadsheet saved as “tenants.csv” still imports — verified in a browser by driving a misnamed .xlsx through the real change handler and watching it take the binary path while a genuine CSV took the text one. One bug fixed on the way through: parseContactsCsv reported refusals by counting the compacted grid, so a single blank line above a bad address pointed the line number at a row that was fine. It reads the row’s own line stamp now, which broker-vault.js has done since the stamp existed.

title: The tester code is typed into Settings now, not the pricing modal
details: Codes go to friends, family and people testing the site, so the place to type one is the panel you open to look at your own account — not a modal you open to look at prices, where it sat behind a "Have a code?" disclosure that nobody who had not already been told about it would ever open. #passkeyRow moved into the Settings panel as an ordinary titled row, directly under Plan because that is what redeeming changes. It MOVED rather than being copied: one code, one control, on the theme toggle's precedent from the day before and the Plan row's from the same week — a second box would have been a second input, a second message element and a second visibility rule to keep in step, for something a person types once, ever. It is a row and not a disclosure because every other row in this panel shows its control, and hiding an input behind a toggle inside a panel that is itself behind a menu is one door too many. Two behaviours changed with the address. Success used to close the pricing modal, which was right there (the plan card behind it already said Pro) and wrong here, where the Plan row sits directly above and refreshProConfig() has just repainted it — closing would hide the confirmation the redemption earned, so it now says what happened and leaves the panel open. And the route's `already` answer to a re-redeemed code, a 200 that the old copy passed over in silence, now reads as success rather than nothing at all. No server change: the route, the secret, the rate limit and the entitlement are untouched, and VAULT_PASSKEY still redeems through the same input by design. Verified in a browser against a real signed-in account on an isolated server — wrong code refused, right code granted with pro_tester landing on the account row, re-redeem reporting `already`, and no row at all for a signed-out visitor at /?settings=1, since the grant has no account to attach to. Four tests pin the move: exactly one input, inside the settings modal and absent from the pricing one, no script still reaching for the disclosure's removed elements (a stale getElementById would throw and take the whole front end down), and the success path no longer closing a modal.

title: The tenant contacts importer asks for a spreadsheet, not a CSV
details: Owner’s call, from reading the workspace. The second door into a firm’s tenant contacts list said “Import a CSV”, which names a file format rather than the thing a broker believes they have: a list of people kept in a spreadsheet. The button, the line under the section heading and the empty state all say spreadsheet now. The format is deliberately still named in ONE place — the empty state, which is the only one of the three that actually instructs (“import a spreadsheet, saved as CSV, with a name column”) — because nothing underneath this changed: the file input still accepts .csv only, CONTACTS.parseContactsCsv is still the parser, and there is no xlsx reader in this repo nor room for one under the no-dependencies rule. So a member who saves an .xlsx out of Excel will still find it greyed out in the picker, and the one line they read while deciding what to upload is the line that tells them why. Copy only: same button, same id, same route, same handler.

title: Pricing moved into Settings, and the app's nav lost another row
details: The theme switch's journey, the same week and for the same reason. Pricing was a row in the Explore dropdown until 2026-08-21 and a bar row after that, on the argument that a B2B site hiding its price reads as one that would rather not say. That is true of the SITE and was never true of this surface: index.html is the signed-in app, and its settings panel has carried a Plan row with a See pricing button — on the identical `live && !pro` rule — since 2026-08-23. Two controls, one question. The nav row is gone and the settings button is the app's one pricing door. Nothing about how the site SELLS changed: marketBar still renders its own Pricing row on every server-rendered page (to /pricing for a stranger, /?pricing=1 for a member), and both deep links still open the modal here, verified in a browser along with the whole Settings path — panel closes, modal opens, Free/Pro/Founding. The move needed a second edit to be safe. Settings is signed-in chrome: its door is the account menu. An anonymous visitor reading a shared report at /r/<id> gets index.html with no account menu at all, so once the nav row went there was no pricing door on the page for them. Every server-rendered footer has carried /pricing since that page existed and this one had not, so it does now — a real URL that works signed out, which is what that reader needs and what a modal could never have given them. The equivalence that makes the removal safe was checked rather than assumed: the retired nav row showed on `live && !pro`, and #settingsUpgradeBtn shows on exactly the same test inside a Plan row whose own condition (`live || admin || tester`) is strictly wider, so there is no deployment or account state where the old control appeared and the new one does not. Proved by booting with billing switched on — the local default has no Stripe key, which hides the whole Plan row and would have made a spot check look like a regression.

title: The header stops selling a report to somebody already working
details: Owner’s call. The red “Run a report” button rode every server-rendered header a member saw, including the four pages where they are plainly in the middle of something else: the vault, the market explorer, the 1031 guide and bulk valuation. On those it is a call to action for a different task than the one on screen, which is the definition of a nag. It comes off all four and stays everywhere else — /brokers, /pricing, /firms and the market pages under the explorer — because those are the surfaces where somebody is still deciding whether to run one. A market DETAIL page keeps it deliberately: it is reached FROM the explorer, and it already carries its own value-a-property form lower down. Two things this is not. It is not a way home: that reasoning is unchanged from the 2026-08-28 round, when the CTA was explicitly ruled out as one, and dropping it is safe only because the Workspace row is on every one of these bars — a future edit that suppresses Workspace here has to put the button back. And it is not a rule about being signed in: the suppression is a list of four paths, keyed on the same ones the nav rows point at so that the row you are standing on and the page that drops the CTA cannot drift into two lists. Pinned from both sides, so a widened set is as much a test failure as a narrowed one.

title: Light and dark goes back to Settings, and stops being two buttons
details: Owner’s call, the same day the sidebar parity work put the theme switch into the nav on both halves of the rail. That fixed the old asymmetry the wrong way round: dark mode is one preference, so it gets one control. The switch is back where it sat from 2026-08-23 — the Appearance row in the settings panel — and the nav copies are gone from BOTH sides, so #themeToggleApp in index.html is now the only theme control in the product. What came out with the server-rendered button is worth more than the button: accountNavSlots no longer renders it, ACCOUNT_NAV_CSS no longer styles its moon and sun, and ACCOUNT_NAV_JS no longer carries a hand-copy of index.html’s click handler that nothing but a comment and a test kept in step. THEME_BOOT stays hand-copied on both sides, because applying a stored choice is not the same act as offering one — a member who picks dark still gets dark on every market page. Every server-rendered page reaches the panel through the account menu’s Settings row, which already pointed at /desk?settings=1. The one case that needed thought: a signed-out visitor has no account menu, so removing their toggle would have trapped a browser that had already stored dark with no way back to light. The wall now lets a bare /?settings=1 through (never /desk?settings=1 — that is still a personal workspace) and the panel opens for them showing its two account-free rows, appearance and plan. Nothing in the chrome points there; it is an escape hatch, not a feature. Choosing a theme is a member affordance now.

title: The vault stopped building its own version of the website
details: Task 9 of the rail plan, the one the plan itself calls the riskiest and the least required. vault-page.js built a whole HTML document — doctype, head, its own header, its own footer — which is exactly what made it the surface that drifted: a third hand-written copy of a nav list two other files already render, an Escape script that closed the dropdown and never stepped back the way every other page does, a footer that carried no links at all until two days ago, and ~34 lines of chrome CSS that MARKET_CSS already defines. It renders a BODY now and marketShell supplies the rest, as it does for /markets, /brokers, /firms, /pricing and /bulk. The twelve-key chrome object the route used to hand it — CN_LOGO, RAIL_CSS, ACCOUNT_NAV_*, FOOTER_*, THEME_*, NAV_SHELL_CLASS — is gone, because every one of those existed only to rebuild by hand what the shell already had. The file is 271 lines lighter and the Escape key works. Two things had to be carried across deliberately. Inter, which MARKET_CSS names in its body rule and which NO server-rendered page actually fetches — they were all designed against the system fallback and this one was not, so the fold would have silently restyled the page brokers use daily; it rides marketShell's head parameter as INTER_FONT_HEAD. And the stylesheet moved INTO the body rather than the head, which is bulk-page.js's pattern and is load-bearing rather than tidy: MARKET_CSS is emitted in the head, so this page's own rules have to come after it in document order to win on equal specificity. That last point is the whole risk of the task and it is not theoretical. Both stylesheets independently use .card, .ledger, .lcell, .btn, table, th and td for completely different components, so every property the vault does not itself set falls through to MARKET_CSS's rule. Measured in a browser against a populated twelve-comp vault, before and after: .ledger and .card each silently gained a margin, .lcell a right border and a flex basis, and the comps table got tabular figures on every column plus a 180px first column. All six are stated explicitly on the vault's own rules now, and test/vault-shell.test.js COMPUTES the leak set from the two stylesheets rather than listing it, so a property added to a MARKET_CSS rule years from now fails the build instead of quietly restyling a broker's book. The before/after diff covered 28 computed styles: 26 identical, and the two that moved are the two that were meant to — main is the wrap element itself now (same 1120px content column) and the privacy sentence moved out of the retired footer into the page, where it is content rather than chrome. The hub is the other half of the task and there it is a decision rather than a port: hub-page.js keeps its own minimal document, because a hub is shown to somebody else's client, who is not inside your product.

title: The two halves of the sidebar now agree with each other
details: Owner-reported: clicking between the rail's rows walked you across a seam. The rail is one shape drawn by two files -- index.html for the app, marketBar plus RAIL_CSS for everything else -- and every fault was a difference BETWEEN them, which is why none of it was visible in either file alone and why the tests for it live in a new test/nav-parity.test.js that reads both. Six of them. The app could not say which row you were standing on: marketBar has written aria-current since the rail shipped and index.html wrote it nowhere, so markNavCurrent() now does, from the four seams that change which view is showing -- including the two report seams, because assembly yields the workspace a minute before renderResults repaints and a highlight left over a view that is gone is worse than none. Workspace was a button, the only row in either rail that could not be middle-clicked, opened in a new tab or previewed on hover; it is an anchor to /desk now, and its handler stands aside for a modified or middle click instead of swallowing it. Clicking it at / pushed /desk over the top of a view that had not changed, so the address bar moved, nothing else did, and Back then appeared to do nothing either; both URLs still serve the workspace, they just stop rewriting each other. The vault row said Your vault in the app and Vault everywhere else, so the row you were looking at renamed itself the moment you clicked it. The theme switch was a row on every server-rendered page and two clicks inside a modal on the app -- right on 2026-08-23, five days before the rail existed -- so it moved back into the nav, same id, same handler, same element. Settings was the reverse case: the panel lives only in index.html and so did its only door, so accountNavSlots grew a Settings row pointing at /desk?settings=1, read and cleared the way ?pricing=1 already is. And /vault's footer was four lines of prose and not one link, which was survivable while its header had an Explore dropdown and a dead end the moment the rail took that dropdown away; it renders MARKET_FOOTER's own columns now, extracted to FOOTER_LINK_COLS and FOOTER_LINKS_CSS rather than pasted a third time, on RAIL_CSS's argument. One more, found while reading: both shells stamp the rail from cookie PRESENCE, which is not the same question as whether the session is still valid -- the app already re-decided after /api/account/me, the server-rendered pages did not, so an expired cn_session left the product's own sidebar standing around a bar reading Log in.

title: Every Florida address was read as one unit of a site
details: unitDesignatorOf gates three things: the OSM footprint size estimate, the Street View or aerial photo on every map pin, and the verified_key that migration 035's portfolio dedupe runs on. "fl" is in its keyword vocabulary and FL is a state abbreviation, so "873 E Citation Ct, Miami, FL 33101" matched as floor 33101 and the whole state was refused — no size estimate, no photo on any pin, and dedupe off, so one Florida building typed three ways saved as three properties with three value histories. Invisible by construction: the vocabulary's own comment notes that a false positive silently costs a size estimate and a photo, which is exactly why the must-PASS direction needed a test and not only the must-REFUSE one. A trailing state and ZIP is now dropped before the vocabulary is applied, which is the general fix rather than an FL exemption — that suffix is never a unit designator whatever the keyword list grows to, and a genuine "Fl 3" still matches once it is gone.

title: Outreach targeting skipped Florida, and any street named after a keyword
details: outreach-draft.js carried its own loose copy of the unit-designator rule — a keyword followed by any word — so it refused "500 Lot Ave", "900 Building Materials Way" and "100 Space Center Blvd", and because FL is a state it refused every Florida address in the corpus. A refusal here only means a building is never written to, so nothing reported it. The file already imports isAggregateAddress from corpus-audit rather than restating that vocabulary, and now uses the same tight rule index.html does, with the two pinned together by a test: neither file can require the other, so the pair is kept honest the way ORG.SHOP_COPY's mirror is. The tests it gained run in both directions, which is what the copy in index.html needed after "Roomy", "Lotus" and "United Nations" all parsed as unit designators on its first pass.

title: A failed report burned the anonymous visitor's one free search
details: The rule stated where the guest gate is built is that the free search is spent only when a report is actually served. The consume ran before gate(), which is not a formality — it runs the radius blend, the comp gate, coordinate attachment and the vault and firm blends, any of which can throw into the handler's catch and answer 502. The visitor got no report and lost the allowance, with the cn_guest cookie already set, so the retry was refused with signin_required for a report that never arrived. /api/explore-market has always had this ordering right, consuming only on a published 200; the report route now serializes first and spends second, and reuses the serialized value at both exits rather than calling gate() again per exit.

title: Import errors cited a line number the broker would find blank
details: parseCsv drops blank rows before returning, so a caller's array index counts rows that survived parsing rather than lines of the file — and both callers that report line numbers computed it from that index while promising the number the person sees in their spreadsheet. One spacer row and the vault said "Line 3" about a row sitting on line 5; a quoted cell spanning two lines pushed it further. Bulk valuation had the same off-by-N in its header branch, surfaced in skipped[] and warnings[] to whoever pasted the list. parseCsv now stamps each row with the file line it started on, counting newlines inside quoted cells too, and both callers read the stamp. The property is non-enumerable, so a row is still an ordinary array of cells to every other consumer — same length, same JSON, same spread.

title: Eight smaller defects found in the same sweep
details: The Market Explorer read its type and state tables with bare lookups, so typing "constructor Boise ID" returned the Object function as a property type and rendered "function Object() { [native code] }" on the button — index.html already guards the identical shape one file over and says why, so the same own-property fix is applied here. The vault's filter dropdown built a quoted attribute with the innerHTML-safe escaper instead of the attribute-safe one defined two lines from it, and the values are markets parsed from addresses a broker typed. DELETE /api/vault/upload lacked the uuid guard every sibling vault route has, so a malformed id answered 502 "could not remove that import, please try again" — telling a broker our storage failed and inviting a retry that could never work; it now 404s like the others. The search-error status line interpolated a raw server message into innerHTML, which the file's two other error renderers both avoid deliberately. The subject last-sale and asking-price links built an href without the protocol check their four sibling link sites apply. refreshDistances drew the comp table before recomputing the value band it reads, so outlier chips could quote a range the hero was no longer showing. applyCuration rebuilt the column list without clearing the sort state, so excluding the last comp carrying a sorted column left the table sorted with no indicator and a blank sort control on mobile. And outreach.js padded the wrong side of a fallback and reported failed addresses as warmed.

title: Reopening a saved report valued it with the last search's square footage
details: subjectRangeFromMeta, askingRangeFrom and subjectCapRate fall back to the live form inputs whenever a report's own meta carries no figure, and the comment on the first of them says a reopened report has no form inputs to read. That is true on a cold page load and false the moment anything has been searched, because renderOwnerHero auto-fills the size box with the size it looked up. So opening a saved house from My Desk after searching a 152,400 SF warehouse priced the house at its own $/SF times the warehouse's square footage — the number CLAUDE.md calls the most expensive in the report, taken from a different building. The price box fed the asking-price check and the cap rate box seeded the DCF the same way. Both reopen paths now restore the form from the report's own meta before rendering, through one helper that rerunHistory shares. Every field is assigned rather than assigned-if-present: the leak happens exactly when the new report has no stored figure, which is the case a presence check skips, so a blank has to be written as blank.

title: A monthly lease rate could be banked as an annual one
details: leaseRentPsfYr trusted price_per_sqft before consulting the rate string, and price_per_sqft is a bare number carrying no basis — the prompt asks the model to put the quoted rate there, which in California industrial and retail is the monthly figure. The same lease therefore answered 1.08 or 12.96 depending only on which field it arrived in, and a two-comp market medianed to $7.02/SF/yr, a rent that describes nothing. Downstream it was worse: leaseQuoteBasis correctly read that comp as monthly-quoted, so the hero divided the already-monthly figure by 12 again and printed $0.09/SF/mo on a $1.08 market. A figure that names its unit now outranks one that does not. The existing refusal of monthly-only quotes stands unchanged and was never the problem — what was broken is that it could only ever be reached when price_per_sqft happened to be empty.

title: Range-quoted corpus prices were treated as having no price at all
details: The radius blend's money reader stripped every non-digit, which welds a real corpus value like "$7.00-$12.00/SF/yr NNN" into "7.0012.00" — a two-decimal-point string Number() rejects. The row then read as unpriced and blendNearbyComps skipped a perfectly good saved deal, so comps that had been harvested never reached a report. corpus-audit.js reads the first numeric run for exactly this reason and says so in a comment, which meant the audit counted the same row as priced while the blend dropped it, and nothing anywhere reported the disagreement. Now reads the first numeric run, so a range yields its low end and commas survive; "Undisclosed" and "Rate Upon Request" still correctly carry no price, and a $/SF-shaped figure in the price column is still refused rather than divided by the size.

title: Sorting the comp table by Date could return an order that does not exist
details: Parseable dates were compared chronologically and anything else lexicographically, which is not a total order: "Sep 2025" beats "Q3 2025" and "Q3 2025" beats "Feb 2026" as strings, while "Sep 2025" loses to "Feb 2026" as dates. Array.sort given a contradictory comparator returns an arbitrary permutation, and this one really did put Feb 2026 first in an ascending sort. The date column holds unconstrained model text and both "Active" and "Q3 2025" are real stored values, so it fired on ordinary reports rather than on edge cases. Unreadable dates now sink in both directions, exactly as unreadable numbers already do in the branch below it.

title: Every unsubscribe link in every email was truncated before it was sent
details: The letterhead's linkifier built its href from a character class that stopped at an ampersand. It runs on already-escaped text, so a query string arrives as ?u=abc&t=xyz and the link was cut at the first parameter. Both unsubscribe builders in the product authenticate with a &t=<mac> token, and every outbound email gets this HTML part, so the "turn these emails off" link in the watchlist digest, the lease renewal notice and hub note emails all pointed at a URL the route could only refuse. Its refusal page reads "it may have been truncated by an email client" — it was truncated here. These three are the only things this product sends on its own initiative, which makes that the one link that has to work. Fixed by matching the & entity rather than adding a bare ampersand to the class, so an apostrophe after a link still ends the URL and a crafted one still cannot escape the href attribute; a trailing entity also no longer gets its semicolon sheared into a malformed &amp.

title: A failed card kept Pro for the whole Stripe retry schedule, not seven days
details: subscriptionRowFrom derived the grace deadline from the current clock while its own comment promised a second past_due webhook could not extend it — it never read the stored row, so it had no way to keep that. invoice.payment_failed and the firm path each patched the value back afterwards; customer.subscription.updated did not, and Stripe fires that on every Smart Retries state change while a subscription is past_due, with the upsert merging the column over the top. The window was therefore pushed forward on every retry and a dead card held Pro for roughly three weeks. The rule now lives in the pure module as an existingGraceUntil argument and every caller feeds it, because three handlers each remembering to re-apply it is three chances to forget and the one that forgot is the one Stripe calls most. Preserved unconditionally rather than only while still in the future, so a window that ran out stays run out; recovery still nulls the column, which is what lets a genuinely new dunning cycle earn a fresh one.

title: The mail runs read a user row too narrow to answer what the reader had paid for
details: findUsersByIds is the third place a user object is built for getEntitlements — the watchlist digest and the renewal watch mail from it — and it selected id, email and digest_optout only. pro_tester and vault_beta therefore read as undefined, then false, so every comped account in a mail run resolved to the free tier with nothing failing anywhere: the exact silent shape vault_beta walked into on 2026-08-12. Measured before claiming it: today the omission changes nothing a watcher receives, because feedRowCap is 20 for free and Pro alike since the free comp cap was retired on 2026-08-21, and the digest never asks for search demand. It is fixed and test-pinned anyway, since both things masking it are one edit from moving and a send advances a high-water mark, so a wrong digest is never repaired by re-running. The same read also gained the chunking and explicit limit every other in.() fan-out here has: PostgREST can honour a max-rows setting by returning fewer rows with no error, which would have mailed part of the list while the run summary counted all of it.

title: The schema checker is now checked, and it was crashing instead of reporting
details: test/migrations.test.js proves verify.js's two lists are complete; nothing proved the script still REPORTS correctly, and a row that silently checks nothing is indistinguishable from a row that checked and passed — the shape of the 2026-07 corpus outage the whole migrations folder was built after. So test/migrations-verify-run.test.js spawns the real script against a stub answering PostgREST's own signals (404/PGRST205 for a table, 400/PGRST204 for a column), the way routes.test.js boots a real server to prove the gates are wired rather than merely correct in isolation. It pins five behaviours, including the one that is pure honesty: a 500 is reported as 'could not check, NOT proof of absence' and never as a missing table, because sending somebody to run DDL against a database that is fine is the expensive wrong answer. Each test was checked against a deliberately broken verify.js before being trusted. It earned its keep the first time it ran: under the suite's normal concurrency the script CRASHED rather than reporting, exit 3221226505 — process.exit() tearing the process down while its fetch sockets were still open, 0xC0000409 on Windows, measured at 13 of 16 concurrent runs and 0 of 16 once the exit became natural. That is worse than it sounds, because a crash is a non-zero exit exactly like a missing table is, so it reads as 'the schema is wrong' while destroying the output that says which migration to run. It now sets process.exitCode and returns, which also guarantees stdout flushes — the way this tool's result becomes evidence in APPLIED.md is somebody redirecting it to a file. A source scan pins that process.exit( never returns.

title: The sidebar carries the whole product, not two rows of it
details: Owner-reported: in some places the sidebar only has Workspace and Your vault. That was the app itself, read by a Pro member. The rail is the header stood on its end, and it hides the Explore dropdown outright — a menu has nowhere to open in a 224px column — so on the app's front door Explore went, Pricing hides for a Pro member, Sign in hides for anyone signed in, and what was left was literally two rows. Reachability had quietly become a question of whether a link was a top-level row or a dropdown item, and no test asked that: every one of them checks whether the link is in the document, and the 1031 guide was in the document on every page and reachable from none of them. So the five product surfaces are rows now, in one fixed order — Workspace, Vault, Market explorer, 1031 guide, Bulk valuation — on all three headers — the one marketBar builds, the one index.html authors, and the one vault-page.js hand-writes. Three headers built three different ways is why the order is asserted as a sequence rather than as five presence checks: nothing else stops the sidebar reshuffling itself as a member navigates between them. The app gained Market explorer, the 1031 guide and Bulk valuation, the last off its own canBulkValue entitlement rather than the vault's flag; the vault page had Markets and the guide buried in its dropdown and no route to bulk at all. The guide left the shared Explore list for the reason Pricing and Markets left it before: it is somewhere a member goes back to, not a browse link. Brokers, For firms and the download stay in the dropdown, which is for strangers — who still see it, on a phone and under NAV_SHELL=bar. And Bulk is called Bulk valuation everywhere now, which is what the page has always called itself.

title: The three refusals that gated the archive: undated deals, a per-sheet rent basis, pinned addresses
details: The 2026-08-28 extraction verdict passed on quality and then showed where the remaining loss was: correct refusals cost 13 of a 16-document set’s real deals, and one behavior destabilized the dedupe key. All three fixes shipped. A closed deal from a document that dates none of its transactions can now be imported as the literal word “undated” (migration 042 — run before deploy — drops broker_comps.deal_date’s NOT NULL): a blank stays refused, the word is a statement, and the stored null keeps the comp out of every report blend and lookback by SQL semantics, unpublishable, and unshareable to a firm — with a named refusal instead of a silent no-op, and an edit-to-undated pulls the firm’s copy rather than leaving it stale. The sentinel is contained to deal_date by an opt-in parser flag, validateEdit round-trips the stored null so an undated comp never becomes uneditable, and the book export writes the word back so export→re-import is a no-op. Second, lease sheets that state a rate but never “annual” or “monthly” — conventionally formatted, close to unimportable — get a per-sheet basis selector on the confirm table: no default, rendered only when a row needs it, stamped visibly into the rows so a hand-typed cell always wins, curing exactly the rows whose only blocker it was; the server re-validates everything on import. Third, the extract prompt pins address handling — street verbatim, “City, ST” completion only when the document itself proves the state — so the dedupe key stops flapping between runs. Proved end to end against the stand-in PostgREST (test/vault-undated-run.test.js) and live in a browser, including the d04-shaped import, the export round-trip, and the firm-share refusal. The fake PostgREST also learned offset paging, which the export’s pagination loop needed to ever see an empty page.

title: The migration folder's paper rules became build failures, and main is protected
details: migrations/verify.js now names everything a read-only probe can see: 035's portfolio_items.verified_key, 038's three renewal-watch columns plus shared_reports.shared_by_name, 039's org_contacts — and three tables it had never listed at all (broker_bovs from 019, broker_csv_mappings from 021, org_contacts again), so a run could answer "Everything present" while three tables were absent. APPLIED.md had named the 035/037/038/039 gap itself as "the obvious next tidy"; the two tables from 019 and 021 nobody had noticed, which is the argument for the second half of this change: a new test/migrations.test.js reads every `create table` out of the migration files themselves — the migration-columns.js approach — and fails the suite when verify.js's TABLES list is missing one, in either direction. The same test enforces migration-number uniqueness, grandfathering exactly the two applied 036 files by name, so the collision APPLIED.md asks never to repeat is now caught by CI instead of by a human reading that row. 037 is documented as the one migration the tool can never see (a CHECK-constraint widening; proving it read-only is impossible, and verify.js writes nothing). Alongside: branch protection is ON for main — the test check is required to merge, force pushes and deletions are blocked, admin bypass stays available for an Actions outage — closing the roadmap's "once PR flow feels routine" item, and the long-merged gifted-lamarr Claude worktree and its branch are pruned.

title: The import confirm table reads like the document it came from
details: Verifying twelve extracted rows was timed at 4m51s against the 60-second bar, with zero corrections needed — the extraction took 9.9 seconds and the person took 291. The cost is the review, not the read, so this takes the two causes that are pure presentation. Figures are now shown the way the source page prints them (,250,000, not 4250000) using the comps table’s own convention rather than a second one: formatted to read, raw on focus to edit, and the raw value is what imports — a dollar sign can never reach the vault. The guard matters more than the formatting: these rows have NOT been through normalizeRow, and the rows a broker most needs to read are the ones holding something it refused, so anything that is not genuinely a number is shown exactly as it was read. An unguarded formatter would have rendered 1.2M as  and erased the only clue about what to fix. The model is also now asked to return rows in the order the document prints them, top to bottom, page by page — out-of-order rows were the biggest single cause, because checking row 4 meant hunting the page for it. And a lease sheet was headed rent_psf and rent_basis: migration 029 added five lease fields to the confirm table’s column list and never to its labels, and the label lookup falls back to the key, so nothing failed and nobody saw it until a lease row was photographed. Every column is now pinned to a label by test.

title: Pricing and Sign in no longer strand a signed-out visitor on the app
details: Clicking Pricing or Sign in from the landing page, then backing out of what opened, left you on the report page with a Create a free account card and no way back to the page you were reading. Both links are doors through the account wall onto index.html, because the pricing modal and the account modal live only in that file. The door strips its own marker from the URL on arrival, and closing a modal only hid it, so nothing recorded where you came from. Two changes. The header's Pricing link now points at /pricing, the standalone rate card, for a signed-out reader; a signed-in member still gets the modal, which is where checkout actually starts, and for whom the app is already home. And cancelling the sign-in modal after arriving through /?auth=signin now returns a signed-out visitor to the landing page. Signup deliberately does not do this: a signup arrival is usually carrying an address typed into the landing page's own form, and bouncing back would throw it away.

title: The live comp lines actually appear — a swallowed ReferenceError, one year of silence
details: The first real streamed Gemini report showed searches, results and the summary arriving live — and not one comp line, while the finished report held four. The streamed-comp callback in server.js calls expandComp, which moved into report-parse.js in the 2026-08-08 extraction and was never exported; the resulting ReferenceError was swallowed PER COMP by makeCompExtractor’s catch, so every live comp event died with no log, no error, and a perfectly fine report. Nothing noticed because the whole streaming path was dark on the default provider until today. The call now goes through the module, the export exists, and two tests pin it: report-parse must export expandComp, and a source scan fails the build on any bare expandComp( call in server.js — the exact shape a future refactor would reintroduce.

title: Vault comps get map pins without the CSV carrying coordinates
details: A broker's private comp only ever earned a map pin if their spreadsheet supplied lat/lng columns, because geocoding it any other way meant the address leaving their browser for a third party — the exact thing the vault promises not to do. The server now locates the buildings an import left blank itself, at import time, through the same in-process Census call our own /api/geocode proxy fronts: never Nominatim, never the browser, never a URL. Up to 25 buildings per import, and books uploaded before today backfill 8 at a time whenever the vault's comps are read for a report. A coordinate the broker typed always wins — the census write only ever fills a building that has none, and a miss or a Census outage leaves the building unlocated rather than guessed, because a wrong pin puts the building on the wrong continent and nobody would recognize it as wrong. The whole path is proven end to end against a stand-in database and a stand-in geocoder, including that a located building's address is never sent anywhere at all.

title: A firm gets one letterhead: firm-level report branding
details: Branding was one profile per member, so a five-broker firm was five people each uploading the logo and one stale copy made the firm look inconsistent to clients. A firm’s owner or admin now saves one branding profile for the whole firm (migration 041, org_branding — its own table read by its own fail-open function, so the 030/036 deploy-order hazard never applies), and a member’s report falls back to it whenever they have no personal profile of their own. The member’s own profile always wins — a fallback, never an override, the auto-share member veto’s philosophy applied to letterheads — and canBrand still gates applying, so a free colleague merely invited to a firm stays unbranded. The share snapshot inherits the same rule (auto-share included), the branding card on the workspace gains a My branding / Firm branding scope row for owners and admins plus a disclosure line for members whose reports are riding the firm’s mark, and everything stays co-branded: the CompNinja attribution and the automated-estimate line survive every configuration. Proved end to end against the stand-in PostgREST: member PUT refused, validation shared with the personal editor byte for byte, the snapshot fallback, and the own-profile win.

title: The workspace tells you when a value has gone a year stale
details: The workspace opened with numbers, then lists, and nothing anywhere on it that was waiting on the member. There is one line under the ledger now, and it appears only when something is actually waiting: "2 properties were last checked over a year ago. Refresh them below to bring their values up to date." On most days for most people it renders nothing at all, which is deliberate: a standing "you're all caught up" banner is the 0-0 scoreboard the vault's first run already taught us not to draw. A year is not a number picked for this line. portfolio-delta.js already draws exactly that boundary and says why: past a year a window "stops being since you last looked and becomes market history", so a property last checked before then does not have a stale-ish reading of its market, it has an answer to a different question. That module is server-side and cannot be required from the page, so the constant is mirrored with a flag on it, the same treatment compWeight and SHOP_COPY carry. It names ONE thing on purpose. New comps are the ledger's fourth cell one line above and a pending firm invitation is the first deck one line below, so repeating either here would be the header's just-removed habit of saying things three times; and lease expiries, the other candidate, were checked and simply never reach this surface. Building it turned up a real inconsistency underneath: the property table said "checked {date}" from updated_at, which is when the ROW was last written by anything, while the new line counts the last time a value was actually produced. A save that produces no valuation moves one and not the other, and the two dates contradicted each other on screen thirty pixels apart. The column says checked and a snapshot is a check, so the row now reads the last snapshot and falls back to updated_at only when there is none. Free desks are excluded with the ledger: a page that never showed a value has no business reporting that values are old.

title: Pricing opens the pricing modal on the first click, not the second
details: Clicking Pricing in the header of any server-rendered page sent you to a bare home page with no pricing on it; you had to click Pricing a second time to see the plans. Those headers link to /?pricing=1, which is a deliberate door through the account wall so a signed-out visitor can read the prices. The door is a one-shot, and it was being spent too early: the billing UI repaints once during startup, before /api/config has answered, and at that moment the page cannot yet tell a deployment with billing switched on from one without it. That early pass assumed off, skipped the modal, and cleared the ?pricing=1 marker from the URL anyway, so the later pass that knew the real answer found nothing left to act on. It now waits for a real answer before spending the link. Same guard the Address Explorer's deep link already uses, for the same reason.

title: Brokers and For firms are back in the Explore menu
details: The Explore menu now reads Brokers, For firms, 1031 Guide, Download the app. The two audience pages left the menu on 2026-08-25 and kept only a footer link, which is not where a stranger browsing the site looks for them. For firms was never in the menu at all. Both are in one list in server.js (NAV_LINKS), so the change lands at once on the app's own header and on every server-rendered page, and each page's own link still gets the current-page style.

title: The live report assembly finally runs in production
details: The comp-by-comp progress card was built 2026-08-09 and has been dark ever since the default provider became Gemini, because its streaming frame shape was unconfirmed and the reader shipped behind a verifier rather than a guess. The verifier earned its keep: its first run disproved the guessed parser outright — the live wire is event_type-tagged frames, not steps snapshots — so the reader was rewritten from the real frames (committed as test fixtures and replayed by the suite), streaming is on, and the STREAM_UNVERIFIED opt-in is deleted. A bonus the non-streaming path could never offer: streamed calls surface the model’s real search queries in the progress card. Rollback without a deploy: STREAM_ANTHROPIC=off.

title: The vault moves into the rail, and the workspace stops showing your face twice
details: Four changes to the signed-in shell, all the owner's call, and the second half of them finishes a job the entry below started an hour earlier. The broker vault was a row inside the account dropdown, which under the rail is pinned to the foot of a 224px sidebar and opens upward — so a broker's daily workspace sat two clicks down a menu while "Workspace" itself was one click away in the rail. It is a rail item now, directly beneath Workspace, and it left the dropdown rather than being listed twice. Nothing about who sees it changed: refreshBillingUI still shows it from /api/config's canUseVault and /api/vault still re-checks server-side, so the link and the page agree exactly as before. The workspace header then lost the rest of its profile cluster. The entry below took the greeting and "Add a photo" and kept the avatar circle, on the grounds that the circle is itself the upload control and that the settings panel had no Remove, so dropping the cluster would have deleted the only way to take a photo off an account. Both grounds were right; the owner still wanted the circle gone, and under the rail the reason is plain, since the account circle is already pinned bottom-left in the sidebar and a second one top-right shows the same face twice on one screen. So the circle went too and the blocker was removed rather than argued with: the settings panel now carries Remove photo alongside Change photo, which is the whole reason that button exists, and the hidden file input stays where it is because settings clicks it. And with that row down to one control, the "Run a report" shortcut is red — it starts the same act as the red button at the foot of the chamber it jumps to.

title: The fourth workspace figure counts new comps, and the header says your name once
details: Two more passes over the workspace strip and its header. The fourth ledger cell counted watched markets, which is a count of a preference sitting beside three facts about the member's book, and the only live thing on the whole strip -- "N new comps waiting" -- was demoted to the 11px note underneath it. The figure is the new-comp count now and the markets are the context: "12 / across 3 markets you watch", or "0 / 2 markets watched · quiet", or an em dash and "watch a market to see new comps here" for somebody watching none, because a big 0 over an empty watchlist states a fact about markets they never asked about. Both writers of that cell were changed together -- renderMyDesk paints a placeholder and renderWatchFeed fills it in a request later -- and a test now pins their labels as well as their markup, since a cell that renames itself a moment after first paint reads as a glitch. The header said who you are three times: the avatar circle, "Signed in as {name}", and "Add a photo", directly beside a nav carrying the same photo and the same account menu. Identity and the duplicate button are gone. The circle stays, because it IS the upload control, because the #avatar deep link points at it, and because clicking your own initial to change a photo is the pattern people already know; it carries the label in aria-label and title instead of in text, and the settings panel keeps an explicit "Change photo" for anyone who wants a written one. Remove stays too, and that was the finding that shaped the change: settings has no remove, so dropping it from the header would have deleted the only way to take a photo off an account. Both removed elements were read UNGUARDED by the page script, so their references went with them. One thing worth recording for whoever next reaches for a before-and-after here: the signed-out app at / is not byte-deterministic, because the market explorer's placeholder rotates -- two runs of identical code differ, so a hash comparison on that surface proves nothing either way. The wall-on landing page is deterministic and is byte-identical.

title: Report branding folds away, and the workspace says what it holds
details: Three fixes to the workspace now that it opens the page. Report branding was a permanently-expanded form on the screen a member looks at every day: measured on a three-property workspace it was 629px tall against 568px for the entire portfolio deck, so a set-once-a-year setting took up more of the page than everything the member owns. It now collapses behind a row that states what is actually on their reports, named rather than counted, because "3 details saved" tells nobody anything: "Colliers Boise · logo set · license shown". The section rule and the explanation stay outside the fold so the deck still reads as furnished rather than as a lone twisty, and the whole page drops from 2371px to 1859px. This is the same call the header gear got on 2026-08-24 — settings belong where you go to change them, not where you go to work. One trap came with it and is handled: the load-failure message lives inside the box, so a branding read that fails opens it rather than reporting into something nobody can see, which is verified against a real 503. The subtitle under WORKSPACE said "Your recent searches and tracked properties" from back when that was the whole of it; the page has since grown the firm shelf, the deal board, sharing, the vault and the report runner, so the first sentence on the page described about a fifth of it. It now reads "Your properties, your firm's shelf, and everything you have shared." And on a phone the four-cell ledger stacked one per row, which meant scrolling past an entire screen of statistics before reaching a property you own; it goes 2x2 under 640px, scoped to this ledger because every other one on the site is a two or three cell strip that stacks correctly. A phone capture also caught the workspace header running together as "WORKSPACERun a report" at 375px, fixed with a wrap and a gap. Nothing behavioral moved: every id the branding save, delete and preview handlers reach is still there and still wired, and both anonymous surfaces are provably untouched by byte-identical before and after screenshots.

title: The workspace opens the page; the search chamber follows it
details: Since 2026-08-28 a member's / has opened the workspace — but the search chamber still sat above it in the document, so the first screenful of the page a member lives on was still "Value a building" and "Or read a market", with their book, their firm and their pipeline below the fold. The chamber now sits below the workspace, moved as one unit, and in desk view it wears a deck-style "Run a report" rule so it reads as one more section of the workspace rather than a page that happens to follow one; the plain home, and a report on screen, both retire that rule. The workspace header carries a "Run a report" shortcut that jumps to the chamber and seats the caret in the address field — an instant jump on purpose, because a smooth scroll paired with a focus proved able to silently go nowhere, and it is what reduced motion would ask for anyway. The ledger is promoted to the workspace's opening statement, Georgia figures and roomier cells, and its third cell stops over-claiming: "Since last checks" read as a portfolio return, and the figure is not one — it compares each property's last two check-ins, over only the properties checked at least twice, with no time window at all. It is now "Between checks", its note names its own sample ("2 of 3 properties, last check vs the check before"), and its tooltip says outright that this is not a return over any period of time; the arithmetic is unchanged and the same figure still feeds the statement's closing total, computed once so the two can never disagree. The deck interiors take one family: addresses go Georgia in the portfolio, the shelf and the shares; the firm's shelf and its people become hairline rows; a share's audience wears a chip so who-can-see-this scans as a state; the watch feed's markets become bordered briefing cards; and the four hard-coded white cards take the themed shell, which also fixes them in dark mode. Every id, render order and behavior underneath is untouched — revoke, invites, checkout polling, the watch form and branding save all run through the same elements they always did — and the signed-out home is provably unchanged: the before and after screenshots are byte-identical, which also caught the one real bug of the build, a deck heading whose display rule out-cascaded Tailwind's hidden class and showed on the signed-out page until it got its own override.

title: The landing page leads with the vault, not the address box
details: Under the account wall, / is the whole product's front door, and top to bottom it was still the single-address comp puller: the hero's call to action WAS an address field, and the exhibit beside it was a one-property report. Everything the product has become since — the private vault, the firm shelf, the pipeline — appeared below the fold or not at all, on a page selling a $100/month subscription whose headline feature is the vault. The page now opens on a broker's own book: "Your closed deals, in every comp report you run", beside a vault sheet showing four of their deals and, underneath, the one thing a broker actually wants answered about a private archive — what leaves it. Then the firm layer, then a Sharing section drawing the same comp three times, redacted by who is looking: everything for you, the comps you opted into for your firm, and $/SF with size and date for your client, with no address, no total price and no notes. The report did not go away, it stopped being the pitch: Method still explains how one is built, and the address field and the sample report moved down together into a Proof section under the heading "See it on a building you know", markup unchanged, so the free-report signup funnel and the sessionStorage handoff work exactly as before. What the page may NOT say is written down now: a broker's archive floors their web-search budget only where the provider supports a search cap, and the default provider does not, so archive-first retrieval is inert in production and copy is forbidden from selling it — BRAND.md carries the rule and a test rejects five phrasings of it. Two other honesty rules ride along: "no total price" rather than "no price", because price per square foot times size implies the price, and the deal board says out loud that it counts contribution to the firm and does not report who is closing what. Head terms were deliberately left alone — the title, the FAQ questions and the WebApplication description keep every term they had, the last of those gaining a vault clause rather than losing anything, and the meta description is now split by route the way the title already was; the thing to watch in Search Console is CTR on /, not position. Eight new assertions pin what nothing pinned before, including the actual instruction (the vault must appear before the address field, and the address field below Method) and the appraisal disclaimer, which BRAND.md has always required on this page and which had never once been asserted on it.

title: The flaky suite names its own cause: a server that died, not a socket that reset
details: npm test still failed about one run in five, always in a different suite, always green when that file was re-run alone, and always as a bare TypeError: fetch failed. The standing theory was Node's keep-alive connection pool handing a test a socket its server had already closed. It is not. Instrumenting the failures shows the first error is read ECONNRESET and every request after it to that same port is ECONNREFUSED — nothing is listening any more, because the child server PROCESS died. A run boots about 179 of them and roughly one in a thousand exits on its own with Windows code 3221226505 (0xC0000409, a hard abort), a few hundred milliseconds after it answered /healthz, having printed nothing: no fatal message even with its stderr written to a file instead of a pipe, no --report-on-fatalerror report, no uncaughtException and no unhandledRejection. Whichever suite owned that child is the suite that goes red, which is exactly why the failure wandered. It also explains why capping --test-concurrency changed nothing, which had been the confusing result: the crash rate follows the number of child boots, and lowering concurrency does not lower that. The idle keep-alive race was tested directly and could not be made to fail even with the client's event loop deliberately stalled across the 4s/5s margin, which fits the earlier finding that raising keepAliveTimeout did not help. boot.js already captured each child's stderr but only ever reported it when the child died inside the health-check loop, so a death after that was silent — that blind spot is why this read as a networking problem through two rounds of investigation. It now watches the child for its whole life and, when a healthy one exits by itself, prints the port, the exit code and the server's last words, and says plainly that any fetch failed below it is a consequence rather than a real assertion failure. This is a diagnostic, not a cure: the crash rate is unchanged and the suite is still about four runs in five green on a loaded 24-core Windows box. Two candidate cures were measured and rejected rather than shipped on a theory — windowsHide on the spawn (no effect on the abort across 1,862 boots, though it did clear the STATUS_DLL_INIT_FAILED that heavy churn provokes) and, earlier, the keep-alive changes. The one lever left with real leverage is the boot count itself: most suites start a fresh server per subtest, and fewer boots would mean proportionally fewer of these.

title: The Home link is in the signed-in header too
details: It shipped signed-out only, on the theory that the signed-in bar's Run a report already points at /. That was the reported bug restated one layer down: Run a report reads as starting a task, not as going home, so a signed-in member browsing market pages was left with the wordmark and a call to action, which are exactly the two things that failed the logged-out visitor. Navigation and a CTA are different affordances even when they share a destination, and the header should not change shape with auth state. The one suppression left is whose home page you are actually on: under the account wall an anonymous visitor at /how-it-works is looking at what / serves them, so a link there would point at the page they are on, while a member's / is the app, so that same URL owes them the link.

title: Public pages carry a Home link in the header
details: A logged-out visitor who opened Explore and landed on one of these pages had nothing that read as a way back: the wordmark links / but is branding rather than a button, and the Escape binding is invisible. Home is now the first item in the nav, left of Explore, on every server-rendered page. Signed out only, since the signed-in bar's Run a report already points at /, and never on the home page itself -- under the account wall that means both / and /how-it-works, which are one render served at two URLs.

title: A tagged link no longer 404s the market pages
details: /markets, every /market/<slug> page and /how-it-works matched on the raw request URL, so a tag on the end of the link made the address stop matching its own route and fall through to Not Found. Facebook appends ?fbclid=... to outbound links on its own, so every market page shared there was a dead link for whoever clicked it, and any UTM-tagged campaign or email link did the same. All three now match on the path, as /brokers and /privacy already did, and the canonical still points at the clean URL so the tagged variants do not become duplicate entries in Search Console. /broker/<slug>, /market-preview/<slug>, robots.txt and sitemap.xml carried the same shape and were fixed alongside.

title: Continue with Google no longer appears in the desktop app
details: Google refuses OAuth inside an embedded user agent — an anti-phishing control of theirs — so in the Electron app the button led to Google's own 500 page rather than a sign-in. It is hidden there now, leaving the password form, which works. It keys on the desktop app's user-agent token ALONE and not on display-mode, because an installed PWA is ordinary Chrome where Google sign-in works perfectly and hiding it there would take away a working door. A site change rather than an app change, so every installed copy got it without a new release. The real fix is a system-browser flow handing the session back through a deep link; that needs a new installer before it helps anybody, which is why this shipped first.

title: A leadership page
details: /leadership — the three people who build CompNinja, with headshots and a group photo, rendered through marketShell so it inherits the site chrome and needs no CSS of its own. Discovered from the footer, under Company, alongside /brokers and /how-it-works; it is deliberately NOT in the Explore menu, which is for the tools a reader might go and use. Listed in sitemap.xml. Each person is one TEAM entry feeding both the markup and a schema.org Person node tied to the canonical Organization, so the page and what crawlers are told cannot drift. Photos are four literal keys on the STATIC_FILES allowlist rather than a directory read.

title: The messaging hub is driven end to end, as two people, in software
details: test/hub-run.test.js walks a broker and their client through one requirement against a real server, a stand-in PostgREST and a stand-in Resend: the hub is created, the invitation opens it with no account, a comp is sent out of the vault, the client signs in and shortlists it, adds a building of their own, they trade messages and poll for what is new, a colleague is added and then taken out, and the hub is closed. Everything but POST /api/hub/message was previously proven only as a pure rule with no server near it, or as a refusal on a bare server where these routes 503 by design long before they reach SQL — and that gap has already cost this feature once, when every vault send failed for a week because the route asked PostgREST to resolve ON CONFLICT against a partial index.
