Each claim was watched go red against a deliberately broken server first: the poll's cursor loosened to gte replays the last message, the vault read losing its user_id scope pulls another broker's comp into the hub, and removal no longer beating everything leaves a removed guest reading and writing. The fake PostgREST learned two shapes to make it possible, both taught deliberately rather than guessed at: the gt. filter the poll sends, and the created_at / added_at defaults these tables declare, without which an ordered thread and a cursor are unprovable.

title: Show password when signing in
details: The sign-in modal's password field now carries an eye button that reveals what was typed — the same field covers creating an account and choosing a new password after a reset, so all four modes get it. It resets to hidden every time the modal opens or the mode changes, because revealing is a decision about one attempt rather than a setting, and a password left legible on screen is not what anyone asked for. Switching to Forgot password hides the whole row, button included.

title: The momentum word comes off the market cards
details: Each card in the /markets grid ended its subtitle with a coloured Expanding / Flat / Contracting — and since only about half the markets carry a current read, the grid ran ragged: some cards ended in a red or green word, the rest just stopped. The subtitle is the figures again. Nothing was taken off the page: the momentum map directly above the grid is still coloured by the same read, its legend still names all three words, and typing one into the filter box still narrows the grid to those markets.

title: A double-clicked Buy can no longer become two subscriptions
details: Checkout now sends Stripe an idempotency key, so two requests carrying the same purchase get one subscription instead of two. The failure it prevents is the quiet kind: org_subscriptions is keyed on the firm, so a second subscription would overwrite the first and the firm would be billed twice while every screen still showed one plan. The key is a hash of the request itself rather than a hand-assembled string, which is what makes the other half safe — Stripe refuses a key reused with different parameters, and the fields that vary are easy to miss by hand (the return origin differs between two hostnames, and the customer field changes shape the moment a customer record exists). Buying more seats later is a different request, so it gets a different key and still works. It does not stop somebody buying a second subscription on purpose; a firm that already has one should be sent to its billing portal, which is a separate change.

title: The momentum map reads like a picture of the country instead of a grey band
details: A look pass on the /markets map after the basemap moved to Esri. Four changes, each answering something visible in a screenshot. Place labels now come off below zoom 6: at national zoom Esri's Reference layer writes UNITED STATES in tracked capitals across the middle of the country and labels Toronto, Monterrey and Havana, none of which this map is about and all of it competing with the pins for the same few pixels — and since clicking a pin flies to zoom 11, the labels arrive exactly when they start being useful (which street, which suburb) rather than never. The frame is taller, 460px against 320px, because the continental US in a squat band read as a detail crop of a bigger map rather than a national picture; phones keep 300px. The fit gets modest padding so the outermost markets are not pressed against the edge. And the tile pane carries a slight contrast lift, because Esri's Light Gray Canvas is built to disappear under data, which at this zoom left land and sea the same tone and the country with no shape at all — scoped to this map, so the market pages' comp map, read at street zoom where the flat canvas is correct, is untouched. One thing tried and rejected on the evidence: fractional zoom (zoomSnap 0) frames the pins beautifully tight and then scales every tile off the pixel grid, leaving hairline seams straight across the map, which is worst on exactly these wide flat greys. The framing is solved by the frame's own height instead, so the fit lands a whole level up rather than falling back to one.

title: Every map drops CARTO for Esri — the “API KEY REQUIRED” watermark is gone
details: CARTO began requiring an API key for its raster basemaps and stamping “API KEY REQUIRED” diagonally across every unauthenticated tile, so every map this product draws was wearing it: the report map, the address-confirm map, the market pages' comp maps, the new /markets momentum map — and, worst of all, the printed and PNG reports a broker hands a client. CARTO also says the raster endpoints are being retired, so buying a key would have bought time rather than a fix. All five call sites now use Esri's Light/Dark Gray Canvas, which is keyless, needs no account and no secret to rotate, and is already this codebase's provider for satellite aerials and imagery — one vendor instead of two. Two things about Esri that will bite anyone editing this: it numbers tiles {z}/{y}/{x}, ROW before column, where every other tile URL here is {z}/{x}/{y}, and getting it backwards mirrors the world into a plausible-looking map of nowhere; and the Canvas base carries no place labels, which are a second Reference layer drawn over it, exactly as satellite imagery has always been paired with its own label overlay. Both are pinned by tests, along with a rule that no keyless CARTO raster URL may return to either file. The print path needed its own answer: CARTO served an @2x retina twin and that spare detail is what made the exported map ~330dpi at the printed width, and Esri has no @2x. The sharpness now comes from zoom instead — one level deeper, where each 256px tile covers half the ground, drawn into a half-size box — so a printed report is exactly as crisp as before, at four times the tiles on an export path that already budgets its time and tolerates a tile failing. Verified in a browser rather than argued: the finished raster matches the tile that should cover its centre with a mean pixel difference of 0.7, against 4.5 for a deliberately transposed control.

title: The momentum map's pre-ship pass: cards carry the word, and every failure degrades
details: A six-angle review of the whole momentum-map branch before shipping it, and the punch list it produced. The visible half: every /markets card now carries its market's momentum word beside the median, in the same colours the pins and badges use, and the word joins the filter haystack so typing “expanding” narrows the grid — the cards were the last market-listing surface saying nothing about direction. The Mixed legend swatch was a green/red split gradient that no shape on the map ever wore; it now matches what a mixed city actually draws, a grey wash inside an ink ring. The invisible half is most of it. cityBoundary refuses a file that parses to null (which would have thrown on every market-page request, i.e. a restart loop) and no longer memoizes a failed read. The market page's map gained the missing window.L guard its sibling always had, so a blocked CDN hides the card instead of leaving an empty rectangle, and its boundary draw is isolated so a degenerate stored geometry costs the shape and never the comp pins. A failed boundary fetch on /markets is no longer remembered for the life of the page — one blip on flaky wifi used to disable every later pin click — and a present-but-undrawable boundary now falls through to the anchored card instead of making the click do nothing. A boundary-only market page stops paying a geocoder round trip to sanity-gate zero pins, and if every comp fails to geocode the card retracts its own “Pins are geocoded…” copy rather than describing pins that are not there. The pin de-stacking groups on the city key rather than rounded coordinates, so two markets of one Explorer city with slightly different stored points still spread instead of hiding each other. The areas blob stopped re-serialising per-market rows the pins already carry. check-market-freshness now fails when reads have ALREADY expired (its header always claimed it did) and refuses a bad --warn-days instead of silently using 30. The monthly Market heroes workflow now fetches city boundaries too, so an Explorer-published city gets its photograph and its shape in one reviewed PR. And the two style functions that must agree across the two maps carry ⚠ MIRROR comments plus a test that pins them, including that every direction word reaches both.

title: Every market page draws its own city, coloured by that market's momentum
details: The market page's comp map now carries the city's real municipal boundary under the pins, shaded to match the Momentum badge already sitting in that card's heading — so the badge and the shape state the same thing by construction, both reading the one freshDirection gate the Explorer dropdown and the /markets pins read. This is where the three entry points converge: searching, clicking a directory card, and clicking a map pin all land here, and the summary, the comps and the coloured area are now one page rather than three places. An unread market keeps its boundary and is OUTLINED rather than shaded, because the wash is a claim and there is nothing to claim; the disclosure line says which it is and why. A market whose comps are all quoted at the submarket level used to get no map at all — it now gets one, headed "Where this market is" instead of "Where these comps are", because a boundary alone still answers that and a heading over zero pins should not claim otherwise. The geometry is inlined in the page's own blob rather than fetched: this page needs one city's shape (314 bytes for Ontario, ~6KB average) where the shared file is 107KB of all of them, and the page already caches for an hour — the opposite trade from the /markets map, for the opposite reason. The view fits the boundary AND the pins together, since a comp just outside the city limit is ordinary and fitting the pins alone would crop the shape the card is describing. A city with no stored boundary renders exactly as it did before any of this existed.

title: Click a momentum-map pin and the city's real carved boundary appears
details: Clicking a pin on the /markets momentum map now opens the city: the view flies in, the city's actual municipal boundary appears washed in its momentum color — Ontario's real city limits in red, the wash stopping at the line where the data's claim stops, which is exactly what a circle or a pin can't say — and a card opens listing every market there, each a link to its market page. The pins stay at every zoom (they are the navigation and the keyboard surface), revealed cities accumulate as you click around, and a click is never a dead end: with no stored boundary, or the boundary file unreachable, the same card still opens anchored to the pin. The boundaries are real OSM administrative polygons, fetched once by scripts/fetch-city-bounds.js and committed as city-bounds.json (the market-heroes rule: Render wipes its disk, and a page surface never waits on a network call at render time); the browser buys the ~110KB file on the first click, never on page load. Carving surfaced a question pins never faced: one city shape can hold markets moving opposite ways (Phoenix industrial expands while its multifamily contracts), so a new pure module, market-area.js, owns the answer — agreement colors the shape, disagreement is a fifth Mixed state with a split green/red legend swatch, no readings is a dashed outline making no claim, and an unread market never turns an agreeing city mixed, because absence of data is not a disagreement. Alongside: dark mode learned to style Leaflet tooltips (both twinned blocks — every hover card was white on dark pages), the map script gained an executed vm test in test/market-map.test.js's mold, and scripts/check-market-freshness.js plus a weekly workflow now watch the one cliff this feature makes visible — every seeded momentum read expires on the same day, 2026-10-12 as of this entry, and the only real fix is a seed regeneration.

title: A US momentum map heads the markets directory
details: /markets now opens with a map of the country, one pin per covered market, colored by the same expanding/flat/contracting read the Explorer dropdown and each market page's map-card badge already show — green expanding, grey flat, red contracting, and a hollow outline for a market with no current read, because “we don't know” must never render as “the market is flat.” Pins click through to the market page, tooltips carry the median $/SF, and a legend names all four states. No geocoding and no new endpoint: every point comes from the committed city-coordinate chain the hero photographs already resolve (now exported as MARKETHERO.coordsFor), and direction comes only through freshDirection, so the map, the dropdown and the badge can never disagree. Two property types in one city spread on a fixed pixel ring instead of hiding each other, and the pins carry visually-hidden labels because Leaflet's alt option never reaches a divIcon.

title: Paste a list of addresses into the search and it values all of them
details: Bulk valuation is no longer a place you go, it is what the search does when you give it a list. Pasting two or more addresses into the main address box opens list mode — the pasted list in a box, one property type for the run, the ordinary lookback — and the run then renders inline where a report would go, rows filling in live, sizes editable, CSV and cancel in place. Its two links are gone: the account-menu entry went on 2026-08-24 and the "Have a list? Value them all" link beside the form goes now, because a feature reached by pasting needs no link. /bulk is unchanged and still holds the history, the CSV upload and every earlier run, and the inline view links to it. The architectural rule is that the run view has exactly ONE source: bulk-page.js renders it, /bulk uses it directly, and index.html receives the same bytes at a BULK_RUN marker replaced at serve time — the NAV_LINKS / INAPP_BOOT / AUTH_BOOT pattern, never a hand-copy, because two copies of a totals strip would eventually quote two different portfolio values for one run. Three things that pattern forced and are worth knowing: the run view's DOM ids are all prefixed bk, since index.html already owns short generic ones (its password overlay is #gate) and rows/msg/run were one refactor from colliding; its CSS carries a fallback on every colour, because /bulk is dressed in marketShell and gets the site tokens while index.html never does — measured in a browser afterwards, it inherits index.html's own palette and follows dark mode for free; and the module now reads no form at all, reporting state through an injected callback instead, because its render used to dereference the /bulk textarea and would have thrown on a page that has neither. A paste is data and never consent to spend: it opens a form and nothing else, the billed call sits behind the button, and that is pinned by test the same way the landing-address handoff is. A visitor without bulk access keeps the first address of what they pasted, so the paste is not thrown away, and is shown the ordinary Pro pitch. Two bugs the checks caught before anyone saw them: an error colour with no dark rule, and five Tailwind utilities (font-mono, resize-y, normal-case, tracking-normal, ml-2) that are not in the vendored build and would have silently styled nothing — the list box is plain CSS in the page's own stylesheet now, and deliberately sets no font-size, because .rd-in pins 16px to stop iOS Safari auto-zooming on focus.

title: A failed extraction run reports why it failed instead of crashing on top of it
details: The extraction harness gates the whole Archive block, and it says whether a run may be read as a verdict through its exit code: 0 means every file scored, 2 means something was excluded and the figures cover only part of the set, 1 means it never ran. On Windows a failed sign-in produced none of those. It printed the real reason correctly and then aborted with a libuv assertion and exit code -1073740791, because it called process.exit() the instant the response came back, while the HTTP sockets were still closing. Reproduced against production, not reasoned about. The sign-in failures now throw and the top level sets an exit code rather than pulling the process down, so Node closes its handles and leaves with the code the harness meant. A test reads the script and fails the build if a process.exit() ever appears after a fetch again, while leaving the pre-flight exits alone, since a dry run that reports its plan and stops has opened nothing. Also recorded, from the same session: a comp sheet row reading "Feb 2026" is extracted as 2026-02-01, silently, and imports as a day-precise date. The prompt both requires YYYY-MM-DD and forbids inventing a date, and the model resolves that by inventing the day. It has to be settled before the truth file is keyed, because it lands on the fabrication rate, and fabrication is the one number the spec calls fatal on its own.

title: The sample report states a search radius that covers its own comps
details: The sample a prospect reads before signing up claimed a search radius of “Immediate submarket, ~5 miles” while its comps sit 8 to 17 miles out, in Grand Prairie and Arlington. Nothing wrong reached the screen: the reconciliation shipped a day earlier spots exactly this and drops the claim rather than print it beside the measured distances. But that left the demo showing no search radius at all — the one report we control was relying on the product papering over its own data on every render, and quietly not demonstrating a line that real reports do show. The fixture now says “DFW mid-cities, ~20 miles”, which is true of its comps and matches the wording the sample summary already uses. A test computes the farthest comp from the sample’s own coordinates and fails the build if a future edit puts the claim back out of reach — deliberately stricter than the live check, which allows a quarter’s slack because a real search’s radius is an approximation, where ours is written by hand and should simply be right.

title: Two labels on the report stop crediting the wrong thing
details: Found by running the app and reading the screen. First: the "Your property vs. market" card printed its market average under the words "from pulled comps", and that figure is the search’s own market-level number, which deliberately does not recompute when you exclude a comp. So excluding one moved the value range, the trust line (which said in as many words that one comp had been excluded by you), the table footer and the spread bar — and left this card quoting the same average, credited to the very comps that had just changed, then computing your pricing position against it. On the sample that read "median of 3 sale comps · $110/SF" in the footer and "$113 · from pulled comps" a few inches above: two figures claiming one source, with nothing on screen saying which to believe. The label now places the figure at the market rather than at your comp set, which is both true and an answer to the question the old one provoked. Display only — no number moved. Second: the Analysis tab told you to "enter an NOI in Property details above", and the form has not had a section by that name since it was retitled "Details for comps", so the one instruction for unlocking those tools named nothing on the page. It names the real section now, and a test pins it to the form’s own label so a future retitle fails the build instead of stranding the sentence again.

title: The extraction scorer stops failing rows the vault would accept
details: The scorer that decides whether we build the Archive was marking correct extractions wrong. Its own rule is that it must never fail a row the importer would accept, and it compares values through the vault's real parsers so that "$1,250,000" and 1250000 count as one value. But it only routed six kinds of field that way; four more that the vault does parse fell through to plain text comparison. Found by running a real extraction against production: a lease quoted at $1.29/SF/mo came back with a rent basis of "/mo" against a truth keyed as "monthly", and scored as a wrong value — while the vault's own parser reads "/mo" as monthly and stores exactly the figure that was keyed. The same held for lease type ("Triple Net" against "NNN") and for both lease dates, which went through as text while the deal date was parsed. Lease expiry and option notice feed the renewal watch, and every lease row in the twenty-file verdict would have carried the same false failure, against a pass condition deliberately fixed before the numbers arrive — so a leasing-heavy set could have read as a fail when the extraction was right. The four fields now compare through the same parsers the vault uses, a genuinely different value is still wrong, and a test reads the vault's own normalizer and fails the build if a field it parses is ever left out of the scorer again.

title: Bulk valuation's door moved out of the vault grouping, beside the search form
details: The only two doors to /bulk were the account menus, where “Bulk valuation” sat directly under “Your vault” — the server-rendered copy even carried the vault's own CSS class — so a tool for running fifty searches read as a corner of the broker's private data store, and nobody standing at the search form learned it existed. Owner's call: out of the vault, discoverable, without ruining the homepage look. The link now lives in the search form's quiet action row as “Have a list? Value them all”, styled exactly like its neighbours (“View a sample report”, “No address? Find one” — the Address Explorer link that already made this row the home for Pro-discovered doors), and both account-menu copies are gone. Same visibility rule as before, only the location changed: it ships hidden and is revealed off canBulkValue — the Buy-button rule — so an anonymous visitor and a free member see a byte-identical row, which is what “without ruining the homepage look” cashes out to. One cascade fact makes the hidden shipping safe and is verified against the vendored tailwind.css rather than assumed: the display utilities end with .hidden, so it beats the link's own inline-flex — the same ordering the menu links' “hidden block” always relied on.

title: The installed desktop app stops offering to download itself
details: The shell was tagged desktop-v1.0.0 at 22:29 on 2026-08-20 and its installers were built a minute later; the commit that taught it to identify itself to the site landed at 00:32 the next morning, two hours after the release. It is the only commit that has touched desktop-app/ since, so every installer anyone has downloaded is missing the one thing it added — the CompNinjaDesktop/ user-agent token. The site's own half has been live the whole time, and it checks four signals: display-mode standalone, window-controls-overlay, navigator.standalone, and that token. Electron reports display-mode browser (measured, Electron 43), sets no titleBarStyle so window-controls-overlay never fires, and navigator.standalone is Safari-only — so in the shipped build none of the four are true, data-inapp is never set, and the Explore menu of the desktop app still carries "Download the app". Installed PWAs were never affected, because they match display-mode standalone; this was Electron-only. Nothing is broken by it and nothing about the site changes here: the app holds no product code, so it has always been current with every deploy. What was stale was the binary, and the fix is a release rather than an edit. Version bumped to 1.0.1 so the new installers do not report themselves as the same build as the old ones — the artifact names are deliberately version-less, so the /download links do not move and need no edit.

title: The market box's example rotates, and can no longer cost a billed search
details: The Explorer's box carried one hardcoded example forever. It stopped being decoration last change, when Tab began typing it in — so it is a working query now, and it rotates through the 27 seeded markets on every page load, round-robin across the four types so three refreshes do not show three industrials. Rotating turned up a real hazard in the fixed example it replaces: industrial-boise-id is NOT in market-seed.json. It exists in production only because somebody explored that market once, and a market with no standing page turns the dropdown's top row into “Explore this market, build the … page →” — so Tab then Enter would have spent a billed search and 30-60 seconds on a build nobody asked for the moment that page aged out. The rotation reads MARKET_PAGES, the committed seed, which getMarketPage always resolves with no database read, so every example is guaranteed free navigation. Substituted at serve time like NAV_LINKS and AUTH_BOOT, and fails safe: it replaces a whole attribute, so if index.html's copy ever drifts the replace no-ops and the static example stands (which is why the fallback in the markup is now a seeded market too). It advances a counter rather than picking at random, so a fresh process always serves entry 0, and MARKET_EXAMPLE pins it outright — scripts/shot.js sets that on both sides of a comparison, because byte-identical PNGs are how “this changed nothing visually” gets proved here. The Tab handler needed no change at all: it reads the placeholder at keypress time, so it types whatever the server chose.

title: Tab fills the market box with the example it is showing
details: The Explorer's search box says “e.g. industrial Boise, ID” and there was no way to take it up on that. Pressing Tab in an empty box now types that query in and opens the dropdown, so Tab then Enter reads a market from a standing start. It only fires while the box is EMPTY and never on Shift+Tab — Tab is the focus key, and taking it from somebody who has typed half a market would trap them in the field. The example is read off the placeholder rather than kept as a second copy of the string, so the two can never disagree about what Tab is about to type. The placeholder itself began rotating in the same release, and Tab needed no change to follow it.

title: The header gear is gone; Settings lives in the account menu
details: The settings panel shipped with two doors — a gear in the header bar and a Settings row in the account menu — and the gear was the redundant one for everybody who could see both. The header is back to Explore / Pricing / My Desk / account circle, and the account menu is now the single door. The panel is therefore signed-in only, which costs a signed-out reader of a shared report the in-app theme switch; every server-rendered header still carries its own toggle, the choice persists across both, and light is the default either way.

title: The search form asks for an address and nothing else
details: Running a report meant answering four questions before the page would do anything: Focus, Lookback, Property SF and a details drawer. The app already held an answer to three of them — two have defaults, the lookback prints "Recommended for Industrial" underneath itself, and the size is looked up from public records or the building footprint on most searches. So the form was asking questions it could answer. Those three now sit behind one line that states what they currently say — "Sales & leases · last 24 months · size from public records" — with Change to open them. Nothing was removed and nothing about the search itself moved: every control is one click away, keeps its behaviour, and the line rewrites itself the moment any of the three changes, including when a saved report or a looked-up building size fills them in. Also fixed on the way past: when a size was estimated from the footprint, the note offering to correct it pointed at "Details for comps", which has not held that field since it moved back onto the form a week earlier.

title: A settings panel, and light mode becomes the default
details: The header gear (where the theme icon sat) opens one panel holding the theme control, the visitor's plan with the upgrade and billing-portal buttons, a watchlist digest email toggle, and the account controls — Change photo and Delete account moved here from the account dropdown, the delete behind a proper two-step confirm whose copy now names the vault. The digest toggle is the first in-app control that column has ever had (it was email-unsubscribe-only) and writes through a new session-authenticated POST /api/account/digest; the email link still works and the panel re-reads /me on every open so the two never disagree. Light is now the default on every surface: the boot scripts no longer consult prefers-color-scheme, so a first visit is light on a dark-OS machine and dark happens only by choosing it — a stored choice keeps working, and scripts/shot.js --dark now seeds that choice since the emulated media query stopped producing a dark render. The plan row hides on a deployment where nothing is for sale rather than describe caps a dark deployment does not impose. Pricing keeps its header link; the panel is a second door, not a relocation.

title: Refreshing while signed in no longer flashes a signed-out app
details: index.html ships one set of bytes to everybody and then corrects them from /api/config and /api/account/me, so until those landed a signed-in member was looking at a signed-OUT app. Measured with the account read deliberately slowed: at 78ms the header reads "Sign in", and at 1170ms — the frame where config has answered and the account read has not — the search form is replaced by the wall's "Create a free account to run a report" card. Then it all snaps back. It is a race, so it is worst exactly when the database is slow, and it hit Pro and free accounts alike. The fix is not a faster fetch: the `/` handler already knew both answers and was throwing them away. It templates that file at serve time anyway (NAV_LINKS, INAPP_BOOT), so authBoot() rides along as one more marker and carries two facts that cost no database read — the wall, which is a server constant, and whether a session cookie came with the request, which is the exact rule the wall itself decides on. Safe to key on a cookie only because index.html is served no-store; /how-it-works does the same swap and has to carry `vary: cookie` to do it. It is a stand-in, not an answer: refreshAccountUI() — the one function that runs after /api/account/me on every path including the failed one — drops both classes and writes the truth itself, which is what makes the !important safe. Without that retirement an expired session would leave the "Sign in" button hidden by CSS the JS cannot reach, i.e. a member who cannot sign back in; that case is tested, and it corrects to the signed-out chrome as it should. applySearchLock() now reads the hint through looksSignedIn() rather than currentUser alone, and accountWall arrives with the page instead of a fetch later — that pair is what fixes the big flash, since the card appeared precisely because that function ran once with the wall off and once with it on. Shared-report readers get the same benefit from the other side: /r/<id> is one of only two doors the wall leaves open to the app, and it now paints the signup card immediately instead of showing a search form that vanishes.

title: Two stray tables from a mis-pasted migration are gone from the scratch project
details: 036-bulk-valuations.sql was first pasted into the wrong Supabase PROJECT — the empty default account project, which nothing reads — where it reported Success and created bulk_jobs and bulk_job_items in a database no code has ever pointed at. It was then run correctly in "Market comp puller" and verified there, so the feature itself was never affected; the two empty tables were simply left behind, and migrations/APPLIED.md has said so since. They are now dropped, and that row records what happened rather than describing a loose end. The part worth keeping is how the right project was identified, because every obvious signal is useless here: no database names its own project ref, both answer to the database name postgres, and the dashboard breadcrumb shows a main PRODUCTION chip in BOTH — that is a database BRANCH label, not a project one, and reading it as a project name is the same class of mistake as trusting the original Success message. The proof was content instead: production carries users, comp_corpus and leads, and the scratch project held only the two bulk tables. The drop then re-checked that for itself, inside a do block that raises rather than drops if it finds any of those three production tables or a single row in either bulk table — so the same SQL pasted into the still-open production tab would have refused instead of destroying live bulk valuation data. Confirmed afterwards by to_regclass returning null for both names and public holding zero tables, down from two.

title: Dark mode stopped painting black bars across the search form
details: In dark mode a blanket rule recessed every field on the site one step below the card it sits on, which is right for a bordered input and wrong for the Research Desk, where the CELL is the field: .rd-cell draws the hairline box and owns the red focus ring, and .rd-in is deliberately borderless and transparent so the form reads as one unit. The two together put a near-black slab under Property address, Focus, Lookback and Property SF -- four bars floating on the form. Those four fields now stay the colour of the cell in dark exactly as they do in light. Every genuinely bordered input on the site, the Market Explorer's included, keeps its recess. The exemption is a :not(.rd-in) on the existing rule rather than an override under it, because that selector carries eight :not([type=...]) and outranks any plain .rd-in rule; autofill follows it and covers the desk's fields with the cell's own colour, since Chrome's sheet is UA-!important and only an inset shadow beats it.

title: The onboarding docs pointed new contributors at the wrong API key
details: A fresh clone followed ONBOARDING.md, put an ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in .env, ran npm start, and got a server that boots, serves every page, and cannot run a single search — because the default provider has been Gemini since 2026-08-10 and nothing in .env.example or the onboarding guide mentioned GEMINI_API_KEY. The banner names the missing variable, but only in the terminal a first-timer has already scrolled past. .env.example now leads with the key the default provider actually needs, says the project must be on a paid Google tier, and gives the free models-list curl that proves a key works without spending anything — including the warning that the key does not necessarily start "AIza", which cost an afternoon of hunting for a key that did not exist. ONBOARDING.md is corrected to match on four further points it had drifted on: the cache window is 30 days not 7, a search costs about $0.36 not $0.75, the suite is a couple of thousand tests in ten seconds rather than a handful in one, and the call deadline is derived per search rather than a fixed 100 seconds. The free four-comp cap it described was retired in August. HANDOFF.md, which still called hosting the next step and named a retired model, is now a signpost to the documents that are actually maintained rather than a third decaying copy of the project description.

title: A hub invitation that could not be sent no longer reports itself as sent
details: Creating a hub, or adding somebody to one, told the broker "each person has been emailed their link" whenever the mail settings were configured. It never asked whether the mail actually went. The send was fire-and-forget and a rejection from the mail provider reached nothing but a log on the server, so a refused invitation and a delivered one looked identical from the app. On the hub page that cost more than a wrong sentence: the People panel hides the invite links when it believes they were mailed, and a hub link cannot be shown a second time, so a refused send destroyed the invitation and reported success. The send is now awaited and the flag is its real answer, per person: anyone the mail provider would not accept keeps their link on screen, and the panel says plainly that they could not be emailed. A hub still cannot fail to be created because of a mail problem, which was the original reason the send was abandoned rather than awaited. Also: the hub and firm invitations phrase the free-account line the way the report-share invitation always has, so three emails from one product stop reading as three.

title: A failed read on the desk says the same reassuring thing everywhere
details: When the desk cannot load your shared reports it hides those sections rather than pretending you have none, which is right and was already the case. What it said was thinner than the portfolio's version of the same failure: one bare line naming the failure, where the portfolio adds that nothing has been lost and to refresh in a moment. The shares line covers the sections that name colleagues and their work, so it is the one where a bare could-not-load reads most like somebody's shared reports having gone missing. Both now say what failed and then that nothing is gone.

title: A firm keeps its own tenant list
details: Your firm page now has a contacts list: name, email, company and a note, typed in one at a time or imported from a CSV. It is shared with everyone in the firm, and each row shows who added it. The one thing it will never do is fill itself in from CompNinja, and that was a condition of building it rather than an afterthought — enquiries that come through this product are routed by the owner and stripped of the enquirer's name, email, phone and address before any broker sees them, and a tenant who agreed to talk to one broker through one message hub did not thereby agree to join that firm's list. So the list holds what the firm typed or imported, and there is deliberately no button anywhere that would change that. The import refuses a row rather than cleaning it up: these are addresses somebody is going to mail, so a mangled one is a message to a stranger or to nobody with the sender believing it arrived. Each refusal names the line number and quotes what was actually in the cell. Two smaller judgments worth knowing. A contact with no email address is perfectly normal and imports fine, but it is never merged with another — two people who share a name may be two people, and quietly deleting one of them is worse than leaving a duplicate somebody can remove. And an email that is already on the list is recognised and reported rather than added twice, so re-importing the same file does not double anything that can be identified.

title: The valuation block leads with the method that produced the number
details: A report lists three valuation approaches and usually only one of them ran. The other two said so at length, and the cost approach spent forty words explaining why nobody models it, so reading top to bottom two thirds of the block was about methods that did not run and the method behind the headline was outnumbered on its own statement. The figures lead now and the approaches that produced no figure collapse behind one line. They are not dropped: an unrun approach is a real disclosure about how the number was reached, it is one click away, and it is always fully shown on a printed report and in an exported image, because those are the copies that get forwarded.

title: A colleague who leaves the firm stops showing up twice on the deal board
details: When somebody deleted their CompNinja account, the firm's deal board split them into two rows: their shared comps kept their name, because that name is copied onto the comp at the moment it is shared, while their shared reports lost it entirely, because there the name was only ever looked up from an account record that no longer exists. The totals were right and the roster was not, and it read as two people where there had been one. The report now carries the same snapshot the comp always has. Two smaller decisions inside it. The stored name is a name and never an email address, matching what the comp side already does: the shelf will fall back to showing an email while an account still exists, but persisting one here would outlive the account it belongs to, which is the opposite of what deleting an account ought to mean. And the live account wins over the snapshot wherever there still is one, which is the reverse of how report branding works and is deliberate: a letterhead should look the way it looked when it was sent, while an attribution should say what a colleague is called today, so fixing a typo in your profile updates your own shelf rows rather than leaving the old spelling behind. It cannot be backfilled, because the names it would need belong to accounts that are already gone, so this fixes the split for anybody who leaves from here on.

title: The download counter stops sounding like a cap on running reports
details: The line under a report's export buttons read "5 downloads left this month · reports are unlimited". Both halves were true and they were joined by a middot, which everywhere else on the site separates facets of one thing, so a reader met a number and the word unlimited in the same breath and had to work out which applied to what. It is two sentences now: what is metered, then what is not. The second sentence is not decoration and should not be cut, because it is the only reason the first is not read as a limit on running reports, which is exactly how the original wording was misread.

title: The renewal watch: one email before a lease deadline, with what comparable space rents for
details: Put a lease expiry and an option-notice date on a comp in your vault and you get one email 90 days before the deadline, naming the building, the date, how many days are left, what that lease pays and what comparable space is quoting in the same market. Filling the two dates in is the whole opt-in; leaving them blank changes nothing about how the vault behaves. It rides the watchlist digest's existing run rather than adding a second schedule, so whatever already triggers that triggers this, and it inherits every one of that feature's refusals: it will not run without a database, and it refuses outright rather than sending blind when outbound email is not configured, because running blind would mark every lease as told and delete a reminder nobody received. The judgments worth knowing are all about when NOT to send. One email per lease, ever. Nothing at all once a deadline has passed, because a message about a date that already went by is not a reminder, it is a notification of a loss the reader can do nothing about. And a lease that records only an expiry with no option notice is described as expiring rather than being told notice is owed, because that would be a wrong statement about somebody's own contract. The market comparison is a decoration and never a gate: when there is no rent figure for that market the email still goes, carrying the deadline alone, because the deadline is the part that matters and staying quiet over a missing nice-to-have would be the worst possible trade. The two figures sit side by side with no verdict drawn between them, quoted in whichever basis the broker recorded the lease in, and the broker's own rate prints exactly as they typed it while the market median is rounded, because one is a number in a contract and the other is a median over public comps.

title: A leases-only report headlines the rent, not a missing sale price
details: Run a search with Leases only and the top of the report used to show three dashes under Low, Likely and High, say "No priced sale comps came back in this window", and offer a button to re-run the whole thing as sales. The search had worked. The comps were right there in the table. The report was just answering a question nobody asked, and it cost a billed search to find that out. A leases-only report now headlines the rent range, reads "What This Building Rents For", and says what that costs at your size: at 5,000 SF, about $68,000 to $75,000 a year before pass-throughs. It quotes the market back in its own basis, so where the comps are quoted monthly, as California industrial and retail are, the tiles read $1.18 per SF/mo rather than $14.10 per SF/yr. The figure underneath is annual either way and is divided only for display, which is the vault's own rule about rent basis: one canonical number, because a book holding two bases quotes three rents for one lease. The basis is read off how the comps themselves are quoted rather than guessed from the address, and anything short of real evidence stays annual. The range is the same function the market pages have used since the market snapshot shipped, reached from the browser rather than copied, so a report and a market page cannot disagree about one building or about whether a rate quoted monthly is a rate quoted annually. It under-claims the way the rest of the report does: two priced leases minimum, never a range built from one, and below four it says out loud that it is a rough guide. The furniture around it follows the same noun, so the chart caption counts lease comps and the disclaimer names comparable leases. The offer underneath follows the same noun: a lease report asks "Talk to a local leasing broker" rather than offering a Broker Opinion of Value, which is a sale price and read as the report disowning the rent it had just published. Only the words change. The introduction is requested, stored and routed exactly as it always was, the same way a house report already asks for a local agent instead. The note explaining how the range was calculated follows too. It used to say that recent, nearby, similar comps count for more and that prices are indexed to the market's trend, which is how the SALE range is built and not how this one is: every priced lease comp counts the same, and the range is the middle half of them. On a house that rents it also dropped the line about residential sales living in the MLS, which is a statement about sale listings and not about rentals. Every rate on the page also says which rate it is now. Where the headline is quoted monthly, the comp table's column and the Market Avg tile still hold the annual figure, so both are labelled $/SF/yr rather than left as a bare $/SF a few inches under a monthly headline. The figures themselves are not converted: that column is shared with sale reports and feeds sorting and the exports, and one column meaning two different things depending on the report is the mistake the vault refuses to make.

title: Tenant rep is a third kind of shop
details: A firm could say it was a broker shop or a development shop. It can now say it is a tenant rep shop, and the product answers in that job's nouns: the invite email and the desk both tell a tenant rep firm its shelf holds lease abstracts, rent comps and market surveys, where a broker shop reads comp sets and BOVs and a development shop reads land comps and feasibility packets. The option is in both places the question is asked, when the firm is created and in its settings afterwards, and changing it is still an owner or admin call because it re-labels every colleague's desk. One deliberate difference from the other two: a development shop's shelf opens filtered to Land, and a tenant rep's opens on everything. Land earned that default because exactly one property type names a development shop's subject, and nothing names a tenant rep's - office, industrial and retail tenant reps are all normal, so any single default would open two shops out of three on a shelf that looks like it lost rows. Nothing is gated on the new kind and nothing is published by it. Existing firms are untouched: broker is still the column default and still what an unrecognized value reads as, so the only way into the new kind is somebody choosing it.

title: The deal board: who shared what to the firm, by market and by month
details: A firm page now shows what its members have put on the shelf — reports and comps opted in from a vault — grouped by person, by market and by month, with a most-shared list for this month and this quarter. It reads only data that was already attributed at the moment it was shared, so there are no new tables and no read was widened; the counting itself lives in a pure module that npm test covers. The one thing it deliberately does not answer is "who is closing what", and the panel says so in as many words: a member's own book and their won and lost log are private to that member, not to the firm, and the only honest number available is what somebody chose to share. That is also the better incentive — a leaderboard of closings rewards the quarter someone happened to have, while this one rewards filling the shelf every colleague reads. Three smaller judgments are worth knowing because they are the ones that would otherwise produce a wrong number that looks right: two colleagues who have left are never merged into one row just because neither has a name left; a share whose date cannot be read still counts in the totals but is declared rather than quietly dropped from the month breakdown; and the month is when something was shared, not when the deal closed, so importing a decade of old deals shows up as this month's contribution instead of vanishing.

title: The home page stops calling our own archive a stale database
details: Method step I on the landing page read "Public records, listings, and news are searched at request time, not read from a stale database." It was written when a live web search was the whole product and it had stopped being true: corpus-first retrieval runs on every cache miss before anything is billed, and its rows are offered to the model, so every search DOES read what we already hold first. Archive-first retrieval landed the same day, putting the searcher's own vault above the corpus. So the line was telling visitors that reading stored comps is the shoddy way to do this, on a page selling a product whose stored comps are the asset. It now reads "We check what we already hold, then search public records, listings and news for anything missing." The heading stays "Search live" on the owner's call: the live search is still the front door and this is a correction, not a repositioning. Nothing else on the page changed, and no other surface carried the phrase.

title: The search radius stops contradicting the comp distances below it
details: A report printed the search model's claimed radius ("Search radius: Immediate submarket, ~5 miles") and then, two lines below, the distances measured from real geocodes ("Located comps sit 13 mi to 20 mi from your property"). Nothing reconciled them, so a reader met two statements about the same thing and had no way to know which to believe. Measurement wins now: when the comps are found well outside the radius the search claimed, the claim gives way and the measured line stands alone. A radius is approximate by nature, so a claim that is merely close keeps its place, and a claim with no mileage in it, or a report whose comps never geocoded, is left exactly as it was.

title: Reports are three times faster, and the comps in them are better sourced
details: A report used to take about 34 seconds; it now takes about 10, and costs a third of what it did ($29.56 to roughly $9.50 per thousand). The change is that the model reasons less before it answers — on this provider thinking was seven of every eight tokens it generated, so it was the whole clock, and every trim to the report itself had been fighting over the other eighth. Measured across four runs before anything was switched, with the full record in docs/evals. What it costs is honest and worth stating: reports come back with about a third fewer comps, and roughly one in five now shows a wider value range because it has fewer priced sales behind it. What it gains beyond the speed is that the comps which do come back are better evidence — the share that could not be tied to a real source fell from as high as one in seven to one in fifty, the best this measurement has ever recorded, and every property in the test set could still be valued. An attempt to have it both ways, by asking the model to keep hunting for more comps, was tried and rejected: it bought almost no extra comps and more than doubled the unsourced rate, which is the one trade this product should never make.

title: The eval's spend preview quotes what will actually run
details: It multiplied the per-type number by six, but the target set is lopsided — four Industrial against one Land and one Residential — so --per-type 2 yields ten targets, not twelve, and the preview quoted $0.74 for a run that costs about $0.62. Over-quoting is the safe direction and nothing was overcharged, but a spend estimate that does not match what runs is the kind of small inaccuracy that stops people trusting the preview at all, and the preview is the only thing standing between somebody and an unintended bill. It now counts the real set, capped per type, and falls back to the old approximation if the file cannot be read — a bad read should cost an approximate quote, never the run.

title: COMP_FLOOR — an answer to the one thing thinking less cost us
details: Measured on a 12-target eval: THINKING_LEVEL=low made reports 66% faster (34.3s to 11.6s) and 66% cheaper ($0.0296 to $0.0102), and returned a third fewer comps — 7.1 down to 4.8, priced sales 6.7 down to 4.5. Both moves are three to five times the run-to-run noise floor, so they are real. The surprise is that the shorter list was BETTER sourced: provenance up 8%, market match up 12%, and the unsourced-estimate rate down from 14% to 2%, the best this eval has recorded. So reasoning less does not find worse comps, it appears to stop looking sooner — satisficing at the low end of the prompt's own "find 3 to N". This adds a floor asking it to keep hunting to six, and the one thing it must never do is buy that count back by relaxing what counts as a comp: the instruction spends its words on searching harder and restates the anti-padding rules inside itself rather than trusting proximity to them, with a test that fails if that wording ever softens. Off by default, because it is a prompt change on the hot path and only worth carrying if the eval says it works. compare-thinking.js gained --candidate-env so the two arms can be run in one session at the same reasoning depth, which controls for the run-to-run wobble that comparing against a saved file does not.

title: The Markets link moved from the Explore menu to the Market Explorer
details: Browsing markets now starts where markets are searched: an “Our markets →” link sits under the Market Explorer's input on the app page, and “Markets” left the Explore menu on every header (one shared NAV_LINKS list feeds them all). Nothing is stranded — the footer on every page still links /markets, and market pages keep their own “All markets” breadcrumbs.

title: The site gets its width back, and Pricing comes out of the browse menu
details: Two site-wide bits of polish on top of the home page pass. The shared container went from 1024px to 1120px on every public server-rendered page (MARKET_CSS and HOW_CSS: the landing page, /markets, every /market/<slug>, /brokers, /1031-exchange, /terms, /privacy). 1120 is not a new number -- /vault has run at 1120 since it was built, so the widest surface in the product had already answered this; 1024 dates from before the market pages carried 3840px photographs and before the comp tables grew their per-type columns. The four dashboards and /bulk keep their own widths, and the signed-in app deliberately stays at max-w-5xl for now, since that container wraps the report itself. Separately, Pricing moved out of the Explore dropdown into the header bar on both front doors, sitting between Explore and Log in. It is the question a prospect arrives with, and a B2B site that keeps its price one click inside a browse menu reads as one that would rather not say. The visibility rule is untouched on both sides (ACCOUNT_NAV_JS's live && !isPro on server-rendered pages, refreshBillingUI's toggle in the app), so it still hides for a Pro member and on a deployment with no billing configured; the id, the hidden class and the click handler are all unchanged. Two things were checked rather than assumed: the dropdown-row utility classes #pricingLink used to carry are used on 40-plus other lines of index.html, so a tailwind purge still emits them for the server-injected NAV_LINKS (verified by regenerating and diffing, not by reading), and the fifth header item still fits one row at 390px with no overflow because the header learned to wrap earlier the same day.

title: The home page stops breaking its own numbers
details: Five layout faults on the logged-out landing page, all on first paint. The value ledger's LIKELY figure wrapped, stranding a lone "$" above "4,730,000": the scroll choreography splits that string into a "$" text node plus an inline-block span so the numeral can tick without shoving its cell, and the split manufactures a line-break opportunity the plain string never had. .fig takes white-space:nowrap and LIKELY takes flex:1.15, because eight digits at 22px measure 115px inside the 108px an even three-way split leaves. On a phone this sheet had no rule to stack the ledger at all, so all three cells stayed side by side at ~77px and drew every figure across three lines; it now folds at 639.98px, matching index.html's .rd-ledger rather than MARKET_CSS's 700px, because the exhibit is a miniature of the report and should fold where the report folds. The comp table overflowed its scroller by 26px and cut "Ridgeline CRE" off mid-word while the column beside it sat on 300px of dead air, so the hero grid hands the exhibit the wider half and the table fits exactly. The search row shrink-wrapped to 326px of a 502px column and the field to 187px, narrow enough to truncate its own placeholder.

title: Both home pages get the footer, the hero and the phone header they were missing
details: index.html carried a Follow column (Instagram, TikTok, X) and no other page did, so the only links to the company's own accounts sat behind the login and every indexable page ended in a footer naming no accounts at all. Follow moves into MARKET_FOOTER, reaching the landing page, every market page and /brokers at once. The landing page was also hand-keeping footer markup byte-identical to that constant, so it is now the constant: that block already carried a "keep the three in step" comment it had not been kept in step with once before. index.html's TikTok href was the raw share-sheet URL, whose "?_r=1%_t=" contains a bare % that is not a valid percent-escape; all three copies now use the plain profile URL. On the landing hero the badge key was a full-width strip spanning both columns while the column beside the exhibit sat empty, so it moves into the claim column where it also reads better, as a key beside the exhibit whose badges it decodes. On the signed-in home the hero stacked kicker, claim and lead down the left of a max-w-5xl band, leaving the right 450px empty and running 326px tall before the search form; the lead now sits beside the claim above 900px, which is 236px and brings the form up 90px. That page's header could not wrap either, so at 390px the theme toggle sat flush against the wordmark and both actions broke across two lines; it takes the same three rules server.js's .hdr already had.

title: Type a size on a bulk row and it re-values for free
details: The first real bulk run found 24 to 27 comparable sales on every address and a building size on only one in three, so two rows showed a $/SF range and no dollars. That is a gap bulk has by construction: valuing one property estimates the size from the building's footprint in your browser during the address confirmation, and a fifty-address run has no confirmation step to do it in. The Size column on a finished row is now a field you can type into. Enter a square footage and the row re-values instantly against the comparables already found — no new search, no charge, and the portfolio total and the saved property on My Desk both follow. It reads the report saved to your desk rather than going back through the search, deliberately: going back would be free today and would quietly start costing a search the day that entry expired, and a button that says it is free has to be free every time. Every finished row is editable, not only the ones missing a size, because a looked-up size that is wrong is the most expensive number in a report. A size that is not a number is refused rather than stored as a best guess. Alongside it, a real bug the work turned up: an unvalued row was exporting as $0 in the CSV instead of blank, because an empty database column reads back as zero — the screen was fine, the spreadsheet was not, and 'a failure is not $0' is the one rule this feature states out loud.

title: A comp ten miles out stops being graded Weak
details: Every comp in a report could read Match: Weak underneath a confident value range. The distance weighting gave a comp a free pass only out to the radius named in the market note, and that note is optional and almost always empty, so it fell back to one mile for every property type. Ten miles is what blend-corpus already treats as in-market for commercial, so the same 13-mile comp was folded into the report as in-market and then graded Weak by it. The fallback now matches. In the sample report the sale comps go from five Weak to three Fair and two Weak, and the value range moves slightly with them. Houses are unchanged at one mile.

title: Press Tab to fill the bulk box with example addresses
details: An empty paste box shows three greyed example addresses. Pressing Tab now drops them in as real text you can edit, so trying bulk valuation no longer means inventing three addresses first. There is a link beside the box that does the same thing, both because the shortcut has to be discoverable and because not everybody wants to reach for Tab. Two rules keep it from being annoying: it only fires while the box is EMPTY — the moment there is anything in it, Tab goes back to moving between fields as it always has, so the surprise can happen at most once and is visible when it does — and Shift+Tab is never touched, so tabbing backwards out of an empty box still works. Ctrl+Z undoes it like ordinary typing. The examples are read from the box's own placeholder rather than written out a second time, so the greyed text and the thing Tab inserts can never drift apart.

title: Bulk valuation has a daily ceiling, and the form says so before you paste
details: One run at a time bounds how many searches happen at once; it does not bound spend. A fifty-address run finishes in about seventeen minutes, so the next could start immediately — roughly $63 an hour of API credit, indefinitely, with nothing in the way. There is now a per-member daily ceiling of 200 addresses (raisable without a deploy). It is deliberately per member rather than charged to the site-wide daily search cap: one bulk run would have eaten a third of that cap and locked out the free visitors it exists to protect. It counts addresses that were actually attempted, so cancelling a run costs what ran rather than what was queued, and the remaining allowance is shown beside the per-run cap and in the hint under the Run button — so somebody with twelve left finds out while pasting rather than after deciding which forty addresses mattered. It fails open if the count itself fails: a paying member must not be locked out of a tool by one bad query.

title: The bulk worker is now proven end to end, not argued for
details: The bulk tests stopped exactly where the money started: with no API key in the test harness, every run was refused before a job was created, so everything from "a report came back" through valuing it, writing the row and putting it on My Desk had never actually executed. A test-only setting now lets the suite stand a stub search provider in front of the real one — the same trick the watchlist digest uses to prove an email really left the building — and a new test runs a whole job through it: the search, the valuation, the desk write, the comp harvest, the cache write, and the job finishing. It also pins the two things that cost real money if they are wrong: two addresses buy exactly two searches, and re-running the same list buys none. And one failed address costs that row and not the run, with the vendor's own error text never reaching the member. Production is untouched by this — the override is unset there, so the real endpoint is the only one that answers.

title: One building typed three ways is one property again
details: My Desk saved a property under the address you typed, matched character for character, so the same building entered three ways was three separate properties — each with its own value history, each counted again in the combined total the desk leads with. That is not hypothetical: a real desk carried "1210N17th st", "1210 N 17th st Boise Idaho 83702" and "1210N17th st Boise Id" as three houses. The app already knew better, because it geocodes and confirms every address before running the report and shows you what it matched — it just threw that answer away afterwards. It now keeps it, and a save lands on the property the address was verified as, whatever you typed. Written to miss rather than guess: if the verified answer is missing or too vague to name a building, saving falls back to exactly the old behavior, because a stray duplicate row is something you can delete while a wrong merge would quietly destroy one of two value histories. An address naming one unit of a building never uses it at all, since geocoders silently drop "Apt 3" and two units would otherwise become one property. Existing duplicates are left alone deliberately — merging two histories is a decision about whose numbers to keep, and nothing should make that silently; delete the spares and the remaining row keeps its history.

title: Market pages say which way the market is moving, on the comp map
details: The Expanding / Flat / Contracting badge that landed in the Market Explorer dropdown yesterday now also sits in the heading row of the "Where these comps are" card, in the same three colours. Same read, not a second one: the page and the dropdown both call freshDirection(), so the 90-day expiry stays one rule and the two surfaces cannot disagree about the same market. A market with no read shows nothing, which is what every market page looked like before. 19 of the 27 seeded pages carry a badge today; the other 8 either have no stored read or have no map card to hang it on.

title: The firm feature's browser half is now tested, and the deploy notes name the right migrations
details: Everything the server does for firms was already exercised end to end — an invitation grants nothing until it is accepted, a removed colleague loses the report immediately, a firm checkout bills the firm and not whoever clicked Buy. What none of it touched was the screen: about 450 lines of desk code across eight render functions, and the vault's firm column, ran in no test at all. So the failures that could still ship were the visible ones — a sole owner offered a "Leave firm" button the server will always refuse, an invitation accepted without the auto-share disclosure that was a condition of building auto-share at all, a "you're reading a firm link" notice left over from the previous report, or a renamed div quietly turning the whole section into nothing. Those 53 new checks run the real functions against a small stand-in browser and assert what lands on screen, and each one was verified by breaking the code and watching it go red. The invitation email is covered too, which was the last thing in this feature argued only in comments: it is now asserted that a colleague already invited is never mailed twice, that a refused invitation mails nobody, and that the message names who sent it, which firm, and that an unaccepted invitation gives nobody access to anything. Separately, the deploy notes had drifted: the section that says which migration must run before the code does named 028, 029 and 030 for work that actually lives in 030, 031 and 032, so anyone following it by name would have run the wrong file — corrected in the notes and in seven code comments.

title: A firm you can click through, with no database
details: The enterprise system is the one part of this app with no local fallback — every firm route refuses without Supabase — so looking at it has always meant pointing a server at a real database. That is a poor trade for an access-control surface, where the failures are visual before they are anything else. `node scripts/firm-sandbox.js` boots the real server against the stand-in database the test suite already uses, seeds a firm through the ordinary routes (never by writing rows, so it cannot produce a state the app itself could not), and prints one URL. Behind it: an owner on Pro, a colleague on the free plan who has accepted, and somebody with an invitation still waiting — click a name to become them. Two reports sit on the firm's shelf, and one comp sits in the owner's vault so the Firm column has something to toggle. Invitations are captured rather than sent and printed on startup, so the invitation copy can be read as mail. Nothing can reach a real book, nothing can spend money — the API keys are blanked — and the whole thing lives in one process's memory and goes when you stop it.

title: The thinking comparison can no longer be poisoned by the .env it sits next to
details: An eval worktree's .env is a SYMLINK to the real one, and the server fills any variable the launcher did not set from that file. Three of them would have wrecked a run: APP_PASSWORD makes every search demand a header the eval does not send, so all twelve targets 401 after the preflight has already announced the run is safe to spend; SUPABASE_URL points an "isolated" run at production's cache, corpus and market pages; and a THINKING_LEVEL sitting in the file would override what the comparison is trying to set, making both halves identical and reading as "reasoning depth does not matter" rather than as a misconfiguration. All three are now blanked explicitly by the launcher, which the server's .env loader deliberately respects. The practical consequence is that nobody has to edit that .env — which was the real hazard, since editing a symlink edits the production file on the other end of it. Proven by planting all three values in a throwaway worktree and watching the run refuse every one.

title: The live search progress is no longer wired to one vendor
details: The code that turns a streaming model response into the comps appearing on screen named eight Anthropic event types directly, which is the real reason the default provider shows a simulated progress bar and then the whole report at once: not that Gemini cannot stream, but that there was nowhere to put a second vendor's event shape. Reading the stream now happens behind the provider seam and hands the server a small vendor-neutral vocabulary, so adding a provider is one function rather than a rewrite of the read loop. Behaviour is unchanged and the invariant that matters is now pinned by tests it has never had: the streaming and non-streaming paths must hand the parser the exact same string, or a report is subtly different depending on a setting nobody thinks about.

title: Groundwork for live comps on the default provider, plus the one call that settles it
details: The Interactions API does stream, and the request form is now confirmed against the live endpoint. What is not confirmed is the shape of the frames it sends back, which is documented only as "each event includes a type and JSON data" — so the reader written for it is explicitly unverified and unreachable unless a deployment opts in. That caution is deliberate: a wrong frame shape recovers no text at all, which would turn every report into an error rather than a slightly worse report. scripts/verify-gemini-stream.js settles it for a fraction of a cent — it runs the real reader over real bytes and either confirms it reassembled the model's JSON, or prints exactly which frame types it did not recognise, which is what a fix needs. When it passes, turning it on is a one-line change and the whole live comp table lights up on the default provider.

title: A portfolio that will not load no longer reads as an empty one
details: If the read behind My Desk failed — a blip, a dropped connection, the database briefly unreachable — the desk said "Run a report — it will show up here", which to somebody with sixteen tracked properties says their book is gone. It also reported "0 properties" and quietly forgot which properties were saved, so the button on a report would offer to save one that was already there. The desk now tells the two situations apart: a failure says so plainly, keeps whatever it was already showing, and states that nothing has been lost, while a genuinely empty portfolio keeps its invitation to run a report. The rest of the desk — watchlist, shared reports, firm, branding — renders either way, so one failed read cannot blank the page. This is the same rule the broker vault, the lead inbox and the hub list each had to learn: never report an outage as an absence.

title: Colleagues on a firm seat are no longer offered someone else's billing
details: Every page outside the app — the markets directory, a market page, the brokers page, how it works, the 1031 guide, the vault — draws its own copy of the account menu. That copy decided who sees "Manage billing" from a slightly older rule than the app's, and the gap was a real one: somebody holding Pro through their firm's seat was offered it, even though the subscription behind their status belongs to the firm's card and not to them. Clicking it either opens a plan they cannot be the one to change or fails outright, since they have no customer record of their own. The header now applies the same test the app has applied since firm billing shipped, plus the app's other condition — a deployment with no payment keys hides the button rather than offering one that can only fail. A test now holds the two copies together, and it was checked by reverting the fix and watching it go red, so it cannot quietly stop guarding this.

title: Details for comps says which figures leave your browser
details: Everything behind the "Details for comps" summary looked alike, so the one real difference between those fields was invisible: the market note and the per-type facts (clear height, beds and baths, unit count) ride to our server with your search and steer which comps come back, while the asking price, NOI and cap rate are read only by your own browser and are not in the search request at all. The section is now two labelled groups that say exactly that — "Sent with your search" and "Yours alone" — which turns a guarantee the code has always enforced into something the form actually tells you. The wording is deliberately "not sent with your search" rather than "never leaves your browser", because publishing a share link does upload the report: your NOI is dropped from that link, while the asking price and cap rate travel on it, and the note under the second group says so. On land, where NOI and cap rate do not apply and are hidden, that sentence adjusts to name only the asking price. Nothing about what is sent changed — verified by watching the actual request with all three private fields filled in.

title: Bulk valuation — a list of addresses in, one portfolio out
details: Pro members can paste a list of addresses, or upload a CSV with an address column, and get a value on each as one portfolio at /bulk. Every finished valuation also lands on My Desk as an ordinary saved property, so the comps behind a row are one click away and every desk feature works on it unchanged. The number in a row is the same arithmetic a single report runs, reached through the same search and serialization path, so a row and the report behind it can never disagree — and a broker's own vault comps and their firm's shared comps blend into their own bulk rows exactly as they do into their own reports. A job is an invoice before it is a feature: every address that misses the cache is its own billed search, so there is one run per member at a time, a hard 50-address cap, and the count and the likely wall clock are said before the button rather than after. Addresses that are places rather than properties, duplicates, and sizes that will not parse are each reported by line number instead of being silently valued or silently dropped, and a total sums only what was actually valued rather than counting a failed lookup as zero. A run outlives the request that starts it, so you can close the tab; if a deploy interrupts one, the next read says so plainly and re-running the list serves the finished addresses from cache for free. Migration 035 must be run before deploying.

title: One search pipeline and one serialization funnel, shared
details: The /api/comps handler's two halves came out into their own functions: runCompSearch (cache, derivable window, daily cap, size memo, corpus retrieval, the billed call, and every side effect that must see the ungated report) and finishReportForViewer (the old gate closure — radius blend, then the paywall, then the private comps). Bulk valuation runs both, so there is one answer to questions like whether a cache hit counts and whether a corpus-strong market shrinks the search budget. The cheapest of those to get wrong, harvesting, swallows its own errors, so a second copy would have drifted with nothing reporting it. Behavior is deliberately identical: the daily cap became a thrown error the handler turns back into the same 429, and the live-progress stream still opens at the last moment before anything is billed.

title: A jump bar for long reports
details: A finished report runs about five screens on a laptop and the comparable-sales table starts three and a half of them down, so getting back to the comps meant a scroll hunt every time. A slim bar now rides the top of the screen while a report is open — Value, Market, Drivers, Map, Position, Comps — with the section you are reading underlined, and clicking one lands it just below the bar rather than behind it. It lists the sections that actually exist in the report you are looking at, so a report with no map does not offer a Map link, and switching to the Analysis tab relabels it to that tab's cards (DCF, Expenses, Debt, Sensitivity, Rent roll) instead of keeping a second list of them. Two rules keep it from becoming furniture: it stays away entirely on a report shorter than two screens or with fewer than three sections to point at, and it never appears while a report is still assembling, since a nav pointing at cards that do not exist yet is worse than none. It is screen-only — printed PDFs and downloaded images have never carried it.

title: The eval scorecard can finally answer "what did that cost?"
details: The harness measured quality and wall clock and said nothing at all about spend — no cost, no token counts — so "is thinking less cheaper AND still accurate?" was only half answerable, and the half it could answer was the half that did not decide anything.
