Every scored report now carries what the search really cost: dollars, input and output tokens, billed calls, and the split that matters on the default provider — thinking versus the report itself. That split is the point. A measured call generates 928 tokens of report and 6,473 of reasoning, so an output figure of 7,401 reads as an enormous report when it is a small report and a long think; without separating them a thinking comparison can show that the clock moved but not that reasoning is why. The numbers ride on an internal-caller-only field attached at serialization, so nothing reaches the cache, the corpus, a market page or a customer, and a cache hit reports no cost rather than a measured-looking $0.00. --compare now prints a per-report trade: time, cost, cost per thousand reports and the token split on top; priced sale comps, provenance, estimate rate and whether a valuation was possible underneath — because a faster, cheaper report that cannot value the building is not a cheaper report.

title: One command runs the whole thinking-level A/B
details: scripts/compare-thinking.js boots an isolated server, scores every eval target at the vendor's default reasoning depth, restarts at a lower one, scores again, and prints the comparison. It replaces a six-step manual dance whose steps existed only because the launch had to be done by hand — and it closes the expensive trap in them: in PowerShell setting SUPABASE_URL to an empty string DELETES the variable, so the .env loader refills it from the worktree's symlinked copy and an "isolated" run writes into production's cache, corpus and market pages. Spawning the server with an explicit environment makes that impossible rather than merely warned about. It also enforces the restart the comparison depends on (the thinking level and the model are read once at startup, and the subject-size memo lives in memory where no file wipe reaches it), refuses to run against the main checkout, verifies through /healthz that the server really is at the depth requested before spending a cent, and prints the estimated bill and stops unless you pass --yes.

title: The comp table now fills before the market commentary is written
details: The model writes the report top to bottom, and the comps are the only part your browser can put on screen while it is still writing — so everything above them was time you spent watching an empty table. The market-level figures (average $/SF, cap rate range, op-ex range, value drivers, market trend, search radius, transactions reviewed, price discovery) now come after the comps instead of before, about 800 characters the live table no longer waits through. It is the better order for accuracy too: every one of those figures is a read of the comps — the average averages them, transactions reviewed has to exceed their count — so the model now describes rows it has actually committed to rather than rows it still intends to write. The plain-English summary stays on top, because it is the one piece of prose the loading card can show you while the search runs.

title: Reports stop restating arithmetic we already do
details: $/SF on a sale comp is the sale price divided by the building size, and the server has always derived that itself and overridden the model whenever the two disagreed by more than 10%. So on any priced, sized sale the field was time spent writing out a number that could never survive contradicting its own row. The model is now asked to leave it out there, and still asked for it wherever it genuinely is not derivable — lease rates, and sales missing a price or a size. The cross-check the field was really doing (does the source's own $/SF match its own price and size?) stays as an instruction. One thing worth knowing: the small calc mark in the comp table now means only that we corrected a figure we were handed, never that we filled a blank one.

title: THINKING_LEVEL — the largest speed lever the search has, wired up and made measurable
details: On the live provider, thinking is not a rounding error on report time, it is report time: a measured call spent 928 tokens writing the report and 6,473 thinking about it, and thinking is generated and billed exactly like output. So roughly seven of every eight tokens the model produces are reasoning — every trim to the report itself is attacking the small half. THINKING_LEVEL (low/medium/high) exposes the other half. It ships unset, so nothing changes until somebody chooses to change it: Google's own guidance calls the default depth the best quality for agentic work, and comp accuracy is the product, so this is a thing to measure with a run-eval --compare pair rather than assume. /healthz now reports the live level beside the model, eval runs record it and --compare prints it, so a pair that differs only in reasoning depth can never be misread as model noise. An unknown level, or one set against a provider that has no tunable depth, exits at boot rather than being silently ignored.

title: A printed report leads with the comps, not your DCF
details: On screen the Market Report and Analysis tabs keep the two halves apart, so nobody saw this: printing forces both halves visible and they print in document order, and the Analysis half was written first in the page. So a PDF — the copy that actually gets handed to a client or a lender — went value hero, then your DCF, expense ratio, debt service and rent roll, and only then the market summary, the map and the comparable sales the value was computed from. The evidence arrived several pages after the number it supports. The two halves swapped places in the markup, which changes nothing on screen (the tabs hide one either way) and puts the market report first on paper. The analysis cards now open on their own page under an "Appendix — your figures: income, debt & risk" header, which says plainly that everything below it was computed from what you typed rather than from the comps above. The appendix header prints only when there is an analysis to head: with no NOI entered, every card below it is hidden and it stays away rather than printing a heading over blank space.

title: One shared-reports table on My Desk
details: Reports you sent and reports sent to you were two stacked lists with two headers and two empty states, and telling "what moved lately" meant reading both. They are now one table under the Sharing deck, sorted newest-first across both directions, with a Shared column that says which way each report went ("By you · Aug 18" / "With you · Aug 20") and an Audience column carrying the status that used to be a line on a card — invited count, "Anyone with the link", the firm's name, or "Link turned off". Every control survived the move: the viewer list with per-person opened status, the wholesale people editor, Start a hub, and Turn off link now live in a detail row that opens under the report it belongs to. A revoked link renders grey with no controls and no link, as before. The firm shelf deliberately did not merge in — it is a firm-level record with its own rules (whole-shelf count, truncation notice, its own search) and stays in the firm deck.

title: My Desk grouped into decks with a reading strip
details: The desk was a flat stack of a dozen identically-weighted sections — Plan had the same visual rank as Portfolio. It now reads as five decks in the vault's Direction-U style (serif label on an ink rule): Your properties, Sharing, Your firm, Broker, Account. The portfolio's book line was promoted to a desk-level reading strip directly under the page header, so combined value, movement and markets watched are the first thing a member sees. A deck whose sections are all hidden hides itself (a MutationObserver recomputes it, so no render function has to remember to), which is what keeps the Firm and Broker decks off a free member's desk. Every section keeps its own id, gating and empty states — this is grouping, not new behavior.

title: The landing page stopped selling yesterday's prices
details: The FAQ on the front page — the same answers Google can serve as facts about the product — still said free reports itemize ten comps and offered a $20 single-report unlock, hours after the free tier went to every-comp and the one-off was retired. This is the second time this exact answer has gone stale after a pricing change (it once denied the subscription entirely), so beyond the correction it is now pinned by a test: the build fails if the page ever again claims a free comp limit that does not exist or sells a product that cannot be bought.

title: The $20 single-report unlock is retired
details: Once free reports began itemizing every comparable, the one-off was left selling only the ten-year window, and the button that offered it — which only appeared when comps were locked — had almost nothing left to appear on. Rather than invent a new reason to surface it, it is retired. If you bought one, nothing changes: your unlock was permanent for that property and stays permanent — the full history, exports and branding you paid for keep working, and a refund on an old purchase is still honored too. Pro is now the one way to get the ten-year window, alongside the vault, the Address Explorer, unlimited exports and branding.

title: A free report itemizes every comparable we find
details: Free reports used to list ten comps and hide the rest behind a lock line, even though the value range above them was always calculated from every comp the search found. So the part being withheld was the evidence for a number we had already published, which is a strange thing to charge for. A free account now sees the whole list, addresses and sources included. Pro is the ten-year window instead of three, unlimited exports, the private vault, the Address Explorer, and your own branding on the report. One knock-on worth knowing: the $20 single-report unlock only offers itself when something is actually locked, so inside the three-year window it will rarely come up now; it still buys the ten-year window and branding for one property.

title: The app stops offering to install itself
details: Open CompNinja inside the desktop app (or the installed web app) and Download the app disappears from the Explore menu — an offer to install what you are already using reads as the product not knowing where it is. Worth being precise about what this does and doesn't do: a website cannot tell whether a program is installed on your computer, because browsers deliberately refuse to answer that question, so nothing here guesses. What it knows exactly is whether the page it is drawing is being viewed from inside the app, which is the case that matters. That takes two different signals — the installed web app announces itself through a standard display mode, while the desktop app reports itself as an ordinary browser window and is recognisable only by a marker it stamps on every request — and a test fails the build if those two ever drift apart, because the failure is silent: the link simply comes back, in the one place nobody thinks to look. The check runs before the page paints, so the link is never drawn and then taken away, and the download page itself still works for anyone who visits it directly.

title: compninja.co/download — the app's front door
details: The download page for the desktop app: one card per platform linking the latest release's installer under a stable URL, an honest first-launch note (Windows and Mac show their standard unknown-publisher prompt until code signing is bought — saying so up front stops the prompt reading as a virus warning), and the no-download alternative for people who'd rather install from the browser. Download the app joins the Explore menu on every page and the sitemap. A test holds the three places that name the installer files — the build config, the release workflow, and this page — in step, because a renamed artifact would otherwise leave the page serving dead links with nothing else failing.

title: A real downloadable desktop app — its own installer, no browser attached
details: The installable web app still visibly lived inside Chrome, and the owner wanted a genuinely standalone program. CompNinja now ships as one: its own CompNinja-Setup.exe for Windows, CompNinja.dmg for Mac (Intel and Apple Silicon in one), and CompNinja.AppImage for Linux, each with the ninja icon, its own taskbar identity, and no browser chrome anywhere. The app deliberately contains no product code — it opens compninja.co in its own locked-down window, so every site deploy reaches every installed copy instantly and there is no update channel to run. Checkout and the billing portal stay in-window so a Pro purchase completes and returns; every other outside link opens in the system browser; no connection shows a branded try-again page instead of a grey browser error. Installers build themselves on a desktop-v tag and publish to GitHub Releases under stable names, so download links never change. They are unsigned for now — Windows and Mac will show their usual unknown-publisher warning on first run until a code-signing certificate and Apple notarization are bought, and the download page will say so plainly rather than let the warning look like a fault.

title: Visitors who haven't signed up can install the app too
details: The install identity was linked only from the app page, and under the account wall an anonymous visitor at compninja.co gets the landing page instead — so Chrome and Edge never offered Install CompNinja to exactly the people a download door exists for. The manifest link now rides on every public server-rendered page: the landing page, the markets directory and every market page, the brokers page and the 1031 guide. A test boots nothing extra and pins that both public head builders carry it.

title: Users can install CompNinja as a desktop app
details: The place to download the app is the site itself: compninja.co is now installable. Chrome and Edge offer Install CompNinja from the address bar, and the footer grows an Install the desktop app button — shown only once the browser actually offers the prompt, the same rule the Buy button follows, so nobody ever sees a control that does nothing. Installing puts the ninja icon on the desktop, taskbar and Start Menu and opens CompNinja in its own window with no tabs or address bar; because the app is the live site, installed copies are always current — no installers to host, no code-signing certificates, no update channel, and no unsigned-download warnings scaring users off. Deliberately no service worker: install no longer requires one, and a cache layer could serve the valuation script stale against the page that depends on it, the exact failure its no-cache rule exists to prevent. The icons are the cut-card mark rendered at proper app sizes, including a maskable variant so Android and Windows don't letterbox it.

title: CompNinja runs as a desktop app
details: npm run desktop opens CompNinja in its own chromeless window — no tabs, no address bar, its own sign-in session that persists like an app's. It is deliberately not an Electron build: this repo runs on plain Node with zero npm dependencies, and every machine already ships a Chromium (Edge on Windows), so the launcher boots the ordinary server on a free port — never 3000, the dev server lives there — waits for it to answer healthy, and opens the browser's app mode with a dedicated CompNinja profile. Closing the window stops the server. --url points the window at the hosted site instead, with no local server and no API key needed, and a Windows script installs the desktop shortcut with the ninja icon, finding the owner's portable no-admin Node where PATH never will. The launcher refuses rather than guesses: a typo'd flag, a non-http URL, or a bad port is an error message, not a silent near-miss, and those rules are covered by the test suite.

title: A stolen port can no longer fail CI or block a deploy
details: The test suite boots real servers on OS-assigned ports, and there is an unavoidable window between probing a port free and the child binding it. Anything else on the machine grabbing the port in that window killed the child with EADDRINUSE and failed the run — it hit the main build today after the identical tree passed twice, and because npm start's prestart runs this same suite, the same race could block a production deploy while the previous build kept serving. boot() now captures the child's stderr (so an early exit finally says why, instead of just 'code 1') and retries on a fresh port up to three times — but only when stderr proves EADDRINUSE, so a genuine boot crash, like the unrecognized-provider test relies on, still fails loudly on the first attempt.

title: One header, served from one place
details: The site had three hand-copied headers — index.html's, the market pages' marketBar, and /how-it-works' own — with comments begging editors to keep them in step, and they still drifted. /how-it-works now renders marketBar itself (its one difference, the aria-current marker, became marketBar's `current` argument, so /markets, /brokers and the 1031 guide now mark themselves in the menu too), and the Explore menu's links live in a single NAV_LINKS list that the server injects into index.html at serve time. Adding a nav link is a one-line edit that changes every page at once; a test pins that the app menu and the server-rendered headers carry the same links.

title: Reports and market pages are doors to each other
details: A report for a Boise warehouse never mentioned /market/industrial-boise-id, and the market page offered no way to value a specific building there. Every served report now carries a market_page cross-link when a standing page covers its market and type (attached at serialization, so a page published later lights up older cached reports), rendered as a line under the Market Summary — and every market page's CTA became a real address form that lands on the search page with the address and type prefilled, for members and anonymous visitors alike.

title: My Desk links out to the markets it tracks
details: A saved portfolio property now links to its market page next to the existing open-report and Refresh actions, and each watched market's name in the feed opens its page — so the desk is the hub everything hangs off rather than a list. Server-side the same marketPageInfo read decorates the portfolio and the watchlist feed; a market with no page simply renders no link.

title: The 1031 guide teaches how to choose a qualified intermediary
details: The QI is the one professional every exchange must have, the industry is lightly regulated, and the failures that made case law lost people their money and their tax deferral in the same stroke. The guide now carries the vetting checklist — segregated escrow in your name, bonding and E&O with certificates, state registration where required, the two-year independence rule, fees in writing including who keeps the escrow interest — plus three FAQ entries (how to choose, what it costs, why your own attorney can't do it). Education throughout: what to verify, never who to hire, and the page says in the same breath that CompNinja is not a QI and holds no funds. The decision this implements: CompNinja refers toward professionals and never becomes the party holding exchange money.

title: The 1031 funnel can be measured
details: Reads of the 1031 guide are now counted (PII-free, obvious crawlers excluded — the page is public and sitemapped, so bots would otherwise be most of the number), split by whether the reader was signed in. A new 1031 guide funnel card on /admin puts those reads beside the BOV requests the guide produced, so whether the page earns its keep is a glance instead of a guess. Deliberately no computed conversion percentage: the counts are small and age differently, and two honest numbers beat one confident-looking ratio.

title: The 1031 guide became a funnel, not just a page
details: Three additions. The deadline widget now hands the 45- and 180-day dates over as a calendar file (.ics), built entirely in the browser like the dates themselves. A BOV request from a browser that recently read the guide is tagged source "1031" — the owner's notification, the broker new-lead alert, and the vault pipeline all say so, because a seller inside a 1031 window is the one lead a broker drops everything for; the lead stays anonymized to the same facts as before, plus that one boolean. And every market page links the guide in context — someone reading a replacement market's numbers mid-exchange is exactly who it serves.

title: An invitation goes to the person you typed
details: Inviting somebody to a hub split the address you typed on the letter s. So sarah@jonesrealty.com invited nobody at all, while the panel still said Invited, and because invitations really are emailed now the link is no longer shown, leaving nothing on screen to check against. Worse, when one of the fragments happens to be a valid address it gets invited instead: a test invitation sent on production went to a stranger, with the broker told it had been sent. An address with no s in it, like bob@acme.com, worked fine, which is why nothing looked wrong. The cause is that this page is built as one long template, where a backslash written once is eaten before the browser ever sees it, so a class meant to match spaces and commas arrived matching the letter s. Only the People panel was affected, and only since 2026-08-16; creating a hub with invitations was always written correctly. Found by sending one real invitation. Two tests now hold it: one reads the expression the page actually ships and checks that an address with a plus in it stays a single recipient, and one fails on any escape the template would eat, anywhere on either page.

title: A firm's seats are the number it actually bought
details: The seat count a firm pays for was written down and then never read back, so it stopped nothing: a firm with two seats could invite a two-hundredth colleague without being told, and every one of them held Pro on a two-seat plan. The seat line on the desk reported the same wrong number to everybody looking at it. Seats now bind where they always should have — on the invitation, on the desk, and on who the plan covers.

title: Hover a comp and its map pin lights up
details: The table and the map carried the same numbers and were otherwise strangers. On a dense block you counted roundels by eye to work out which dot was the $116/SF sale, which is the one thing a map beside a table is supposed to save you. Hovering a row now lights that comp's pin, and hovering a pin marks its row, so the two read as one thing. It works in both directions because either one can be the thing you are looking at. Nothing lights for a comp that has no pin, which is the ordinary case for one you excluded or one we could not place rather than a fault. A row that disappears under your cursor, from a sort or a filter or excluding it, leaves no pin lit behind it. Touch devices are untouched, since there is no hover to read.

title: Land comps identified by their corner are no longer thrown away
details: A vacant parcel has no building to number, so the market names it by its corner (“NEC 159th & Brentwood St”). The individual-property rule was written for buildings and demoted three real priced Olathe land listings to “estimate” — 38% of that report's comps on the 2026-08-19 eval. That is not padding being caught, it is real provenance being discarded: “estimate” is excluded from corpus retrieval and from the accuracy backtest, so those deals were lost rather than merely mislabeled. enforcedSourceType now takes an optional property type and exempts corner and intersection addresses for Land only. Deliberately narrow: it needs an ampersand between two tokens or an explicit corner designator, reads the street line only so an “&” in a company suffix cannot qualify one, refuses the word “and” (which appears in ordinary names), and the aggregate test still applies on top. Replayed against the real report the estimate rate goes 38% to 0%, while the same addresses under Office stay demoted.

title: A subject size of nothing no longer carries a provenance claim
details: The 2026-08-19 eval's Atlanta report came back with subject_size_sqft "" and subject_size_source "public_record" — a source citing no value. index.html happens to read the source only where a size exists, so it never reached a screen, but the orphan was written into the cache, the harvest and every share, where the next reader has no reason to expect it. normalizeSubjectSize keeps the pair together or drops it, the same rule normalizeSubjectLastSale already applies to a price with no date.

title: subjectSizeFoundRate is documented as a target-set property, not a model score
details: It read as the weakest number on the eval at 50%, and it is largely not about the model: across the 3.6 Flash and 3.7 Flash runs it agreed on 9 of the 10 shared targets and the same four missed in both. A miss is also often correct, since the prompt tells the model to return an empty string rather than guess a size it cannot source for that exact address. Recorded in eval-set.json so nobody tunes the prompt against it. The --compare target-selection guard now also carries the target COUNT, because eval-set.json is designed to be added to and two runs could otherwise both report “full set” over different targets.

title: Gemini 3.7 Flash scored on the eval set for the first time
details: The default search model moved to 3.7 Flash on 2026-08-13 without a run, so every quoted accuracy, speed and cost figure still described 3.6. Scored now on a balanced slice, one or two targets of each property type: 10 of 10 valued, 0 failures, 6.5 comps and 6.3 priced sales per report, provenance 0.77, in-window 98%, market match 94%. Roughly twice as fast as the 3.6 pipeline run (30s mean against 57s) at $0.030 per search measured from the run's own logged tokens. Two soft spots: Multifamily returned only 4 comps on both targets, and the Land target padded 38% of its comps to estimate provenance. Subject size is still found on only half of targets, unchanged from 3.6, and it feeds the hero directly. Summary: docs/evals/2026-08-19-gemini-3-7-per-type-1787106363919.json.

title: Evals can run a balanced slice per property type, and record which model ran
details: run-eval.js gains --per-type N (at most N targets of each property type; --per-type 2 is 10 of the 12 targets, one or two per type). --only could not answer a per-type question, because eval-set.json leads with four Industrial targets, so --only 2 was two Industrial searches. Runs now also record the model /healthz reports rather than the MODEL env var the runner was started with: four of the five summaries in docs/evals say “(server default)”, which is why the committed record could not say whether Gemini 3.7 Flash had ever been scored. The target selection is recorded alongside it, and --compare warns when two runs used different selections, since a per-type slice reweights every aggregate against a full-set baseline.

title: Gemini cost-per-report constants were billing the wrong rate
details: USD_PER_MTOK in search-provider-gemini.js held Google standard pricing ($1.50/$7.50 per Mtok), which does not take effect until 2027-01-01 — every report through then is billed at the introductory rate ($0.75/$3.75). Real cost per report drops from the documented $0.092 to about $0.045. Updated the constant, outreach.js COST_PER_REPORT, the comment in server.js, and the pinned test in test/search-provider-gemini.test.js.

title: Only a licensed broker can publish a comp
details: The Verified badge on a published comp tells whoever reads that report that a named licensed broker vouched for the deal. Nothing checked the licensed half, so anybody who reached a vault could put the badge on a comp, which would make it say something that is not true. Your broker profile now takes a license number, and publishing is refused without one. It is asked for once, in the same place you set the name your comps are credited to, and it is never shown to anyone: it stands behind the badge rather than beside it. The line above your book now says which of the two is missing before you press Publish rather than after, and both the single Publish and Publish a whole view read the same rule, so neither can drift from the other. Saving your name still does not require the number, since a broker setting up a vault often does not have it to hand.

title: Firms can buy seats for their people
details: A firm owner buys seats and every colleague on one gets Pro — their own reports, their own vault, covered by the firm's plan. The desk shows how many seats are used and how many are free, so an invitation refused for want of a seat makes sense before it happens. Buying fewer seats than your firm has people is refused rather than quietly downgrading somebody, a colleague on a firm seat is told whose plan covers them instead of being offered a billing page that is not theirs, and anyone who already pays for themselves keeps their own plan.

title: Share a comp from your vault with your firm
details: A Firm column on your comps table lets you hand one comp at a time to colleagues, who then see it inside their own reports with your name on it. It does not go into CompNinja's public records, it is left out of every download and client link, and you can take it back at any time. Fix a price and their copy updates; delete the comp and it disappears from theirs. Your vault header stops saying visible only to you the moment that stops being true, and says exactly how many comps are shared.

title: Your firm can share new reports automatically
details: A firm owner can switch on Share new reports with the firm by default, and every report a member runs from then on lands on the shelf without anyone remembering to send it. Off unless somebody turns it on, never applied to reports already run, and each member has their own switch: choose Never and an admin cannot override it, however many times the firm setting changes. Every auto-shared report says so on screen with an Undo, and an invitation tells you the firm's setting before you accept it.

title: A firm link says it is a firm link
details: Open a report a colleague shared with the firm and it now says who shared it and that only people at your firm can open it. Without that line it looked exactly like a public link, and the mistake it prevents is forwarding one to a client and finding out it was refused after you sent it. The line never prints and is not in the downloaded image — it is about the link, not the building.

title: Your firm's reports, in one searchable shelf
details: The firm section on My Desk is now the firm's whole record: every report anybody has shared with it, newest first, with who shared it and when. Search by address, market, type or colleague. The count above stays honest while you filter — 7 reports · 3 markets is the shelf, not the search — and your own shares are on it too, marked shared by you, because a record missing your own work cannot answer whether anybody here has valued a building.

title: Share a report with your whole firm
details: Create a firm on My Desk, invite colleagues by email, and Share now offers My firm alongside a public link and named clients. What lands there shows up on every colleague's desk — including people who join later — so a BOV reaches the third person who asks for it without another email. Everyone keeps their own reports, portfolio, watchlist and private vault: a firm shares only what somebody shares with it. Invitations must be accepted; nobody joins because their address was typed in, and no firm is ever joined automatically by email domain.

title: See how often your published comps are cited
details: Publishing a comp is paid in credit — your firm named in every report that uses it — and the broker who earned that credit was the only person who could not see it: the count already existed and already showed on the public contributor page, which only exists if you opted into having one. Each published comp in your vault now shows how many reports have cited it, and the ledger totals them under Published. The count is a floor, not an impression count: it rises when a report is generated, and a cached re-run of the same report is not counted twice.

title: Publish a whole view of comps at once
details: Publishing was one button and one identical confirm per comp, so a broker with 60 clean sales read 60 dialogs and in practice published none of them. There is now a Publish button that covers everything currently on screen — one confirm naming the count and the firm the credit goes to. Comps that are not ready (no price, no size, no street number) are skipped and the reason is named, rather than the whole batch failing.

title: A deleted comp can be put back
details: Delete was final behind a single confirm. It now offers Undo while the message is on screen, which re-adds the comp through the ordinary add route so it is validated like anything else you type in. Two things it says out loud rather than leaving you to find out: the restored comp is a new entry and no longer belongs to its original import, and a comp that was published does not go back into the public records — you publish it again when you are ready.

title: Find a comp in your vault by typing part of it
details: A book of 400 comps had two dropdowns and a scrollbar. There is now a Find box beside them that filters as you type, over the address, the notes, the market, the type and the tenancy — so "sherwin" finds the deal you remember by its tenant, and two words mean both words. It composes with the Market, Type and Deal filters instead of replacing them, Esc clears it, and a search that matches nothing now says so with a Clear link rather than telling you your vault is empty.

title: Leads reach the broker one town over
details: Coverage matched a lead's city exactly, so a broker watching Boise industrial never saw a Meridian industrial lead — even though those cities trade as one market and the site already keeps a curated list saying so. The inbox, the introduction request and the new-lead email now all read that list. The property type is never widened with it: a shared suburb does not make a retail enquiry an industrial broker's. Each coverage chip says how many nearby markets it reaches, so a lead from a city you did not type is explained rather than surprising.

title: The vault handles leases, not just sales
details: A leasing book used to carry no figure anywhere — the template said to leave price blank on a lease and write the rent into notes, so every market card read “no priced sales yet”. Leases now have rent_psf, rent_basis and lease_type columns, a median in $/SF/yr, their own year chart and a Sale/Lease filter. rent_basis has no default on purpose: $1.35/SF is a normal California monthly rent and an impossible annual one, so we ask instead of guessing and storing a number 12x wrong. A view holding both sales and leases states no median and says to filter, since the two are different measures rather than a wider spread of one.

title: Tell us the condition of your house, and the range narrows to your half of it
details: House reports now ask one more question — Needs work, Original, Updated or Renovated — and report the same thing for each comp, in a new Condition column. Answer it and the estimate stops being neutral about the largest thing it cannot see: if your home is renovated and most of the comps are not, the report says so and points at the upper half of the range. It does not move Low, Likely or High, and it says nothing at all when your house sits among its comps. Comps whose listing does not state a condition stay blank rather than being guessed at.

title: Addresses stopped riding in the geocoding URL
details: Every pin on every map is placed by looking the address up through our own proxy, and that address travelled in the web address of the request, which means it was written into the hosting platform's request logs and handed to any site the page linked out to. It now travels inside the request instead, where none of that happens. This matters most for a broker's private comps: those are deliberately looked up through our proxy and nowhere else, precisely so an off-market address never reaches a third party, and logging it in a URL gave back a good part of what that bought. The old form was removed rather than left working alongside the new one, because a door left open is one forgetful change away from putting the addresses back. Market pages already cached in a browser show no map for up to an hour after this ships, then come back on their own.

title: A refunded report is actually taken back now
details: The handlers for refunds and for delayed payments shipped in early August and had never been switched on at Stripe, so a refunded buyer kept their report forever and a payment that settled after checkout took the money without unlocking anything. All nine events the code handles are now enabled on the live endpoint. No code changed; the code had been waiting.

title: A comp a client adds cannot carry a price with no deal type
details: The Sale or lease box on Add a comp you found defaults to Not sure, which is right for a client who has an address and nothing else. It was also accepted alongside a price, and $/SF is only ever worked out for a sale, so the comp landed as a bare figure in the column every other row is read down: $1,200,000 that might be a purchase and might be a year's rent, with nothing on the row to say which. Sale or lease is now asked for once a price is typed, and only then. A building with no price still goes in with nothing else filled, which is the case the box was built for.

title: A hub says when your client has opened it, without a reload
details: The People list shows whether each person has opened the hub, and then never changed it. A broker who sent comps and sat watching the page saw not opened yet long after the client was reading, because the fifteen second refresh updated the comps and the notes and left the guest list alone. It updates with the rest now. Whether somebody has opened a hub is the one fact on that page that changes through another person's action rather than your own, so it was the last thing that should have needed a reload, and it was the only thing that did.

title: The vault picker in a hub reads as a list again
details: Choosing which comps to send a client showed a stack instead of a list: the tick box sat on its own line above each building, and the address ran into the deal and the price with no gap, so a city and a sale type read as one word. The rows had a layout all along; a broader rule for the panel around them was overruling it. Found by opening the panel and sending a real comp.

title: The trust line puts the warnings first and folds the mechanics away
details: Under a house report the explanation had grown to 1,034 characters — nine sentences of small grey text — and the most useful line in it, what the estimate cannot see about condition, sat ninth of nine. Everything was disclosed and none of it was read. The line now shows only what is specific to your property: the comps it used, a size that does not match, a listing that disagrees, the condition spread. How the weighting works, and the note that house sales live in the MLS, move behind How this range is calculated. A typical house report reads 394 characters instead of about 800. Printing or exporting the report opens the whole thing again, since that is the copy that gets forwarded.

title: The condition gap points at the thing that can close it
details: An estimate cannot see condition or finish; a person standing in the property can. The condition line now says so and hands the reader the free agent introduction that already sits below it. On screen only — the button is not on a printed page or in an exported image, and a report should not point at a control that is not there.

title: The report says what it cannot see about a house
details: A valuation prices size, age, location and provenance. It cannot see condition, finish, or how the last owner kept the place, and until now nothing said so: a gut-renovated home and an untouched one on the same street, same size, same vintage, came back at the same number. Residential reports now close the trust line with the spread the comps still show once size, age and distance are accounted for, in $/SF and as a dollar swing on your own square footage. It is read off this report's own comps rather than a stock percentage, so a single-builder subdivision honestly reports a small number and a mixed-vintage street reports a large one.

title: Gain the market did not hand over
details: When a report knows both what a property last sold for and what it asks today, it compounds that old price forward at the market's own annual trend and names the difference: bought for $400,000 in June 2021, worth about $540,000 at this market's +6%/yr, asking $700,000 — $160,000 the market did not hand over, which often means work was done since. It is the closest honest answer to how much went into a renovation without permit records, and it is evidence only: it never enters Low/Likely/High, and the line says so. Silent without a market trend, silent below the same 25% bar the listing-gap note already uses, silent past ten years, and silent in the other direction, where the causes are unknowable.

title: Property SF is on the search form
details: You can type your property's square feet without opening anything: one optional box on the form beside Asking price, where Focus and Lookback are. It went down to Details for comps in August because public records and the building's footprint usually answer it — but both can miss, and correcting them meant backing out of the confirm dialog to hunt through a collapsed section. The controls row is two-by-two now: Focus and Lookback on top, Property SF and Asking price under them. It is one figure, not a range — the old min-to-max pair is gone, and the label reads Property SF for every property type instead of changing to Building size / Lot size / Living area as the type resolves. Reports you saved with a size range still show it. Nothing changed about how the number is used: it still overrides the looked-up size, still narrows which comps we pick, and still skips the model's size lookup. Details for comps keeps NOI, cap rate, market note and the per-type specs, and no longer advertises a size field it does not hold.

title: Vault comp cells are as wide as what is in them
details: Making every cell an input cost the table the width its text used to give it: an input has a fixed default width and never wraps, so a long address sat clipped inside a box narrower than the address. Cells are now sized from their own value, so the column follows the longest one, with a cap past which the table scrolls as before. Spreadsheet notes get the same treatment.

title: A hub shows who is in it, and can be added to or closed
details: Two more things a hub could not do: invite anybody after it was created, and finish. Both routes existed with nothing calling them, so the only people who could ever be in a hub were the ones named when it was made. A hub now has a People section for the broker who owns it, listing everyone and whether they have opened it, with a box to invite more and a remove beside each name. Removing somebody stops their link working immediately and leaves everything they posted in place. Closing asks first, keeps everyone their access to what is already there, stops new posts, and hides the controls that would then fail. Clients never see any of it: who else is in a hub is a broker relationship, not something a fellow guest is owed.

title: Hub invitations can be emailed, the moment a sending domain exists
details: Hubs shipped with copy and paste invitations and nothing that could ever send one, so verifying a domain would not have made them start working. Creating a hub, or adding somebody to one, now emails that person their link through the same gate every other outbound mail uses. On a deployment with no verified sending domain it logs and does nothing, exactly as before, and the broker copies the links by hand. The panel also stops claiming CompNinja does not email them, which was true when hubs shipped and would have become a lie the day a domain was verified: the server now reports whether the invitations actually left, and the panel says whichever is true.

title: A hub list that fails to load no longer says you have no hubs
details: The vault deck treated every failure the same as not being allowed, so a server hiccup rendered No hubs yet, create one when you have comps to put in front of a client. An outage read as you have none, to the one person who would know that was wrong, and it happened during a deploy. Being told you are not allowed still stays quiet, since there is nothing to act on, but anything else now says the hubs could not be loaded and keeps the invitation hidden. Create your first hub is the wrong thing to say to somebody whose hubs simply could not be fetched.

title: A broker can actually send comps into a hub now
details: The hub shipped with no way to put a comp in it. The route existed, was gated and was tested, and nothing called it, so the core act of the feature was reachable only from a browser console. A hub now carries Add comps from your vault, for the broker who owns it: the book loads on first open, comps already in the hub are listed but cannot be picked again, and the confirmation reports how many actually landed rather than how many were asked for. It sits on the hub rather than on every vault row because that is where you are already thinking about one client.

title: Escape leaves My Desk too
details: Pressing Escape on /desk now returns to the home view, mirroring the report-close handler: an open modal or the fullscreen map still own Escape first, and a focused field just loses focus. /how-it-works already had this.

title: The vault's comp table is edited in place — no Edit button
details: Every cell in Your comps is typed into directly and saves when you leave it, the way the spreadsheet view already worked; Esc puts the stored value back. Prices and sizes still read as $1,250,000 and swap to the raw number the moment you click in. Market and $/SF stay read-only — the server derives both — and now refresh straight after an edit instead of showing a stale figure. The spreadsheet stays as the place to reach cap rate, tenancy, year built and notes.

title: My Desk removes a property with a trash icon
details: The portfolio row said Refresh Remove — two words competing, and the destructive one shouting as loud as the useful one. Remove is now the same quiet trash icon the broker vault uses on its comp rows: grey ink that turns red on hover, with the confirm unchanged. Refresh still reads as a link.

title: A soft market photo is replaced with a satellite aerial
details: When /admin/heroes marks a city Needs a look, the live header skips that JPEG and uses Esri World Imagery of the same city. Ontario, CA is still Ontario, CA — not Canada. A better Commons file restores the photograph automatically once it passes the grade.

title: A page to judge whether market photos are any good
details: /admin/heroes shows every city header at the same 340px crop visitors see, with a file-size and dimension grade beside it. OK is not a good photograph — look at the crop. HQ flags any that need a look.

title: The empty search form no longer asks you to pick a property type
details: Find addresses already fills the type from the chip, but the line under the address still said chosen when you run the report / pick it now on a blank form. That line now stays empty until a type is actually known. The confirm dialog still asks if detection cannot tell.

title: Market page photos are sharp on a retina screen
details: The header was a 1600px JPEG stretched across a full-width 2x display, so Dallas looked soft. Heroes are now 3840x800 with a 1920w srcset sibling; a phone does not pull the 2x file.

title: Find addresses picks the property type for you
details: The Address Explorer used the form's type (Industrial unless you clicked change), so Tabbing through the chips could not tell a warehouse from an office. Each chip now names its class, Find addresses returns a mixed list, and Tab on a rotating example fills that building's type too.

title: A 2.5-mile market note is the neighborhood, not a 1-mile trim
details: The house-radius fix assumed 10-mile extras. The report's market note was 2.5 miles: 19 comps already inside that circle, cheaper pocket still setting a $2M home to $1M. A typed mile radius now is the blend radius and the distance free-pass, so 2.4-mile comps are in-market. Cheaper sales more than 1.5x off the asking $/SF floor in the range, which is what actually separates two products that sit 2.5 miles apart. The search prompt yields to the same note instead of shrinking it to one mile.

title: A house is no longer valued off cheaper sales from 10 miles away
details: The corpus blend auto-included every saved deal within 10 miles, the CRE radius, so a $2M home could show ~$1M with 19 comps drawn from the next pocket over. Houses now blend only inside 1 mile, drop extras more than 1.5x off the asking $/SF, and use a 2-mile distance half-life in the range. CRE is unchanged. When the estimate sits well below the ask, the trust line names a cheaper pocket, not an ambitious list price.

title: Market pages open on an aerial photograph of the city
details: Every /market page header is now a drone or skyline photo of that city, with the title over a dark overlay. Photos are Wikimedia Commons files we host ourselves (Ontario, CA is not Ontario, Canada). Explorer markets without a curated shot fall through to an Esri aerial when we have coordinates.

title: Map pin photos no longer flash the roof before Street View
details: The aerial tiles were still in the popup, just hidden under an opacity-0 Street View image, so the prefetched roof painted for a frame then swapped. Street View is now its own tree with no Esri imgs in it, hover waits until that JPEG has settled, and a 404 is the only thing that swaps in the roof.

title: The market field's example shows the state
details: Or read a market's placeholder ran past the narrow chamber and WebKit's search cancel gutter, so 'ID' in industrial Boise ID was clipped. It is now the same e.g. shape as the address field, with a comma, and the native search chrome is off.

title: Map pin photos show the street view on hover, not the roof first
details: Hover used to paint the aerial, then swap to Street View once the JPEG landed. The roof now stays hidden until Street View 404s, and eligible pins prefetch the facade after the building snap so a hover is the street-level photo.

title: Comp table marks are words, and the type chip names the real count
details: Residential reports showed gray † ‡ § next to Size and $/SF; the section mark next to a dollar figure read as a second $. Those are now calc / size / adj with a legend. The chip beside the property type is the table's own comp count, so a bare 5 can no longer sit next to Residential while the map holds 8.

title: Map pin photos show the building from the street when the camera is actually there
details: Aerial still paints on hover so the popup stays snappy. Street View overlays it only when a camera sits within 35 m of the snapped building and is aimed at it. A fence, a neighbor, or the street in front of a warehouse 404s and the roof stays. The Google round-trip is billed only for the pin you hover, not for the whole map.

title: Pasting an address no longer turns the field blue
details: Chrome paints a light-blue autofill sheet when it recognises a pasted street address, and the existing cover only ran in dark mode, so the desk address field went blue on a white card. An inset shadow in the card colour now covers it in light too, including the focus state Chrome restyles after the paste.

title: Focus and Lookback show one chevron in dark mode
details: The desk selects restored the native arrow after a background shorthand wiped the site chevron, so dark mode stacked three or four arrows on Focus and Lookback. They now keep the one SVG. The pointer row under the desk used a gap class that was never in the vendored CSS, so the middle dot overlapped For brokers.

title: The loading ninja actually jogs
details: The 20-60s wait showed an 18px blob hopping 2.5px on the red bar. It is now a side-on silhouette with a two-frame stride and a 1px bob, planted on the track ahead of the fill so the red scarf stays visible. The cycle freezes when the report is ready, and for reduced-motion.

title: The search desk's corners follow the card again
details: Straightening the title hairline put a square white header on the market chamber. The desk cannot overflow:hidden (that clips the explorer dropdown), so the square fill poked past the 6px card at the top-right. The heads now carry the radius themselves; stacked on a phone, both top corners sit on the building head and the market head stays square.

title: Map pin photos are the roof, and hover is snappy
details: Hovering a comp pin waited 120ms, faded the popup in, then fetched Street View through our proxy — often a fence, parking lot, or the building next door, half a second late. Moving off waited another 320ms plus Leaflet's fade. Popups now show the aerial close-up of the snapped building (Esri tiles, prefetched after the footprint lands). Open is 60ms, close is 80ms, no fade.

title: The line between Value a building and Or read a market is straight
details: The two chamber titles now sit on one shared hairline, same padding and line-height on both sides, so the rule runs straight across the split instead of stopping under the building form. The hidden property-type select also moved out of the address row: a sibling there kept the address cell from matching :last-child, so that row painted a second right border on top of the desk divider and the vertical line jogged for the length of the address field.

title: A comp hub no longer sells anything to the client reading it
details: A client opening their broker hub was shown Pricing in the header, and once signed in a free account also got an Upgrade to Pro button in its account menu. That is a pitch aimed at somebody else guest, inside a workspace the broker owns, and it is exactly what the hub design ruled out: the client side is free forever and carries no upgrade prompt. Hubs now show nothing about Pro. Every other page is unchanged. Nothing about what a client can DO changed: they never had the vault or any paid feature, and a client who wants to buy can still reach pricing everywhere else.

title: A hub page has a way back to the app, and its Post note button is readable
details: Two faults from a real client using a real hub. The page was built with a flag that strips both the My Desk and Sign in links from the header, copied from a page that renders its own; the hub renders neither, so a client who left the hub could not find it again and had nothing to click when told to sign in. Both links are back, and a hub a client belongs to already lists on My Desk under Comp hubs. Separately the Post note button styled its label with a colour variable that does not exist, so the declaration was invalid and the text fell back to the same colour as the button, leaving a blank rectangle. Every colour the page uses is now checked against the ones the theme really defines.

title: An account can have a profile photo
details: The account circle was an initial. Signed-in members can now add a photo from My Desk (or Change photo in the account menu): it replaces the initial in the app header, on every server-rendered page, and on the desk itself. Stored as a data URI like a branding logo, but off the users row so the session lookup never pulls the bytes; a short content hash on the account tells the circle to fetch GET /api/account/avatar. PNG or JPEG, square-cropped in the browser, sniffed on the way in so a URL or an SVG cannot be stored. Remove clears it. Not Pro-gated.

title: A hub tells a client to sign in and now gives them a way to
details: Opening a real invite link showed the dead end: the page said sign in with the address this hub was shared with, and there was nothing on it to click. The note box that carries the account prompt is hidden from exactly the people that line is written for, and the header sign-in links do not render on this page. So a client could read their broker comps, go to reply, and stop. The line now carries a Sign in or create an account link. A closed hub still says only that it is closed, because signing in cannot reopen it.

title: The proof line no longer says up to 12 comps
details: Nearby saved deals join the table, so a city report can carry far more than the search ask. The desk and the landing both dropped the cap. They still say cited comps, about a minute, every source disclosed.

title: Dark mode reads more clearly, and leftover light chrome is gone
details: Labels on charcoal were sitting at the contrast floor on cards and failing it on slabs. The ink ramp lifts a notch so body copy and workhorse muted text clear AA, without moving the paper or card floor. The toggle now shows a sun once you are in dark, Chrome autofill no longer paints a cream sheet over the field, select chevrons and menus pick up the same card lift, and the form focus ring follows --red so it is visible on a dark cell.

title: A house comps table is compact, and tenancy is gone
details: Residential reports showed CRE tenancy (often empty, sometimes a long NNN string) as a wide canyon before Year Built, and the first handful of rows sat taller than the rest because notes restated beds and year built and wrapped. The house table no longer carries tenancy. Notes stay on one line. Row padding is the same compact height for every row. The prompt stopped asking for house tenancy and stopped dumping beds and year into notes.

title: Sending vault comps into a hub works
details: Every attempt to send a comp from the vault into a hub failed with a generic error. The insert asked Postgres to ignore duplicates against an index that only covers live rows, and Postgres will not match a partial index that way, so the whole send was refused. Duplicates are now filtered before the insert instead: sending the same comp twice is still a no-op, and a comp that was removed can still be re-sent, which is how a corrected price reaches a client. Found by sending a real comp into a real hub.

title: The broker introduction band no longer pitches a signed-in member
details: The band that offers a free opinion of value on a covered market page was written before the call to action below it split into signed-in and anonymous variants, so the two would have stacked: a member on a market with a covering broker would be sold an introduction at the top of the page and offered a CSV of the same comps at the bottom. The band speaks to a property owner arriving from a search engine, so it is anonymous-only now, which is the same line the call to action already draws. It renders on no market today, since no broker has opted into being listed, so nobody saw either version.

title: Vault row delete is a trash icon
details: The red Delete word next to Publish was a second shout on the row. Compact table and spreadsheet now share a quiet trash button: ink until hover, same as removing an import. The confirm still names the action.

title: A house number glued to the street still gets a value
details: The Low / Likely / High hero hid itself unless the address had a space after the street number, so it could skip city-only searches like Boise ID. People type 1210N17th st. That failed the space check, the whole What This Home Is Worth block stayed hidden, and a Residential report with 38 sale comps looked like it had no estimate. The hero now uses the same houseNumberOf helper as the type detector, which already reads a leading run of digits, glued or not. Boise ID and One Wilshire Blvd still skip the hero unless the visitor typed a size or price.

title: An uploaded vault spreadsheet opens in CompNinja
details: After a CSV or PDF import, the vault can open that book as a grid — Open spreadsheet on the comps table, or Open on the import itself. Each cell is an input; leaving it PATCHes that one field through the same route and parsers as the compact Edit form, so a 1.2M still fails instead of storing 1.2. Tab and Enter move like a spreadsheet. A published comp still retracts. The compact Edit form stays for a single-row change.

title: Dark mode chips, inner tiles, and the map follow the charcoal page
details: Estimate and vault badges had no dark pair, so they sat as cream pills; they now have --est-* and --bv-* that keep sienna and purple instead of borrowing the listing or verified tokens. Inner tiles and the Likely ledger cell use --wash-2, which is a no-op in light and a second step in dark. The Carto dark_all basemap is still the provider — a tile-pane filter lifts it toward the page, and Street View and aerials are not in that pane. The Likely tile keeps a red label and drops the full red border, so the accent is a mark not a box.

title: Dark mode cards sit above the page
details: The August 13 lift already raised the floor off near-black. What still read as one charcoal slab was paper, card, and wash sitting too close, with no step between them. Cards now take a dark-only --lift: a 1px inset highlight plus a short drop. In light mode --lift is none, so nothing moves. Print and PNG still strip shadows. Native form controls follow the page via color-scheme. Public-record badges and the hero scatter ticks pick up tokens in dark instead of sitting as cream pills.

title: A house report now reads as a house report
details: Zillow is more useful for residential because it is a listing portal. CompNinja cannot be that, and should not try: no MLS, no listing photos, no homes-for-sale browse. What it can be is the cited fair-price check for a house someone already found. A Residential search no longer opens as a commercial real estate analyst write-up with LoopNet/Crexi lane copy. The model is told to match bedroom count as well as neighborhood and vintage. The comparison card is list price vs Low/Likely/High whenever the listing (or a typed ask) exists, and no longer waits for a Refine size. Year built sits under the hero with last sale and ask. The Analysis tab and its NOI/DCF toolkit stay behind Details until someone types an NOI, so investment SFR still works and a house shopper does not land on hold-or-sell. The size field says Living area. The CTA says Talk to a local agent; the lead is still source bov and we still connect you with a licensed local broker, never claiming to be one.

title: Nearby sales pull the value more than sales across town
details: Distance used to be a table column the map filled in after the pins settled, and the Low / Likely / High treated a next-door sale the same as one nine miles away. It is now a fifth compWeight factor: a free pass inside a mile, then a 4-mile half-life, missing distance still neutral so an unplaced search comp is not punished. The mile figure rides locked_basis (never lat/lng) so a free report's range stays in step with Pro. Saved radius deals stamp it at blend time; comps that already have coordinates get it just before the paywall; once the map geocodes the rest, the hero re-runs.

title: A comp hub now has a shortlist, notes on each building, and comps the client adds
details: Hubs shipped as a way to send comps to a client. They are now somewhere the two of you work. Every comp carries where it stands (not decided, shortlisted, toured, passed) and the CLIENT can move it, because a shortlist only the broker can change records what the broker hopes rather than what the client decided. One line above the table says where the requirement stands, counting only what somebody actually decided. Notes can be filed against a single building and read under that building rather than in one stream, which is the thing an email thread cannot do. A client can add a building they found themselves: it is marked as theirs, never wears the broker badge, and is refused in the vault importer's own words if a price is written as 1.2M rather than 1200000. Two people in a hub at the same time now see each other's comps and decisions without reloading, and a half-typed note survives the other person's activity.

title: The brokers page is two ledgers, not two cards
details: What you get for submitting comps and Pro: the Broker Vault sat as peer bullet cards, so the page still read as a feature list after How it works had already drawn those trades as a statement. They are now two stacked hairline ledgers — Contribute (Credit with the Verified chip, Intros, Profile) then With Pro (Book, Pipeline, Private) — so the vault does not look like it comes with a submitted comp. The one Submit button, the 1031 card, and the compliance line are unchanged.

title: Saved deals within 10 miles join the next report
details: Every search already stored its priced comps, but a later search in the same area only reused them if the model picked them or the visitor clicked Add. Saved deals of the same property type, inside the lookback, with coordinates, and within 10 miles of the subject now fold into the report at serialization so they hit the table and the Low / Likely / High math. A free report turns extras into locked_basis, same as extra search comps. Harvest geocodes new rows before writing them; a deal with no point is skipped rather than guessed as same-city. Cache and market snapshots stay search-only, so a later nearby search still picks up deals saved after the cache write. CORPUS_RADIUS=off restores search-only reports. Vault rows are never read.

title: A signed-in search lands in Portfolio on its own
details: Free and Pro alike keep every report they run, on any device, without pressing Save. The same address updates the existing row and appends a value snapshot. Free My Desk is an address list; Pro keeps the likely-value ledger and sparklines, and upgrading reveals history Free already stored. Caps are 100 and 500, enforced on insert only. The Save button remains as a retry when the auto-save fails or the list is full. The $20 unlock is unchanged.

title: What brokers get is a ledger, not a leftover paragraph
details: The landing's Brokers block had collapsed to one paragraph that named Private, Credit, and Leads in a single breath, so it still read as Method's leftover. Those are trades, not steps: they now sit as hairline rows with the real Verified · via Your Firm chip on Credit, the same chip the sample report already shows. Method keeps its 3-up. Copy pins (privacy sentence, firm name, /brokers link) are unchanged.

title: Tab fills the example address
details: The search box's rotating e.g. placeholder used to be display-only: Tab jumped to the next field and left the box empty. Tab on an empty address field now types in the current example, without the e.g. prefix, so a visitor can try a real building without inventing one. A second Tab moves on because the field is no longer empty; Shift+Tab is still back. The same shortcut sits on the shared-report lock field. A placeholder that is not an example is never a fill.

title: The signed-in search page is one Research Desk
details: The report form and Market Explorer used to sit as two products on the same page, with a stale 3-6 cited comps line under them. They are now one bordered desk with two chambers: Value a building (the existing form, ids unchanged) and Or read a market. The explorer is a sibling of the form, not a child, so typing a market and hitting Enter cannot submit a building report. The COMMERCIAL COMP REPORTS kicker is back, the proof line is Up to 12 cited comps, and How it works and For brokers share one pointer row. The public landing is untouched.

title: The digest card says when it last actually mailed anybody
details: The digest is driven from outside this process on purpose, which buys a schedule somebody chose and costs the thing every external scheduler eventually does: it stops, and nothing says so. A cron that quietly dies looks exactly like a quiet few weeks, with no error and no bounce, just people not being mailed. The card on /admin now reports when the digest last sent, how many went out, and how many runs are logged, with never run as a real answer rather than an empty space. Previews are counted separately and never set the last-sent stamp, because a card reading last sent two days ago off somebody clicking Preview would report a healthy schedule while nobody had been mailed in a month, which is worse than reporting nothing. A previews-only state says so in those words. The date is rendered in the reader's own timezone rather than sliced off the ISO string, since an evening run in Mountain time otherwise renders as today followed by tomorrow's date and reads as a bug in the dashboard. Pinned by tests in all three states and confirmed by mutation.

title: A search's plan was passed to the analytics log and thrown away
details: Three /api/comps call sites have passed the visitor's plan to logEvent since the Pro tier shipped, and logEvent's row never had a plan field, so the value was built and discarded on every search for months. Nothing failed, and the code read as though do free users search more than Pro ones was answerable when it never was. It is the same silently-inert shape as vault_beta missing from getSessionUser's narrowed return, which is the second time this exact class of bug has landed here, so the fix comes with a pairing test: every dimension a logEvent call site passes must appear in logEvent's row, read out of server.js on both sides, so adding one at a call site fails the build until it is recorded. The column rides along in migration 026 rather than a fourth migration, since it is the same table and the same unrun deploy. /admin gains a Searches by plan table: anonymous, free, or the paid plan name. Rows logged before today carry no plan and show as unknown rather than being dropped, so the table still totals to the Searches tile.

title: A signed-out /desk lands on the sign-in door, not the marketing page
details: Under the account wall, asking for /desk without a session redirected to the homepage, which answers somebody who already has an account by telling them to go read about the product. It now redirects to /?auth=signin, a door the wall already exempts so the account modal has somewhere to live. The wall's actual rule, that a personal workspace never renders anonymously, is unchanged, and so are the 302 and the no-store; only the destination moved, and ACCOUNT_WALL=off still serves /desk as the app so the rollback lever stays exact. It surfaced because the watchlist digest's only call to action is see them all in your desk: a reader signed in on that device was always fine, which at a 90-day session is most of them, but a new phone or cleared cookies dead-ended the email on marketing copy. Any future mail linking to /desk inherits the fix. The account-wall test that pinned the old target now pins the new one, plus a second case proving the target really serves the app, because a redirect to a door that bounced back would be a loop that looked exactly like the bug it replaced.

title: The digest can be run from the page you already have open
details: The digest route is deliberately manual, because a timer inside the process fires at an hour nobody chose, again after every deploy restart, and twice the day this runs on two instances, and all three end with real people mailed the same comps again. But manual meant curl with an admin key, which is a feature nobody runs. /admin now carries a Watchlist digest card: Preview builds every email, sends none and marks nothing, so the copy can be read before anyone gets it; Send now confirms first and says the send cannot be recalled. Preview is the primary button and Send is the quiet one, because a dialog on the safe action trains people to click through the one on the unsafe action. The refusals show their reason rather than a status code, since no database and no outbound mail configured are different problems with different fixes. One property is load-bearing and now tested: opening /admin must not send email. Every other card on that page fetches its data on load, so the obvious way to write this one is the wrong way and the mistake would be invisible, the page looking identical while the mail had already gone. Both that and the confirm were checked by mutation.

title: The digest is now tested by actually sending one
details: The watchlist digest deliberately has no file fallback, so with no database it stops at a 503 and every test stopped there with it. The cutoff arithmetic, which markets get marked, the opt-out, and the rule that a second run mails nobody twice were all argued in comments and had never executed. test/helpers/fake-supabase.js is a stand-in PostgREST and Resend, so the run can be exercised end to end: fifteen cases now assert who was mailed, what the body said, and what the run left behind. It caught a real hole immediately, though not the one expected. The outbound-mail guard, the subtlest refusal in the feature, turned out to be untestable in the database-free suite because the database refusal fires first; deleting the guard entirely left every existing test green. It has its own case now, and both it and the cutoff rule were confirmed by mutation, meaning the guard was removed on purpose and the suite was watched to go red. One correction worth recording: the same work looked at first like it had found a live in.() encoding bug in findUsersByIds, and that was wrong. Percent-decoding restores the separator commas for values that contain none, so uuids were always fine. The helper that replaced it is consistency with the market-key idiom, not a fix, and the comment says so. The fake refuses a filter it cannot parse rather than matching everything, because a fake that matches everything reports a user-scoped read as working while it hands back another account's rows.

title: The brokers page shows the badge, the path, and the questions
details: https://compninja.co/brokers told the Verified trade in words and left the right half of the hero empty, then repeated the Pro headlines as their own body copy. The claim now sits beside an illustrative report exhibit that shows Verified via Your Firm on a real row, a three-beat path (four facts, we review, your name) sits between the two ledgers without reusing Method's steps, and a broker FAQ (free to submit, who sees owner contact, what Verified means, vault privacy, review) feeds both the accordions and the FAQPage JSON-LD. One Submit door, the 1031 card, and the compliance line are unchanged. The answer about vault privacy names both ways a comp can leave your vault — publishing it, or sharing it with your firm — rather than only publishing, which is all there was when this page was written.

title: /1031-exchange is an identification worksheet, not just a guide
details: The page still explains what a 1031 is, underneath. On top it is now a worksheet: the building you are selling, the closing date (day 45 and day 180, calendar days only), and up to three replacements you type yourself. Each row values that building through the existing report handoff. Copy link puts the worksheet in the URL fragment so a street address never hits a server log, and reading stays free with no account. The page says it is not a written identification and not an exchange CompNinja created; a qualified intermediary still has to receive the signed list. The brokers page card now points at the worksheet rather than a plain guide.

title: The watchlist can reach out, instead of waiting to be opened
details: watchlist_items and the feed have been live since July and are read only by somebody who already decided to open the app. Every loop in the product is pull. POST /api/watchlist/digest mails each watcher the markets of theirs that have new comps, using the send path that was already built: sendOutboundEmail and the branded letterhead, which has named market alerts as an intended category since the day it was written. The copy and the is-this-worth-sending rule live in the pure watchlist-digest.js, and buildDigest returns null rather than an empty string when there is no news, so nobody can mail a blank digest by forgetting to check. The feed computation is now shared with the page, so the two can never quote different numbers for one market. This is the only thing CompNinja sends on its own initiative, so the refusals are the feature: admin-gated and manually triggered rather than a timer, because a setInterval fires at an hour nobody chose, again after every deploy restart, and twice the day this runs on two instances, and all three end with real people mailed the same comps again. It refuses without a database, and refuses without outbound mail configured, because sendOutboundEmail is a silent no-op when the keys are unset and running blind would advance every high-water mark and delete a digest nobody received. Dry run builds every email, sends none and marks nothing. Markets are marked only after the send and only where there was news. The send cutoff is the later of last mailed and last seen, so the email can never tell somebody what they already saw on screen and an active user quietly stops getting digests without unsubscribing. Unsubscribe is a self-authenticating token link whose GET only shows a confirm button, because mail scanners fetch every URL in an email and a one-click GET would opt people out of mail they never opened; the same link turns them back on.

title: The event log can finally say whether one person did two things
details: analytics_events recorded what happened and nothing about whose visit it was, so it could count signups and count reports and never say whether the same browser did both. That is the question the first broker cohort raises, and the August 6 measurement had to answer it by hand-assembling rows out of Supabase. Two columns fix it (migration 026): visitor_id, an opaque random id in a new cn_vid cookie, and user_id once a session resolves. The id is a random number handed to a browser, not derived from IP or user agent or anything else about the person, so the events stay PII-free; the privacy policy names the cookie. /admin gains a Visitor funnel card reading arrived, hit the sign-in wall, created an account, ran a report, as cumulative sets over distinct visitors so the gap between two lines is a real drop-off. Rows predating the migration are excluded rather than bucketed as one unknown visitor, which would have invented a single visitor who did everything the product has ever seen, and percentages are withheld below ten arrivals where they are noise. The cookie is minted only on document navigations, because a page load fires a dozen parallel requests and minting on whichever arrived first would split one visit across ids that never appear again. Worth knowing for anything else built on the request context: AsyncLocalStorage does not reach a req.on end callback, which is where every route with a body logs from, so a plain run around the handler attributed every GET perfectly and recorded every signup, lead, share and vault import as anonymous. Measured, not assumed, and enterWith does not fix it either. The listener registration is bound instead, and a test pins the POST case specifically.
