details: Found by a leak scan across all nine pages after the footer fix, not by reading a diff. index.html carries a block of dark Leaflet chrome for the report map; the market pages have their OWN comp map (#mktMap, MARKET_MAP_JS) and had none of it, so in dark the container showed leaflet.css's own #ddd -- a light grey slab the size of the map, visible through every tile gap and for the whole of a slow tile load -- under white zoom controls, a white attribution strip and a white popup. Worse, the basemap was pinned to CARTO's light_all, so the map was a bright white rectangle in the middle of a charcoal page whatever the chrome did. The chrome is now a shared LEAFLET_DARK_CSS interpolated into MARKET_CSS, and the basemap follows the theme the way index.html's basemapUrl() does, with the same brightness lift over dark_all's near-black tiles. A theme change reaches the layer through a MutationObserver and swaps the URL rather than re-adding the layer, because the toggle lives in the shared header and can fire long after the pins are placed, and rebuilding would drop them. Three tests: that the two Leaflet blocks agree selector by selector (they are a hand-copy, since index.html is static and cannot share a constant), that light and dark visitors get the right basemap, and that a toggle swaps the URL without losing a pin. The map test's fake Leaflet was returning undefined from addTo where the real one returns the layer, which would have passed code that cannot work in a browser; it was corrected in the same commit.

title: The markets directory shows the city, and a failed photo no longer costs a city its picture
details: Two follow-ups to the market page photographs. The markets directory listed every market as a line of text, so the page that exists to help somebody pick a market showed them nothing about any of them; each card now carries a small photograph of that city, the same picture that heads the market's own page, cropped identically so a card can never show a differently framed version of what it links to. They are a third stored size rather than the big file scaled down in the browser, because that page carries every market at once - full-size files would have made it a ten megabyte page - and they load only as they scroll into view. The second fix is subtler. A stored photograph is checked for being the right size and sharp enough, and a file that fails is skipped in favour of a satellite aerial. That check was recorded against the CITY, which was right while a city could only have one photograph and wrong the moment a city could have both a hand-picked one and a found one: one bad file took the good one down with it. It now records the FILE, so a hand-picked photograph that fails hands off to the found one instead of dropping the city to a satellite. Ontario, CA is the case that prompted it, and it is also the honest limit of it: its picture is a real aerial of Ontario that is simply too small for the slot, and there is nothing better on Wikimedia - six archival elevations of one packing house - so it is still showing a satellite. Those archival surveys are now refused outright as a class, and the search also reads every photograph a city's Wikipedia article uses rather than only its lead image, which is where a small town's one real cityscape usually lives. Nampa, Vero Beach and Woodland Hills were re-checked with that wider net and still have nothing; they keep their aerials. Finally the whole thing can now run on a schedule: a monthly job finds photographs for markets published since the last run and opens a pull request with them, because a model approving a crop is not the same as somebody having looked at it.

title: Dark mode stops drawing its boxes heavier than light mode does
details: Review said the dark pages read as a drawn grid. The first instinct was to revert --line, which had been lifted from 1.28:1 to 1.42:1 earlier the same day, and measuring is what stopped that from shipping as the whole answer: by painted border length in dark, --edge accounts for 80% of every line on a market page and 90% on a report, against --line's 2% and 7%. Reverting --line alone would have been a change nobody could see. --edge had never been touched by the dark-mode work at all: it shipped at 1.76:1 against the card while light's equivalent is 1.48:1 against white, so dark has always drawn its boxes about 19% heavier than light, which makes this a correction rather than a preference. --edge goes #3D4B5F to #333E4F (1.45:1) and --line goes back to #2A3648, leaving the dark ladder at hair/line/edge 1.22 / 1.28 / 1.45 against light's own 1.15 / 1.30 / 1.48. --hair keeps its lift, because 1.06:1 was not a visible line and the comp table's row dividers were genuinely missing. Light mode does not move: all three are dark-only values on tokens whose light values are untouched.

title: The app's search card stops reading as a drawn grid
details: The surface the complaint was actually about, found by measuring it instead of guessing a third time. The card that holds Value a building and Or read a market draws EIGHT rules on one small card: the divider between the two panes, one under each heading, one under the address row, one under the Focus/Lookback/Property SF row, one under Details for comps, one above the buttons, and two verticals between the three control cells. Every one of them is --hair, and --line is not used on that card at all, so the --edge and --line work in this same branch barely touched it. --hair had been raised from 1.06:1 to 1.22:1 to fix comp tables that genuinely had no row dividers, which was right, but 1.22 is heavier than light mode's own 1.15 and on this card it turned eight invisible rules into a grid. It goes to #222F40 (1.15:1), exactly light's weight, so the card is ruled no more heavily than the same card is in light and the table dividers it was raised for are still there. That puts all three rule tokens on light's ladder: hair 1.15 against 1.15, line 1.28 against 1.30, edge 1.45 against 1.48. The lesson is written into theme.js: which token draws the lines on a given page is not guessable and was guessed wrong twice here, and three surfaces gave three different answers.

title: The extraction test is one command
details: scripts/extraction-eval.js runs the Archive block's gate end to end: real comp PDFs through the live /api/vault/extract, scored against hand-keyed truth by the pure, tested extract-score.js — recall, per-field precision, and the fabrication rate that decides the feature, with every miss and invention itemized. Comparison goes through broker-vault.js's own parsers, so a formatting difference the importer would accept never scores as an error. The scorecard lands in docs/evals/ with the correction-time blank left for a person with a stopwatch — the half no harness can fake.

title: Archive-first retrieval: a broker's own book cuts their search bill
details: Retrieval order is now archive → corpus → web. Four or more usable comps in the searcher's own vault for that market and type floor the web budget at 2–3 searches, exactly as a strong public corpus does — their rows still join the report only at serialization, and nothing vault-derived ever reaches the prompt. One finding the plan didn't have: a vault-subsidized report is deliberately NOT written to the shared cache, because the cache is keyed by property and a later visitor would be served the thinner report without the private rows that justified it. Rules pure and tested in blend-comps.js; test/archive-first.test.js proves the wiring against a real server and a stub provider that records max_uses off the wire. Rollback: ARCHIVE_FIRST=off.

title: Archive-first retrieval stops firing where it cannot help
details: Shipped hours earlier and wrong on the one provider production actually runs. The feature floors the web-search budget when a broker's own vault is strong — but Gemini's search tool accepts no cap, so that number was silently ignored and the call was identical to a full-budget one, while the report was still kept out of the shared cache. It bought nothing and cost a cache entry, and nothing on screen would ever have shown it. The strength flag now requires a provider that can actually honor a budget, so on Gemini the path is inert and every search caches normally; it becomes a real cost lever the moment the provider is switched to Anthropic. A test boots the same seeded vault against Gemini and fails the build if the flag ever fires there — verified by reverting the fix and watching it go red.

title: The health check says which build is serving
details: /healthz now reports the deployed commit and the time the process booted. Render auto-deploys and a blocked deploy looks exactly like a slow one from outside — in one case two failed back to back and the old build served for an hour with every page answering 200. The only check available was grepping a served page for a string the change introduced, which cannot work at all for a change with no visible byte (a server-side rule, a search budget, a caching decision) and reports a perfectly healthy deploy as failed whenever the grep reads the wrong page. Neither field is a secret: the repository is ours and the commit is already public.

title: A development shop can finally see whether the project pencils
details: CompNinja knew what a property was worth and nothing about what it cost, so a development shop got different words on its desk and no arithmetic. Five fields — land, hard costs, soft costs, a contingency and how long the build takes — now turn the valuation the report already computes into the four numbers a build decision is actually made on: total cost and cost per foot, yield on cost, the spread over the market cap rate in basis points (coloured against the conventional 100–150bp hurdle, because that is the build-versus-buy call), and an unlevered IRR. Every figure is gated on the inputs it genuinely needs and says what is missing rather than showing a zero — a 0% yield on cost is a real number describing a disaster, and nobody could tell it apart from an empty NOI field. Costs are private like the NOI and the loan terms: they stay in the browser and the owner's own portfolio, never reach the search, and never ride a shared link. Deliberately unlevered and all-cash with the exit at completion, and the card says so — it is the screening number, before anyone models a capital stack.

title: The extraction test can no longer report a false failure
details: An audit of the harness before its first real run found two problems that would have corrupted the verdict it exists to produce. The extract route allows eight calls per five minutes per IP and counts refused calls too, so the old retry-on-429 slid the window forward and dug the hole deeper on a twenty-file run; the runner now paces itself to seven per window and never trips it, announcing the wall clock up front so a healthy run that pauses is not mistaken for a hung one. Worse, a file that failed for any reason was scored as an empty extraction — so a rate-limited file counted as zero percent recall, a false failure on the precise number that decides whether the archive gets built. Infrastructure failures are now excluded by name and the run exits non-zero, while a genuine empty extraction is still scored as the real miss it is. Also added --limit, so the pipeline can be proven on two files before twenty are spent.

title: The Explore menu opened off the side of the screen on every phone
details: The header nav wraps to its own row below about 450px, which puts the Explore dropdown at the left edge of the page -- and it was anchored right:0 to its own trigger, so 105px of a 176px menu hung off-screen and every label was clipped to its last few letters. It affected every server-rendered page (the landing page, /markets, each market page, /brokers, /how-it-works, /1031-exchange), which is exactly the anonymous search traffic most likely to arrive on a phone. The menu is now anchored to the header itself below 640px and opens as a full-width sheet. Anchoring rather than flipping to left:0, because the wrap point moves with what the nav holds -- signed in versus out, and a hub drops Pricing entirely -- so a trigger-anchored menu is off-screen on one page and correct on the next with no way to tell from the CSS.

title: The comp list on a phone is half as long, and can be sorted
details: Sorting lived only in the comp table's column headers, and that table is hidden under 640px, so a phone could not reorder comps at all. There is now a Sort by control above the card list, built from whichever columns that report actually has, and each choice names its direction outright instead of toggling. The cards themselves led with every field a comp carries -- 564px each on the sample report, so five comps was a 3,000px scroll -- and now show the seven a reader scans a list by (date, type, size, price, $/SF, distance, match) with the per-type specs, tenancy, vintage, notes and source behind a More details disclosure: 324px a card, measured. Nothing was removed: the CSV, the print copy and the PNG all still carry every field, the last of those because downloadImage's onclone opens each disclosure first (verified against real html2canvas -- the capture grows from 1527px to 2727px).

title: A dialog can no longer put its own button out of reach on a short screen
details: The confirm-address, sign-in and lead-capture overlays centred their card with align-items, and a centred flex child that outgrows its container has its TOP pushed out of reach with no scrolling able to recover it. Measured on a 375x420 viewport, the confirm dialog -- the one that gates every single search -- put Yes, run the report at y=436 in a 420px window. The card now clamps to the viewport and scrolls inside itself, so it still centres on a desktop where it fits. Also: the landing page's address field went from 14.5px to 16px, below which iOS Safari zooms the page on focus, so the reward for tapping the one field that page exists for was a zoomed, sideways-scrolled page; the header links and the hero's two disclosure links got their hit areas extended to 28-40px with an overlay that has no layout effect at all (padding was tried first and moved the header 5px); and the market pages' comps table, 640px wide in a 295px window, now shows a scrolling shadow so it no longer reads as a table with its right-hand columns simply missing.

title: Four things the firm surfaces got wrong, all found by clicking rather than reading
details: From the hand-driven enterprise run of 2026-08-19, the four that were still live. (1) Undoing an auto-share revoked the link but left the publish memo holding it, so Share to the same firm handed the dead URL straight back under “Link copied. It is on <firm>’s desk now.” — nothing published, nothing for a colleague to open, no error. The memo keys on the audience and on object identity and a revoke changes neither, so the Undo now clears it, the way curation already does. (2) A share carried the sender’s own note about sharing: currentMeta was posted verbatim, so meta.autoShared was stored inside the share payload and a colleague opening a LIVE firm link was told “Removed from <firm>. Your colleagues can no longer open this link.”, or handed an Undo button for somebody else’s share. It is stripped from the copy that goes over the wire, and the notice no longer renders at all on a shared report, which also settles the links already written that way. (3) A colleague’s comp named them only in a title attribute — a desktop hover with no touch equivalent, so on a phone the attribution did not exist. The name now sits on screen beside the From <firm> badge, in the verified credit’s shape but in neutral gray, because a firm share has not earned the green Verified colour. (4) The vault’s comp table is ~1200px wide inside a ~1070px scroller and macOS draws no scrollbar until something is already moving, so the Firm column — the Share control that is the shared vault’s only entry point — sat off the right-hand edge with nothing saying the table went further. It gets the scrolling shadows the market pages’ comps table already uses. Both copies now take their shade from --edge rather than 13% black, which was invisible over a #1A2433 card — so the market pages, where that pair shipped on 2026-08-23, get their dark mode fixed too: a comps table that reads as one with its right-hand columns simply missing was exactly the failure the shadows were added to end.

title: Checkout was broken for five days, and nothing noticed
details: Buying anything — Pro monthly, the founding annual, firm seats — answered "Could not start checkout. Please try again." It had done so since 2026-08-21, when the $20 single-report unlock was retired: that change deleted the reportId variable but left one reference to it behind, as the idempotency key handed to Stripe. An undeclared name is a ReferenceError rather than undefined, so every checkout that got as far as calling Stripe threw, and the product was quietly unbuyable. The whole test suite stayed green throughout, because every checkout test in it is a refusal that returns before Stripe is ever called — so the fix comes with the thing that was actually missing: a test that drives a SUCCESSFUL checkout against a stub Stripe and checks what Stripe was asked for, including that a four-seat firm is billed for four seats. It was found by trying to buy something.

title: New pricing: Pro is $100, and a firm can buy seats
details: Pro monthly comes down from $129 to $100 and the founding annual from $990 to $840 (so "founding" still means roughly three and a half months free rather than two). Firms can put a whole office on one plan at $79 a seat. A firm plan starts at two seats, and that is a rule rather than a preference: a seat grants Pro, so a one-seat firm plan would just be a cheaper Pro for one person — two seats bill above the individual price, which closes it without refusing genuinely small shops. The price figures were only ever written in the pricing modal and the landing FAQ, with nothing keeping them in step; a test now pins those two to each other.

title: The firm-seats launch has a written runbook
details: PRO-BILLING-SETUP.md now covers the third sellable plan: what the code already enforces (owner-only, seats ≥ headcount, the two-seat minimum, seats written from the subscription, the firm as its own Stripe customer), the Stripe and Render steps, and a $1-temp-price verification round trip in the E6 pattern before the real price goes in. It also records why env vars are set before the copy deploys — the other order advertises a price lower than the one being charged — and that existing subscribers never move to a new price on their own. The status table caught up with history it had missed: Pro's public launch, report branding, and the single-report retirement.

title: Brokers and How it works leave the Explore menu
details: The Explore dropdown now carries the 1031 Guide, Download the app and — on the vault header — Markets and Run a report. Neither page moved or lost a door: /brokers and /how-it-works keep their footer link on every surface, and the landing page still links both from the line under its hero. One edit did it everywhere, because the app menu and every server-rendered header render from the same NAV_LINKS list.

title: Remove import works in the broker vault
details: Removing an import from /vault deleted the comps server-side and then left the screen exactly as it was — the import still listed with its comp count, its comps still in the table — whenever the broker had opened that import’s spreadsheet first, which is the ordinary way to get there since the other button on the row is Open. The handler treated closeSheet() as an alternative to reloading, and closeSheet only redraws from the rows the page is already holding. It now always refetches the book, and it checks the response: a refused removal (a lapsed subscription, a Supabase outage) used to take the success path and look identical to one that worked, and now says what happened.

title: The extraction verdict is declared: a provisional pass, with its conditions written down
details: The gate on the whole Archive block has an answer. On the pilot set the extractor found 33 of 36 hand-keyed deals with every field it reported correct, and the one file reviewed by hand row by row — twelve county sales pages, forty-eight values — needed no corrections at all. The verdict is a pass, and it is marked provisional in the same breath, because three documents is not the twenty the spec asks for and none of them is a scan, so it is an upper bound on the messy half of what brokers actually send. The judgment the pass turns on is written out rather than buried: fabrication came in at 1.8%, which the spec calls fatal regardless of everything else, and every instance is either an address the source truncates for display which the model completed, or a year taken from a range the page prints for a property with several buildings. Neither is the failure that rule exists to catch, which is a well-formed invented number nobody can detect; no invented price, size, date or whole deal appeared anywhere in thirty-six rows. Three conditions ride on the pass: re-run it on twenty real broker files including scans before anything is built on it, decide whether completing a truncated address should be stopped or simply recorded, and take a real correction-time measurement on a file that actually needs correcting. A reader who weighs the fabrication question differently should read the same numbers as a fail, and the document says so.

title: The extraction test has its first real numbers, and they are not the verdict yet
details: The scoring harness has existed since the 21st with nothing to score. It now has a pilot: nine real comp documents gathered from the public web and vetted by reading each one, five of them keyed into a truth file and run against production. Recall 91.7%, field precision 100%, fabrication 1.8%, nothing refused. Three of the five files were perfect. The verdict is deliberately NOT declared — the correction-time measurement is half of the pass condition and needs a person with a stopwatch, and three documents is a pilot rather than the twenty the spec asks for, with no true scans in it, so a pass would be an upper bound. What the run did settle is worth more than the numbers. The first pass reported 13.9% fabrication, a clear failure, and every one of those twenty-eight counts turned out to be an error in the truth file rather than the model: the county pages print an adjusted year built and a land area on every page and the truth had simply omitted them, so twenty-one correct reads scored as inventions. The spec says the truth file is the test; this is what that means in practice, and it is the thing most likely to produce a wrong answer on the real twenty. The other finding is that the same page read as a PDF and as an image behaves differently — the PDF path completed three addresses the document truncates for display, which is where the remaining fabrication comes from, while the image render of the identical page reproduced what was visible and scored a clean seven of seven.

title: A note in a hub now reaches the person it was written to
details: Posting a note in a comp hub wrote its row and told nobody. The hub polls every 15 seconds but skips a hidden tab by design, so the only way to see a reply was to be looking at the page when it landed: a broker sent comps on Tuesday, the client replied on Thursday, and the broker found out whenever he next opened the vault. For a product whose pitch is one place instead of an email thread, the email thread was winning the round that mattered. A note now emails everyone else in the hub, the client and the broker alike, with the note itself in the body and a link straight to it. The rule is one nudge per absence: somebody who has been mailed and has not come back is not mailed again however chatty the thread gets, and opening the hub re-arms them, so ten notes posted while a client is away is one email rather than ten. Anyone watching the hub as a note lands is left alone, since they are already reading it. Every one of those decisions is a pure function with its own tests, because too many emails is a failure that never throws: it just makes somebody stop reading them. Turning them off is one click from any of these emails and needs no account, which matters because a client can read a hub on an invite link alone and is exactly the person most likely to want out. Replies now go to the person who wrote the note, too. Every outbound CompNinja email had its reply address hard-coded to the site owner, which is right for a lead and wrong for relaying one person's words to another: hitting Reply on a note about somebody's deal sent it to a third party's inbox, losing the message and disclosing the deal in the same click.

title: Pro shows how many people searched your markets
details: Every market on your watchlist now carries a line saying how many people looked at it in the last 30 days, and how many searches that was. Your own searches are never counted, so the number is other people rather than a reflection of your week. A market nobody searched says so plainly instead of going blank. Free accounts see that the figure exists; the count itself is Pro.

title: Continue with Google (dark until the OAuth client exists)
details: The account modal offers Google sign-in on its Sign in and Create account tabs — one click instead of a password, aimed at the signup wall where the visitor funnel loses people. Zero dependencies: the OAuth code exchange is plain fetch, and there is no migration, because identity here is the email — a verified Google email lands on the same account a password sign-in does, and an account born from Google gets a random password hash so the password door treats it like any wrong guess (the existing reset flow, which mails the address Google verified, is how it gains a password later). The whole feature ships dark: until GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID and GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET are set, the routes 404 and the button never renders. Tokens must carry a verified email, our client id and Google's issuer or nobody is signed in; the flow is CSRF-guarded by a one-shot cookie nonce the privacy policy now names; and the suite runs the entire exchange against a stub endpoint, including the case where a refused token must leave no session behind.

title: The extraction verdict is in, and it found two ways a comp sheet could import a wrong number
details: Importing a broker's PDF or screenshot has been gated all along on one question nobody had answered: is the extraction good enough that correcting it beats typing the comps by hand? It is now measured on fourteen real documents from eleven organizations — brokerage comp sheets, a lender BOV, county sales books, a capital-markets report — against 132 deals keyed by hand from the pages themselves. It found 85.6% of them, got 98.7% of the individual figures right, and left nothing out that it was unsure of. It also found two faults, and both are the kind that matter most here, because both put a number in your records that looks perfectly reasonable and is wrong. Every cap rate came back a hundred times too small: a page reading 5.10% became 0.051, which is a legal percentage, so nothing downstream could object — it would simply sit in the vault as a cap rate of 0.051%. And on a lender's valuation, three properties that were merely listed for sale were recorded as completed sales, dated to the day they were listed. Neither is the model being weak; in both cases it was never told the convention — what unit a percentage should be in, and that a listing is a thing that exists. Both are one-line corrections, and until they are made the email-ingestion work stays where it has been, waiting. Two things the verdict says about itself rather than hiding: no proprietary broker files were available, so every document in it is one published on the open web and therefore typeset, and there is no photograph of a printed sheet anywhere in the set — so these numbers are the best case, not the average one. Worth recording that the first scoring of this same run looked far worse, at 4.2% invented data, and was wrong: twenty-one of those were fields the documents genuinely stated and the answer key had missed. The test grades against a hand-written key, so a careless key fails a working extractor — which is exactly what happened the first time this ran, in July, and now twice.

title: Importing a comp sheet no longer divides every cap rate by a hundred, or turns listings into sales
details: Two faults the extraction verdict found, both fixed in the instructions the reader is given rather than in any code that runs afterwards, because in both cases it had simply never been told the convention. A cap rate came back as 0.051 from a page reading 5.10% - a hundred times too small, and a number the vault had no way to argue with, because 0.051 is a perfectly legal percentage and would have sat there as a cap rate of 0.051% for as long as the comp existed. It now asks for the figure the way the page writes it. And on a lender's valuation, three properties that were only listed for sale were recorded as completed deals, dated to the day they were listed, because the sold rows beside them looked the same and the list date was the nearest thing to a date on the row. It is now told plainly that a row with no sale price and no sale date is a listing, and that a date on a row is not a sale date unless the row says a sale happened. Such a row is skipped rather than guessed at, and the import screen says why. Both rules are pinned by tests that quote the measurement, so a later tidy-up of the wording cannot quietly undo either one.

title: The two import faults are fixed, measured against the same sixteen documents that found them
details: Yesterday's test found that importing a comp sheet got every cap rate a hundred times too small and turned three properties that were merely listed for sale into completed deals. Both are now corrected and, more to the point, re-measured rather than assumed: the same sixteen documents went through the live site again, and cap rates went from none correct to all of them, invented sale dates from three to none, and the share of individual figures read correctly rose to 99.6% - one wrong number in the entire run. The headline count of deals found reads lower than before, and that is the fix working: three of them are the listings, which are now set aside with the reason shown instead of being recorded as sales that never happened. Counting only the deals the vault would ever accept, it found 94.5% of them. Two things the measurement turned up that no wording can fix. Requiring a sale date and requiring lease rent to say whether it is annual or monthly cost thirteen real deals across these sixteen files - both refusals are right, and both deserve a proper answer rather than a relaxed rule. And picture quality quietly corrupts figures: on a deliberately poor-quality copy of a page, one sheet came back empty and another read a price of 566,000 as 560,000 with everything else on the page correct. That is the same kind of wrong number as the cap rate - one nothing downstream can question - and it is the reason the confirm screen before an import is not decoration.

title: The last unmeasured thing about importing a comp sheet now has a number, and it is not the one anyone expected
details: The whole case for importing comp sheets rests on one question: is correcting an extracted file faster than typing the comps in by hand? Everything else about the extraction has been measured for two days; this half never had a stopwatch on it. It does now. Twelve rows, checked against the original document, took four minutes and fifty-one seconds - and not one of them needed correcting. The reading is the cost, not the fixing. That is four times over the sixty-second bar the test set for itself, and the four reasons are all in how the rows are presented rather than in how they were read: they do not come out in the same order as the sheet they came from, so checking row four means hunting for it page by page; the figures are printed without commas or decimals against a document that has both; the row says Retail where the page says the name of the actual business, which is how a person recognises which property they are looking at; and every document gets the same columns whether or not it had them. The extractor produced those twelve correct rows in ten seconds. A person then spent two hundred and ninety-one confirming them. One thing worth saying plainly rather than burying: nobody has ever timed the other side of the comparison. Typing twelve comps by hand has not been measured, so "correcting beats typing" is still a reasonable belief rather than a demonstrated fact, and it is now the cheapest thing left to find out.

title: Firm accounts have a public page for the first time
details: Everything about firm accounts has worked on the server since migration 030 — the shared shelf, invites, auto-share, shared vault comps, per-seat billing, three shop kinds — and none of it had a public surface. Nothing in the nav, nothing in either footer, no tier on the pricing modal. The only door into the feature was an invite email, which only ever reaches somebody a member already knows, so a broker asking what it costs for their team could not be sent a link. /firms is that link. It renders through marketShell like /brokers and /leadership, so it carries no CSS of its own and cannot drift from the rest of the site's chrome. The three shop kinds — broker, development, tenant rep — describe themselves using the exact sentences org-access.js already hands the invite email and the create box, passed in rather than retyped, and a test fails the build if any of those sentences is ever hand-copied into the page. The privacy section restates three promises the code actually keeps: colleagues see only what was shared, automatic sharing is never retroactive and a member's own setting beats the firm's, and a vault comp travels one at a time with its owner's name on it. Those reach search engines as public claims, so each was checked against the code before it shipped.

title: Pricing has a URL, and the firm tier is finally on it
details: Pricing lived only in a modal inside index.html. A modal cannot be linked, indexed, or sent in an email, so the answer to "what does this cost" could not be given as a URL and Google never saw a price at all. The gap that mattered more: that modal carried Free, Pro and Founding and no firm tier, while the /how-it-works FAQ had been quoting "$79 a seat, minimum two seats" in prose for weeks. The product's own seat price was stated where a crawler could read it and nowhere a buyer could click, even though per-seat billing has been sellable since migration 033. /pricing puts all three tiers at an address, in the market pages' own tile classes so it adds no CSS and cannot drift from the site's chrome. The figures now come from one PRICING constant that the FAQ answer reads too, and a test pins index.html's modal to the same numbers — the modal's own comment had conceded that nothing caught a drift between its hardcoded prices and anywhere else, which was true of a figure typed into three files. The Firm tile's call to action is "how a firm works", not a buy button: a firm subscription is bought by an owner for a firm that already exists, with a seat count checkout validates against the current headcount, so there is nothing on this page for somebody who has not made one yet. The page never calls /api/checkout at all; buying is handed back to the app, where the session, the entitlements and the ownership check already live.

title: The signed-in chrome can stand on its end
details: NAV_SHELL=rail lays the header out as a persistent left sidebar at 900px and up, on every server-rendered page a member sees. The thing worth knowing is what it is NOT: it is not a new component, and it moves no content. Every surface already renders the same header shape — brand, nav, account slots, inside a centered container — so the rail is that same element re-laid-out by one class on <html>, and the markup is byte-identical in both modes. A test asserts exactly that by diffing the two renders, because the moment a second markup branch appears the eight-page header assertions are only checking one of them. Nothing else moved: .wrap keeps its own centering, so with the body padded on the left every band re-centres itself — measured on /markets, where main lands at 1120px wide beside a 224px rail without a single wrapper being touched. Below 900px the class does nothing at all and today's wrapping bar returns, which is the whole mobile answer: no drawer, no focus trap, no scroll lock. Anonymous visitors never get it, because it marks being inside the product and a marketing page read by a stranger is not that. NAV_SHELL=bar restores the old chrome exactly and is the rollback lever; an unrecognized value exits at boot rather than being accepted and quietly ignored. Two things came along because the rail forced them: the Explore dropdown has nowhere to open in a 224px column, so its links move to the footer — which finally puts the download page in a footer at all, having been in the Explore menu and in neither one, making the page that answers "where do I download it" the hardest on the site to find.

title: Bulk valuation had no link anywhere on the site
details: Not in a menu, not in a footer, not in a header. The only inbound link to /bulk was from inside /bulk itself, so a Pro member could reach it by typing the URL or by pasting a multi-line list into the main search and discovering the mode by accident — and no other way. It is a billed feature with real per-run cost, and it was unfindable. Markets was nearly as bad: 27-odd standing market snapshots reachable from the footers and one line inside the app, with no header link on any surface. Both are now nav destinations, beside the vault, which moved up out of the account dropdown to join them. That is what the rail draws as rows, and it is the right shape in the horizontal bar too: a tool one click inside an account menu reads as a setting rather than a place to go. Vault and Bulk hydrate after paint from the entitlements /api/config already carried, so both ship hidden and appear together once the account resolves — which is exactly why the rail is a fixed width, since an item arriving a beat after paint must not reflow the page around it. One consequence worth stating: hub pages build their header from the account slots and not from the site bar, so a hub no longer shows a vault link. That is correct for a client-facing page whose spec asks for minimal chrome.

title: The app wears the rail too
details: index.html gets the same sidebar every server-rendered page got, from the same class, so a member moving between the app and a market page no longer watches the chrome change shape under them. It rides authBoot, which already runs inline in <head> before first paint — the sidebar is never drawn and then taken away, which is the whole reason that mechanism exists. One difference from cn-in and cn-locked, and it matters: refreshAccountUI retires those once the real answer lands, because they are stand-ins for something the page is waiting on. nav-rail is not. It is a layout choice, so it stays, and a test asserts it is absent from every classList.remove call in the file. Written as plain CSS in the style block rather than as utilities, because tailwind.css is a vendored purged build and every utility a rail needs — inset-y-0, top-0, h-screen, ml-*, pl-*, border-r, z-30 and every md: variant — is missing from it, so a class would have silently not styled. That is the precedent .rd-appbar, .rd-desk and .rd-heroband already set, and using var() tokens keeps the colours out of the per-utility dark-mode bridge rule as well. Measured at 1440px: the header is fixed at 224px and full height, the body carries 224px of left padding, and the hero, the search desk and the footer all re-centre themselves inside it with not one wrapper edited. At 375px the class does nothing and the wrapping bar returns. One test had to change rather than being made to pass: auth-boot.test.js pinned the boot script's class list exactly, which was right while auth owned that script alone. It now filters to the cn- prefix, so it asserts what the page is told about the visitor instead of breaking every time something else legitimately needs the same before-paint timing.

title: Your firm leads My Desk
details: It was the third of five decks, below a member own properties and their shared reports, so the shop work sat past two decks of personal work - the opposite of a product whose pitch is that the firm is the centre. It now leads. Nothing about the deck changed in the move: the block is byte-identical, verified by a script that refused to write unless the moved text matched exactly and every div, closing div and section count in the file was unchanged, so every id, gate and renderer inside it is untouched. A solo member sees no change at all, because refreshDeckVisibility still hides the whole heading for somebody who is in no firm and holds no invitation.

title: The workspace can start a report without leaving it
details: My Desk hid the search desk, so the page a member is meant to live on had no way to start the one thing the product does - you had to leave it first, which is a strange thing to ask of a home. The form now stays. What matters is that it is the REAL form and not a compact copy: #compForm is one form with one set of ids, read by targetRange, the footprint estimate, every report restore and the address confirm dialog, so a second launcher would have been a second address input to keep in step and the first to drift. Verified in a browser: one #address input on the page, the desk sitting above the decks, and the wall signup card still winning where it should because applySearchLock still governs it. Two seams had to learn that a report now yields the workspace rather than rendering under it - renderResults and, earlier, beginAssembly, which puts comp cards on screen up to a minute before the wholesale repaint. Without both, a search started from the workspace would have streamed its comps in below the firm shelf and the deal board. Checked the round trip by hand: workspace to report to workspace, with the search desk present throughout.

title: Home is the firm workspace
details: For a signed-in member, / now opens the workspace instead of the search page. That is the reorganization in one line, and it was only safe to make once the workspace carried the real search desk at its top - landing somebody on a home page with no address field would have been worse than the page it replaced, which is why the test asserts both facts together. The decision reads the boot hint rather than currentUser, because it runs before the account bootstrap resolves and every member would otherwise see the marketing stack for a beat; a forged cookie buys the sight of an empty workspace and nothing else, since every section inside it fetches its own authenticated data. Two exclusions matter. A shared report is somebody else s link and must render the report, never the reader own desk, so /r/ is excluded by name and verified in a browser with a session cookie present. And /desk is kept working rather than redirected to /: it is linked from Stripe checkout returns with a query string, from the watchlist digest, from org invite emails and from /bulk, so a 302 would have dropped the query and dead-ended those. Home moved by opening the same view, not by moving the URL. The back button follows the same rule as the boot, so going Back to / no longer drops a member on a marketing stack they never asked for.

title: My Desk is called Workspace
details: Sixteen user-facing strings, in two registers on purpose. The nav LABEL is Workspace - a proper noun for a place, matching the rail own row, so a member reads the same word wherever they are. PROSE says your workspace in lower case, because Watch it on Workspace is not English. Code comments were left alone: they are about the desk view and its history, and rewriting a hundred of them would churn the file to say the same thing. Done as explicit before-and-after pairs rather than a blanket replace, so a string that had drifted would fail loudly instead of being silently missed - and so the comments could not be swept up in it. Two tests that pinned exactly one My Desk link per page now pin exactly one Workspace link; the invariant they protect, one link and never two, is unchanged. One thing deliberately NOT changed, and left as a question in the code: for a member, Home and Workspace are now the same destination, which is the kind of duplicate row this whole reorganization exists to remove. Suppressing Home for members was tried and reverted, because two tests defend that link for signed-in visitors by name and the decision behind them was made the same day. Whether Workspace now answers the objection those tests were written for is a product call, not a refactor.

title: Two real causes of the flaky suite, and an honest account of what is left
details: npm test failed about two runs in five, always in a different suite, always green when re-run alone. Two causes were found and fixed; a third is characterised but not solved, and the numbers below are measured rather than hoped for. FIRST, and a genuine correctness bug rather than only a test problem: every server the suite boots has SUPABASE_URL blanked, so all of them fall back to local JSON files - and those files were the repo root, shared by the twenty-odd suites node --test runs at once. account-store.json is the one that bit. The server loads the whole store into memory once and writes the whole thing back, so two children that each load ten users and each add one produce two eleven-user writes, and the second silently destroys the first user. The fixed .tmp path raced as well. A DATA_DIR env var now points the thirteen gitignored scratch files somewhere else, defaulting to the repo root exactly as before so production is unchanged, and the test helper gives every child its own directory under the OS temp dir. The suite also stops leaving 48KB of account state in the working tree. devlog.json and market-seed.json deliberately stay on __dirname: they are committed repo content, not scratch. SECOND, ports are never reused within a worker. Node global fetch pools keep-alive connections per origin, and every server here is localhost, so the origin is just the port; when a child is stopped its sockets die, but a pooled entry can outlive it, and if the OS hands the same port to the next boot the next request goes out on a dead socket. WHAT IS LEFT: a rarer ECONNRESET that neither fix removes. Measured across twenty-two runs, green went from about sixty per cent to about eighty. Two things were tried and rejected on evidence rather than taste: raising the server keepAliveTimeout to 72 seconds made it WORSE, three green in six, and was reverted rather than shipped on a theory; capping test concurrency at four or six did not help either, six in eight. The remaining failure is at the connection layer and the durable fix is probably for suites to stop calling bare global fetch, which is a change across twenty test files and a decision somebody should make deliberately.

title: The iOS app gets the broker's book, and a signed build reaches App Store Connect
details:
A native SwiftUI client, built against the same endpoints the browser uses, with no server changes at any point. It now carries the broker vault's read, write and analysis surfaces: the whole book with four composing filters, adding and correcting a comp, deleting one with an undo that restores through the ordinary add route so it revalidates, the market rollup and median-by-year and repeat properties, and the gut check. Plus the pipeline deck, where leads and BOVs share one list exactly as they do on /vault.

Two rules travelled with the data rather than being reinvented. A comp out of the broker's own vault is badged "From your vault" and is filtered out of the share sheet, because the app had been receiving blended private comps since it existed and would have mailed a broker's book to whoever they shared a report with. And the gut check's verdict is computed ON THE DEVICE from public benchmarks, because /api/vault/benchmarks takes only bucket keys and reads no vault rows, so moving the verdict server-side would have traded that privacy property for a duplication one. GutCheck.swift is a second copy of gut-check.js's client half, labelled as one on both sides, and pinned to that suite's own cases.

Signing is manual and must stay that way: automatic signing insisted this was a development build and died on "your team has no devices", which names devices but is really about asking for the wrong kind of profile. Version 1.0 build 1 is uploaded to App Store Connect and not submitted. iPhone only, so one screenshot set.
